t.nanxun section of jiangnan canal@30.9,12:
Nanxun is one of the water towns of the Yangtze delta, south of Lake Tai, where life has revolved around canals for more than a thousand years. In the nineteenth century, it became immensely rich through the silk trade, and its merchant families, known by nicknames like the four elephants and the eight bulls, built mansions that mixed Chinese courtyards with European columns, stained glass and Western-style furniture, an unusual blend you will not find in many other water towns. The canal running through the town is part of the Grand Canal, the immense waterway linking Beijing with Hangzhou, which UNESCO listed in 2014.

Walking along the canals, under arched stone bridges, past whitewashed houses with black-tiled roofs reflected in the water, is the essence of a visit. The Little Lotus Villa, a garden estate with a lotus pond, and the Jiaye Hall library, a private book collection housed in a beautiful building, are highlights, as is the Zhang Shiming residence, with its Western-influenced interiors. Nanxun is less crowded than better-known towns like Wuzhen or Zhouzhuang, especially early in the morning, when locals do tai chi by the water and the mist hangs over the canals.

Now the practical side for riders. Foreigners in China generally need a Chinese driving licence to ride, motorcycles are banned from expressways, and many cities restrict or prohibit them entirely, so independent motorcycle travel requires serious planning, often through a specialised tour operator. The roads in the delta are flat, straight and busy, crossing an endless network of canals, fish ponds and mulberry fields, with heavy traffic of trucks, cars and electric scooters. The old town of Nanxun itself is pedestrianised, so you will explore on foot or by boat.

Huzhou, about thirty kilometres away, and Wuzhen, about sixteen, have full services, and Nanxun has plenty of restaurants and guesthouses in and around the old town. Local specialities include freshwater fish and shrimp, braised pork and sweet rice cakes. The climate is humid, with hot summers, a rainy season in June and July, and cool winters. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant times to visit, with mild temperatures and clear skies.
t.classical gardens of suzhou@31.3,120.5:
A classical Chinese garden is a whole landscape squeezed into a courtyard: rocks stand in for mountains, ponds for lakes, and a winding covered walkway reveals one framed view after another, each window cut in a different shape. Suzhou, a canal city west of Shanghai, perfected the art over centuries, as scholars, officials and merchants built private retreats behind high white walls. Nine of its gardens are listed by UNESCO as the Classical Gardens of Suzhou, among them the Humble Administrator's Garden, the Lingering Garden and the tiny, exquisite Master-of-Nets Garden, and the Retreat and Reflection Garden in the water town of Tongli.

The point given here lies near Mudu, an old town on the western edge of Suzhou, close to the hills that rise towards Lake Tai. Mudu has its own historic gardens and canals, and the hills behind, such as Lingyan Shan, have temples and walks with views over the lake. Lake Tai is the source of the strange, eroded limestone rocks prized in Chinese gardens, and you will see them everywhere, full of holes and twisted shapes.

Suzhou is also famous for silk, embroidery so fine it looks painted, Biluochun green tea grown on the hills by the lake, and, in autumn, hairy crabs from the nearby Yangcheng Lake, a delicacy people travel across the country to eat.

Riding here requires preparation and realism. Foreign visitors generally cannot ride in China on a home licence, and arranging a temporary licence and permits for a motorbike is complex and often requires an organised tour. Many Chinese cities restrict or ban motorcycles in their centres, and expressways are generally closed to them. Electric scooters fill the streets, often silently and without lights, and traffic rules are interpreted creatively. If you do ride, the roads around Lake Tai and onto its peninsulas and islands are the most rewarding, with water views, tea terraces and orchards of loquat and bayberry.

The gardens are best visited early, as soon as they open, before tour groups arrive. Fuel, food and every service are easy to find in Suzhou. Try a bowl of Suzhou noodles in the morning, light and delicate, and a cup of Biluochun tea in a garden teahouse while rain falls on the pond.
t.wuxi city section of jiangnan canal@31.6:
The Grand Canal is the longest artificial waterway in the world, stretching from Beijing to Hangzhou, and some of its sections have been in use for more than two thousand years. In the Jiangnan region, south of the Yangtze, it flows through a landscape of rice paddies, lakes and old towns, and in Wuxi it runs right through the city. The canal was listed by UNESCO in 2014, and the Wuxi section includes historic streets, bridges and warehouses along its banks.

The most charming stretch is around the Qingming Bridge, an old stone arch over the canal, with narrow streets of whitewashed houses with black-tiled roofs, small shops and teahouses. Barges still chug along the water, heavily loaded with sand, gravel and coal, a reminder that the canal remains a working route. At night, red lanterns reflect in the water.

Wuxi lies on the northern shore of Lake Tai, one of China's largest freshwater lakes, and the lakeside is its main attraction. Yuantouzhu, a peninsula shaped like a turtle's head, has gardens, pavilions and cherry blossoms in spring. Further west, the Lingshan scenic area has one of the tallest bronze Buddhas in the world, overlooking the lake. Wuxi is also known for clay figurines from Huishan, colourful little dolls with chubby faces, and for its cuisine, which is famously sweet: try the spare ribs braised in soy and sugar, or soup dumplings that are sweeter than those of Shanghai.

If you are thinking of riding, be realistic. Getting a licence to ride as a foreigner in China involves bureaucracy, motorbikes are not allowed on expressways, and urban areas may have restrictions on motorcycles. Electric scooters and bicycles fill the streets, and traffic rules are loosely observed. For most visitors, the canal and the lake are best explored on foot, by boat or by bicycle.

The roads around Lake Tai, however, can be lovely, with water views, tea plantations and fruit orchards, and the islands in the lake, linked by bridges, offer quieter riding if you can arrange it. Wuxi is a large city with fuel, food and every service. Take a boat trip along the canal in the evening, and sit in a teahouse with a pot of green tea and a plate of sweet pastries while the barges pass.
t.jiaxing hangzhou section of jiangnan can:
The Grand Canal of China is the longest artificial waterway in the world, a chain of canals and rivers linking Beijing with Hangzhou that was begun in sections well over two thousand years ago and unified under the Sui dynasty in the seventh century. Its southernmost stretch, the Jiangnan Canal, crosses the flat, watery plain between Jiaxing and Hangzhou, and this section is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site. Grain, silk and salt moved north along it for centuries, and the towns that line its banks grew rich on that traffic.

The landscape is the classic Jiangnan picture: canals with stone humpback bridges, whitewashed houses with black tiled roofs, mulberry fields that once fed the silk industry, and fish ponds stretching to the horizon. It is completely flat and intensely farmed, with factories and new housing pressing in from every side, so the old beauty comes in pockets rather than wide vistas. Water towns such as Wuzhen to the north and Tangqi near Linping keep stretches of the old canal townscape, though they can be very crowded at weekends.

Riding here takes preparation. Foreign riders need a Chinese driving licence and properly registered bikes; temporary permits for overland travellers usually require an organised tour with a guide. Hangzhou restricts motorcycles in its urban areas, and motorcycles are generally not allowed on expressways in much of China, so you will use the older national and provincial roads, which are often busy with trucks, scooters and electric bikes. Stay alert at junctions, where right of way is a matter of interpretation.

Food makes up for a lot. Jiaxing is famous for zongzi, sticky rice dumplings wrapped in leaves, and Hangzhou's cuisine, from Dongpo pork to Longjing tea shrimp, is among the most refined in China. Fuel stations are plentiful along major roads. Spring, with mild weather and blossoming trees, and autumn are the best times; summer is hot and very humid, and the plum rains of June can be relentless.
t.hangzhou xiaoshan shaoxing section of zh:
Shaoxing is a city built on water. Its canals, bridges and narrow stone-paved lanes have made it one of the most photogenic towns in eastern China, and the Zhedong Canal, which links Hangzhou, Shaoxing and Ningbo, is its great artery. The canal belongs to the Grand Canal system, the longest artificial waterway in the world, which UNESCO listed in 2014. The Zhedong section carried grain, silk, tea and travellers for more than a thousand years, and in Shaoxing you can still see black-awninged boats, arched stone bridges and old warehouses along the banks.

The town has a literary history too. The writer Lu Xun grew up here, and his stories of village life and Shaoxing's odd characters are set in places that visitors can walk through. The city is famous for its rice wine, called huangjiu, a golden, mellow drink made from glutinous rice and the clear water of Jian Lake, which is served warm in small bowls with dried plums or with the local stinky tofu. Pottery jars of aged wine line the shelves in shops across the old town.

For a motorcyclist, the area is flat and heavily built-up, with expressways, bridges and dense urban traffic, and the pleasure is more about the culture than the riding. Foreign riders in China need a Chinese licence and registration, and in many cities motorcycles are restricted or banned from central districts, so a visit here is usually made by other means. Where riding is allowed, expect fast electric scooters, delivery vans and constant horn use, and watch out for slippery stone bridges in the rain. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summer is hot and humid.

Shaoxing has abundant fuel, food and accommodation, and the canal-side districts offer tea houses, restaurants and guesthouses in restored buildings. Walk along the old canals at dusk, when lanterns are lit and the water reflects the bridges, and order a plate of drunken shrimp and a bowl of warmed wine. The pace is slow, the air smells of water and rice wine, and the city is a pleasure to explore at walking speed.
t.paris@48.9,2.3:
It is a gift from the ruler of Egypt, about three thousand years old, and it was set up here in 1836 on the spot where the guillotine stood during the Revolution. Louis XVI was executed on this square in 1793, and so, in the Terror that followed, were over a thousand others. Now the square is a roundabout with fountains, ringed by traffic and framed by the Tuileries gardens on one side and the Madeleine church on the other. The banks of the Seine in this part of the city are UNESCO listed.

The honest advice for a rider is to treat Paris as a city to park in. The Périphérique ring road is fast, dense and unforgiving, and central Paris is a web of one-way streets, bus lanes, cobbles and tram lines. Paris also has a low-emission zone, so find out if your bike needs the Crit'Air sticker before you ride in, and look up the latest rules on parking. Motorcycle bays are common at the edges of the centre, and a garage near a metro line is the sanest option. Petrol stations are rare in the middle of the city, so fill up on the outskirts, in Levallois-Perret or Clichy, which are only a few kilometres away.

On foot, the area is easy. You can walk the Tuileries to the Louvre, cross the Pont de la Concorde to the Assemblée nationale, or head up the Rue Royale to the Madeleine and the smart shops of the Faubourg Saint-Honoré. The Champs-Élysées begins at the square's northwest corner and runs gently uphill to the Arc de Triomphe. Early morning, before the coaches arrive, gives you the best light on the stone and the fewest crowds.

If you want a break, take a coffee at a pavement cafe and watch the traffic rotate around the obelisk. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light and fewer tourists. The metro station at Concorde is a good way to move around if the bike stays in the garage.
t.le havre@49.5,0.1:
Le Havre was flattened. Allied bombing in September 1944 destroyed the old centre, and the French state hired the architect Auguste Perret to rebuild it, which he did in reinforced concrete, with straight boulevards, uniform apartment blocks and a grid of open squares. At first the town seemed grim. Today UNESCO calls it a masterpiece of postwar reconstruction, listed in 2005, and in the right light the concrete takes on a warm, pale-gold tone. The tower of the church of Saint-Joseph, over a hundred metres high, is the landmark, and inside, the light through its coloured glass is dazzling, a thing worth ten minutes of anyone's time.

The city has an older story as France's Atlantic port. It was founded in the early sixteenth century by King Francis I because the nearby harbours were silting up, and it later became the departure point for ocean liners. Monet painted the harbour at sunrise in 1872, in the picture that gave Impressionism its name, and the town still holds a museum with a fine collection of his circle. Sainte-Adresse, along the cliffs, was his subject in another painting, and its pebble beach and old villas have kept a seaside feel.

For riding, Le Havre is a gateway more than a destination. The Pont de Normandie, a long cable-stayed bridge opened in 1995, carries you across the Seine estuary to Honfleur and the Normandy coast, and on a clear day it is a thrilling bridge to cross, though the wind can be strong. To the north, the Pays de Caux plateau offers quiet farm roads, flint-walled villages and the white chalk cliffs of Étretat, around thirty kilometres away. Weather can change in minutes, with sea fog and sudden rain, and wet painted lines on the city's roads are slippery.

Fuel is easy in a city of nearly two hundred thousand, and ferries to England leave from the port. Parking for a bike near the centre is simple. Eat moules-frites near the harbour, and in summer look out for sea-salt caramel from local bakeries. Early morning, when the sun picks out the concrete and the harbour is grey and gold, is the time to be on the front.
t.the lingering garden@31.3,120.6:
The Lingering Garden, called Liu Yuan, is one of the four most famous gardens in China, and a masterpiece of the Suzhou school. It began in the sixteenth century as the private garden of an official of the Ming dynasty, and was later rebuilt by a Qing dynasty owner, whose family name, Liu, gave it its present name, which also means lingering or staying on, and that is exactly what visitors want to do. It belongs to the UNESCO listing of the classical gardens of Suzhou, from 1997, and it covers a couple of hectares, with halls, pavilions, corridors, ponds and rockeries arranged in a design that seems to turn a small space into a landscape.

The art of the Chinese scholar's garden is in the surprise. Covered walkways wind and turn, with windows of different shapes that frame a view, such as a bamboo, a rock or a bit of water, like a painting. The Cloud Capped Peak, a tall, perforated rock from Lake Tai, is considered one of the finest garden stones in China. Water, rock, plants and architecture are balanced, and the white walls with their grey tiles form a backdrop. Visit in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the crowds are thin, and in rain, when the roofs drip and the pond ripples, the garden is at its most poetic.

Suzhou, an hour from Shanghai by fast train, is a canal city, often called the Venice of the East, though its waterways are quieter and more domestic than that comparison suggests. Silk has been woven here for centuries, and the city has a very good museum designed by the architect I. M. Pei, whose family came from Suzhou. The Retreat and Reflection Garden at Tongli, a water town nearby, is another listed garden, and the old street of Pingjiang Road is a pleasant place to walk.

Riding in China as a foreigner is highly restricted, so most visitors come by train and use taxis or hired bicycles. Suzhou has fuel and services everywhere, and the local food is sweet and delicate, with freshwater fish, river shrimp and noodles in broth. Spring, with the flowers, and autumn are the best seasons, and the summer heat can be heavy.
t.the mountain villa with embracing beauty:
Suzhou has been famous for its gardens for centuries, and the Mountain Villa with Embracing Beauty, known in Chinese as Huanxiu Shanzhuang, is one of the nine that UNESCO lists among the classical gardens of the city. It lies in the western part of town, a short way from the old centre, and it is quieter than the more famous gardens on the tourist trail. The name suggests a mountain retreat that holds beauty within it, and the design delivers on that: a pond at the centre, pavilions around it and a large rockery of weathered limestone that is the best-known feature.

The idea behind such gardens is to build a world in miniature. A wall hides the street, a doorway frames a view, a zigzag bridge slows your steps and a window with a pattern of tiles turns a bamboo grove into a picture. The rocks are taken from Lake Tai, nearby, and are chosen for their holes and twists, which suggest mountains and caves. The gardens were built by officials, scholars and merchants who had retired from public life or made their fortunes in silk, and they were places for tea, poetry and conversation with friends.

Suzhou itself is a canal city of more than five million people, with white walls and grey tile roofs, stone bridges and willows. The old moats and canals are still part of daily life. Be aware that riding conditions are quite different from Europe. Motorcycle regulations in Chinese cities are strict, many centres restrict petrol bikes, and traffic includes dense flows of electric scooters, buses and cars, so look into local rules and paperwork well in advance. In practice, visitors usually see the city on foot, by bike or by taxi.

The best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the air is mild, while summers are hot and humid. Early morning is quietest, before the tour groups arrive. Suzhou cuisine leans toward the sweet and light, with dishes such as sweet-and-sour mandarin fish and noodles with a clear broth, and tea houses offer a place to sit with a pot of green tea. Pingjiang Road, a restored canal street, is a nice place for a stroll and a snack in the evening.
t.area of yaoshan site@30.4,120.0:
Five thousand years ago, on the plain north of Hangzhou, people built a city with a water system so sophisticated that archaeologists still marvel at it. This is the Liangzhu culture, and the Yaoshan site is one of its most intriguing pieces, thought to be a ritual platform where elites took part in ceremonies and where beautifully worked jades were buried. The Liangzhu people carved jade into discs called bi and tubes known as cong, with delicate, mask-like faces, and these objects were symbols of status and belief. The whole Liangzhu complex has been a UNESCO site since 2019.

The scale is the astonishing thing. A walled city, a network of canals and a series of dams in the hills to the northwest that controlled flooding show that this was a well-organised society, built on rice farming, with no written records. Much of what we know comes from decades of patient excavation, and the Liangzhu museum on the plain tells the story with finds that are hard to forget. At Yaoshan itself there is less to see on the ground, and the value is in understanding what lies under the fields and the low hills.

The country around is soft and green, the sort of landscape for which this region, south of the Yangtze, is known: rice paddies, bamboo, tea bushes on the hills and small canals threading the plains. Deqing is a town of about 88,000 people 14 km away, and Hangzhou, with its West Lake and its tea plantations, is only about 20 km away. Roads are flat and well surfaced, though busy, and traffic includes many trucks and scooters. Spring brings blossom and green tea, while summer is humid and often rainy.

Practicalities for a motorcycle rider need care. Foreign riders can find it hard to ride in China, as local licensing and plate rules apply, and motorbikes are barred or restricted in many urban areas. If you are on the ground here, hire a car and driver or a bicycle, and use the time to see the jade and the museum. Hangzhou's Longjing tea, grown on the hills near the lake, is the thing to try, and a pot of it in a quiet tea house is a calm way to end the day.
t.cistercian abbey of fontenay@47.6,4.4:
The Abbey of Fontenay lies in a narrow, wooded valley in northern Burgundy, a few kilometres from the small town of Montbard. It was founded in 1118 by Bernard of Clairvaux's circle and became one of the earliest and best-preserved Cistercian houses in Europe. The Cistercians wanted a life of simplicity, work and silence, and they built accordingly: plain stone, no carvings of saints, no coloured glass, and a site chosen for water and seclusion. The result is a place of extraordinary calm.

What survives is remarkable because much of it is original twelfth-century work. The abbey church is long and austere, with a pointed barrel vault and light that falls in clean, plain shafts. The cloister is a quiet square of arches and the dormitory has a vast timber roof. There is even a forge, built by the monks beside the stream, where iron was worked using water power, which reminds you that these were farmers and engineers as much as contemplatives. After the Revolution the abbey became a paper mill, and was later bought and restored by a private family, which is partly why it was saved.

The ride in from Montbard is gentle, along small roads through oak and beech woods, with farmland on the plateau above. This is not high or dramatic country; it is soft and rolling, the sort of road that is a pleasure at moderate speed with a bit of dappled light. Cars and coaches arrive in summer, so mornings and weekdays are best. The car park is a short distance from the gate, and there is ample room for motorbikes.

Montbard, with about five and a half thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and it also has a handsome park laid out by the naturalist Buffon, who lived there in the eighteenth century. Bring a jacket because the stone buildings stay cool even in August, and allow at least an hour to walk around inside. The countryside nearby produces good cheese, notably Époisses to the south-east, and the bakeries do sound business all day.
t.the climats@47.1,4.9:
The Climats of Burgundy are, in plain terms, the vineyard plots of the Côte d'Or, each one with its own name and character, worked and described by monks and growers for nearly a thousand years. The word means little parcels of land with a specific soil, slope and exposure, and the idea is that two vines a few metres apart can yield wines that taste different. Near Ladoix-Serrigny and Beaune the slope faces east and south-east, and the great hill of Corton rises above the villages, covered in vines and crowned with woods.

History is soaked into these slopes. The Cistercians at Cîteaux and the Benedictines at Cluny began mapping the best ground in the Middle Ages, and the dukes of Burgundy later regulated and protected the wines. In Beaune the Hospices, a hospital with a brightly tiled roof founded in 1443, still owns vineyards and holds a famous charity auction every November. The patterns on the roof are glazed tiles in green, red, yellow and black.

For a rider, this is gentle, civilised country. The Route des Grands Crus, which runs along the foot of the slope from Dijon to Santenay, is a fine road for an easy day: smooth, lightly curved and lined with stone walls, village after village with famous names on the signs. Speeds are modest, the villages have speed bumps and cameras, and in the autumn harvest tractors and grape-laden trailers share the road, so patience is part of the deal. Wet leaves and mud from the vineyards can make the surface slick.

Beaune, four kilometres away and a town of about twenty-four thousand, has fuel, restaurants and a lively centre inside its old walls. Burgundy cooking is rich: beef bourguignon, eggs in red wine sauce, gougères and, in the season, fresh snails. Late September brings the colours; May has the vines in fresh green. A tasting is pleasant, but remember that you are riding.
t.archaeological ruins of liangzhu city@30:
Liangzhu is a city that existed before writing. About five thousand years ago, on a marshy plain south of the Yangtze, a Neolithic people built a walled capital with a palace platform, canals, workshops and cemeteries, and they carved jade into ritual objects of astonishing skill. The city covered several square kilometres, and its walls, built of rammed earth on a base of stone, were up to sixty metres wide at the base. UNESCO listed the archaeological ruins in 2019 as evidence of an early regional state.

The most famous objects are jade discs, called bi, and jade tubes with square outer shapes, called cong, many carved with a stylised face that combines a human and an animal. The jade came from a distance, and the workmanship shows specialised craftsmen working under strict control. Burials of elite people contained dozens of jade pieces, while ordinary graves held little. It is evidence of a society with strong social ranks and a shared religion.

Today the site is an archaeological park on the edge of Hangzhou, with a museum designed by the British architect David Chipperfield, which holds many of the finds. The ruins themselves are low mounds and ditches that have been landscaped and marked, and visitors can walk or cycle through the park. It is easy to confuse a field with a city, so the museum is a good place to start. The excavations are still going on, and new finds come out regularly.

Hangzhou has more than six million people, with every kind of service, and Deqing is smaller but also has facilities. The area has rice fields, tea gardens and bamboo forest, and local food includes fish from West Lake and the tea called Longjing. The climate is humid, with a rainy season in early summer and typhoons in late summer. Autumn is best. Foreign riders usually face restrictions in China, so check the rules before you go, and take the museum and the park at an easy pace.
t.immeuble locatif a la porte molitor@48.8:
Le Corbusier lived at the top of this building for more than thirty years and, in the end, swam away from it for the last time. The block at the Porte Molitor, on the edge of Paris where the sixteenth arrondissement meets Boulogne-Billancourt, was designed in the early 1930s as a set of apartments, and the architect kept the two top floors for his own flat and studio. It has a glass-and-steel facade, an open plan and a curved roof, and it was one of the first buildings to show that the white geometric language of modernism could work in a Parisian street. UNESCO listed it in 2016 as part of his body of work, and the apartment can be visited on guided tours, so check the opening hours before turning up.

He died in 1965 while swimming off the coast of the south of France, and the studio remains much as he left it, with the rough-cast walls, painted canvases and rooftop views. Next door stands the Piscine Molitor, an art deco swimming pool of the 1920s that fell into ruin and has since been restored as part of a hotel. Roland Garros and the Parc des Princes, the great tennis and football grounds, are only a short ride along the avenue.

Riding in this part of Paris means urban habits: patience, awareness of buses and cyclists, and a firm grip on the clutch. The périphérique runs close by, and the traffic on the boulevards of the sixteenth is dense in the morning and evening. The tarmac is generally good, apart from tram tracks and the occasional metal plate. Parking for motorbikes is available in designated bays, but it is not free everywhere, so check the signs. Paris and its suburbs have low-emission zones that can affect older bikes, so look into the rules before you arrive.

Fuel is available in Boulogne-Billancourt, which has more than a hundred thousand inhabitants and filling stations on the main roads. Cafes and bakeries are everywhere. If you want a break from the traffic, the Bois de Boulogne lies a few minutes west, and its quiet lanes are a pleasant place to unwind. Early morning on a Sunday is the best time to ride here, when the streets are empty and the light hits the glass.
t.the canglang pavilion@31.3,120.6:
The Canglang Pavilion is the oldest of Suzhou's classical gardens, and in a city famous for them, that gives it a certain quiet authority. Its origins go back to the Song dynasty in the eleventh century, when a scholar and poet named Su Shunqin, disgraced and out of office, bought a piece of land and built a retreat beside a pond. He named it Canglang, meaning blue waves, after an old poem about washing one's cap strings in clear water, and the garden has been associated with scholars in exile ever since.

What makes it different from most Suzhou gardens is its openness. Instead of being enclosed entirely by walls, the Canglang Pavilion borrows the view of the water outside, with a long covered corridor running beside the canal, and its walls are pierced with carved lattice windows, each a different pattern, framing little scenes of bamboo, rock and water. Artificial hills of rock and old trees give a feeling of a mountain landscape in miniature. UNESCO lists the classical gardens of Suzhou as a group, with an addition made in 2000.

Suzhou is a city of canals, stone bridges and whitewashed houses with dark roofs, often called the Venice of the East, and a saying goes that there is paradise in heaven and Suzhou and Hangzhou on earth. Silk and embroidery have been made here for centuries, and the local noodle soups and sweet-savoury dishes, often with a hint of sugar, are well known. Come early on a weekday to have the garden almost to yourself, and spring brings blossom and autumn gives clear skies.

Roads in and around Suzhou are busy, with electric scooters, buses and a heavy flow of traffic, so exploring the old city is easier on foot or by bicycle. Fuel, food and lodging are plentiful, and Mudu, a smaller town about eleven kilometres away, has a famous classical garden of its own. Check the rules for foreign motorcyclists in China before bringing a bike.
t.ruteng@-8.6,120.5:
Ruteng sits on a cool plateau in the middle of Flores, about twelve hundred metres above the sea, in country that feels more like the Alps in a heat wave than the tropics. Mornings here are cold enough for a jacket, mist hangs over the rice fields, and the hills are green with coffee, vanilla and clove plantations. About thirty-five thousand people live in the town, the main centre of the Manggarai region, and the majority are Catholic, a legacy of Portuguese traders and later Dutch missionaries that makes Flores unusual in mostly Muslim Indonesia. The cathedral is a large and busy landmark.

The Manggarai have their own distinctive culture, and the most striking evidence of it is in the fields. Around villages such as Cancar, a short ride from Ruteng, the rice paddies are laid out in great circular patterns called lingko, with the plots radiating from a central point like a spider web. The design reflects traditional land allocation by the village elders, and viewed from a nearby hill it is among the most unusual agricultural landscapes in the world. The old whip-fighting ritual called caci, in which men in buffalo-hide costumes duel with whips and shields, is still performed at festivals.

Ruteng has a place in science as well. In 2003, in the limestone cave of Liang Bua, a short distance north of town, archaeologists found the skeleton of a tiny human relative, nicknamed the hobbit, and named Homo floresiensis. It lived on Flores as recently as about fifty thousand years ago and stood only about a metre tall. The find changed ideas about human evolution, and the cave can be visited with a local guide.

The road here is a joy. The Trans-Flores Highway climbs from the coast through forest and farmland, with long curves and views of terraced fields and volcanic cones. Take care with the weather, since rain falls heavily in the wet season, from about November to March, and landslides can block the route. Fuel is available in town, and warm food, such as noodles and rice with chilli, is welcome on a damp evening. A cup of the local coffee, strong and slightly earthy, is the right way to warm up before the next stretch.
t.moni@-8.7,121.8:
Moni is a small village on the lower slopes of a volcano, and it exists largely because of what lies above it. About thirteen kilometres up a winding road is Kelimutu, a peak of around 1,640 metres whose summit holds three crater lakes in different colours, one of them often turquoise, another green and the third dark red or brown. The colours change over the years, depending on gases and minerals, and no one has fully explained why. Local belief holds that the souls of the dead go to the lakes, the young to one, the old to another and those who lived evil lives to the third.

Visitors usually leave Moni in the dark, around four in the morning, to reach the top for sunrise. The road is narrow and steep, and mist often fills the crater, so it can feel like a gamble. When the cloud lifts and the light strikes the water, the colours glow in a way that seems unreal, and the effect is worth the cold. By mid-morning the mist usually comes back. The climb from the car park to the viewpoint takes a few minutes on a paved path, and the air at that height is thin and chilly.

The village itself is simple, with a few guesthouses, small restaurants and shops, and weavers who sell ikat cloth, woven from dyed threads in traditional patterns, in the nearby market. Women in nearby villages still dye and weave by hand. Rice, vegetables and strong coffee are the staples of a Moni breakfast. The nights are cold, and many travellers are surprised by the need for a blanket in the tropics.

Moni lies on the Trans-Flores Highway, a winding road that links the island's towns, between Ruteng in the west and Maumere in the east. The nearest large town is Ende, about twenty-three kilometres to the south, where fuel and supplies are plentiful, and where Indonesia's first president, Sukarno, spent four years in exile in the 1930s, developing ideas that would shape the republic. Moni itself has little fuel, so fill the tank in Ende first. The dry season, from roughly May to October, offers the best chance of a clear dawn, though the volcano makes its own weather. Allow extra time for the winding road, and take warm clothes for the early start.
t.paris ile de france escapes@48.9,1.4:
Ézy-sur-Eure is a modest town of three thousand on the river Eure in Normandy, close to the border of the Eure and Eure-et-Loir, and its neighbour, Saussay, is a hamlet. The place is a few kilometres from Anet, a small town with one of the most celebrated châteaux of the French Renaissance, built in the 1540s by the architect Philibert de l'Orme for Diane de Poitiers, the favourite of King Henri II. The château, with its elegant courtyard and its famous carved entrance gate, is open to the public, and the story of Diane, who was about twenty years older than the king and ruled his heart for decades, is told in the rooms.

The Eure is a calm, clear river that runs among meadows and poplars, past mills and washhouses, and in summer people swim in the shallows and picnic on the banks, so the point is tagged for swimming. The water is generally cool and the current gentle, but check for signs, since not all stretches are supervised. The Chantilly and Ermenonville, named in the ride, lie well to the north-east, in the Oise, so this valley is a quiet western detour.

For a rider the Eure valley is a gentle place. The road follows the river with long, easy curves, passing small villages with stone houses and church towers, and now and then climbs onto the plateau for a view over the wheat fields. The surface is mostly good, and traffic is light on weekdays, with more cyclists and walkers on weekends. Because the lanes are narrow and the hedges high, watch for blind corners and farm vehicles. Fuel is available in Anet and Pacy-sur-Eure, and bakeries and cafés in the villages offer simple meals.

The region is famous for its cereals, and the plateau is covered with a patchwork of golden wheat in July. Evening is a lovely time, when the sun slants through the poplars and the river is still. In autumn the mist sits in the valley, and in winter fog and frost are common, so allow extra time. A visit to the château in the morning, before the crowds arrive, is worth the detour if you have an hour to spare.
t.paris ile de france escapes@49.5,3.2:
Blérancourt is a village of about twelve hundred in the Aisne, in the green country between Soissons and Noyon, and it houses an unexpected museum: the Musée national de la Coopération franco-américaine, in the remains of a seventeenth-century château. It was founded by Anne Morgan, the daughter of the American banker J. P. Morgan, who came here after the First World War to help the villagers rebuild, and the museum tells the story of the friendship between France and the United States, from the American Revolution to the world wars. A fine garden and a pair of pavilions survive from the old château.

Folembray, a village of about fifteen hundred, lies on the edge of the forest of Saint-Gobain, a large area of oak and beech woodland, and not far from the medieval castle of Coucy, which once had the largest keep in Europe, a cylindrical tower fifty-five metres tall, before the retreating German army blew it up in 1917. The ruins of the walls and towers still make a dramatic sight above the village of Coucy-le-Château. The country is a mix of woodland, farmland and small valleys, in the shadow of the First World War, with cemeteries and memorials scattered across it.

The point is part of a ride that centres on Paris and the Île-de-France, and it is tagged for swimming, with lakes and ponds scattered around the forest, though you should look for signed and supervised places. Laon, the hilltop cathedral city, is about thirty kilometres to the east, and Soissons and Compiègne are within easy reach. For fuel and food, Chauny, Noyon and Soissons are the nearest places of any size, and the villages may have only a bakery.

Roads through the Saint-Gobain forest are among the best in the region for a quiet ride, with long, gentle curves under tall trees and little traffic. The surface is mostly good, although forestry vehicles can leave mud, and deer cross the road without warning, especially at dusk. In autumn the colours are rich, with the smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke, and in spring the woods ring with birdsong. Fog is common in winter, and the shaded roads can be icy. Please treat the memorials and cemeteries with respect.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@45.8,4.0:
The Lignon du Forez comes out of the Monts du Forez with a cold, clean hurry, and by the time it reaches the plain around Boën it has cut itself a shallow gorge through old volcanic rock. This is the country west of Lyon and north of Saint-Étienne that most people cross on the autoroute without noticing, and that is exactly why it is pleasant. The Forez plain is a wide, flat bowl of pasture and orchards, and the mountains stand along its western edge like a wall with the road folded into the foot of it.

Sail is the one to remember: above the village a ruined medieval castle, Couzan, perches on a rock spur, and you can see it from the road long before you reach it. Boën is the practical neighbour, a small town with shops, a bakery or two and the usual fuel station, and it sits in the middle of the little Côtes du Forez wine area, a thin-skinned red country built on gamay. Saint-Germain-Laval, a bit further north, is a pleasant old market town. For anything larger, Montbrison is about twenty kilometres away and has everything.

The riding here is gentle rather than dramatic. Departmental roads run along the river and up into the hills with tight little bends, short climbs and a lot of blind crests where the hedges close in, so keep the speed honest. Surfaces are generally decent but patched, and farm traffic is the real hazard: tractors, loose gravel at field entrances, and mud after rain in the lower lanes. The best hours are early, when the mist lies on the plain and the hills above are already clear, and late in the day, when the light goes yellow on the stone farms.

The river is why this stop is marked for swimming. In summer the Lignon has pools below the bridges where locals wade in, but the water is mountain water, so it is bracing even in August, and levels change quickly after storms upstream. Pick a spot with a gravel bank, leave the leathers in the shade and give yourself time to warm up afterwards.

This is a fine place to start or end a day if you are heading for the Vanoise or the Jura, because you are on the quiet side of Lyon and the roads east are an easy morning's transfer away. Bring cash for the smaller villages, where the one bar may not take cards.
t.morvan southbound weekend@49.0,2.5:
Nobody plans a holiday around Goussainville, and that is fine, because this stop exists to get you out of Paris with a full tank. Aircraft pass low overhead on their final approach, so loud that conversation stops and restarts, and the sky is stitched with white contrails.

For a rider heading south toward the Morvan, the point is simple. Goussainville has about thirty thousand people and plenty of petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, and Gonesse is nearly as big. Fill up and eat properly here, because the first stretch beyond Paris is motorway or fast trunk road with services that charge a premium. If you are coming back on the Sunday evening, this is also where you will find yourself stuck in the returning traffic, so a coffee before the last push into the city is not a bad idea.

There is real history underneath all the concrete, though. Gonesse was famous in the Middle Ages for its bread, which was carried into Paris to feed the city, and the town still carries the name. Goussainville has an odd survivor: the old village centre, Vieux-Pays, was largely abandoned after the airport opened in the 1970s and the noise became unbearable, and a medieval church with its tower still stands among empty houses. In June 1973 a Soviet Tu-144 supersonic airliner crashed onto the village during the Paris Air Show, killing everyone aboard and several people on the ground. Locals do not forget it, and a short detour will show you the church, although the area is quiet and residential, so keep the engine down.

As for the riding, there is little to say. Roads are flat, signalised and full of roundabouts and speed cameras, and the surface is the tired asphalt of an industrial belt. The best advice is to leave early on a weekend morning, before the delivery lorries wake up, and aim for the forests and rolling farmland south and east of Paris. The Morvan, with its granite hills, lakes and beech woods, is a long way from here, which is the whole point of stopping.
t.ende@-8.8,121.7:
Ende sits on the south coast of Flores, a long, volcanic island in eastern Indonesia, and it is a place where history has left a small, quiet mark. In 1934 the Dutch colonial government exiled the nationalist leader Sukarno here, and he lived in a modest house for four years, writing, staging plays and thinking. According to local tradition, he came to the idea of the Pancasila, the five principles that became the foundation of the Indonesian state, while sitting under a breadfruit tree on the seafront, and the spot is now a small memorial park.

The town has some 77,000 people, a busy port and a market, and behind it rises Mount Iya, a volcano whose slopes shape the weather. The coast is rugged, with black sand beaches and a harbour full of wooden boats. Fuel is easy to find in Ende, and it is the last big town before the road east climbs toward the villages of the highlands. About fifty kilometres along lies Moni, the base for visiting Kelimutu, where three crater lakes change colour from turquoise to red to black, depending on the volcanic gases and minerals in the water.

The Trans-Flores Highway, one of the great rides in Indonesia, connects the towns along the island's spine. It is mostly a narrow, twisting road, with endless bends, steep gradients and sudden views of terraced rice fields, coffee plantations and green mountains. The surface is patched and rough in places, with potholes and landslides in the wet season, from December to March, and the pace is slow. A day's progress is often measured in a few dozen kilometres.

Expect to share the road with trucks, buses, motorbikes, chickens and goats. Take it patiently, and stop often to stretch, drink coffee and talk to people, who are friendly and curious. Local food is simple and good: rice with fish, vegetables and chilli sambal. The evenings are warm, the stars are bright, and the air carries the smell of clove smoke and the sea.
t.fontainebleau@48.9,2.8:
Louis Braille was born in Coupvray in 1809, and the house where he lived is now a small museum, a short ride from this point.

After a day in the Fontainebleau forest and along the Loing, it makes a quiet end. The roads near the river are flat and gentle, with long views over fields and a surface in good condition. Traffic is moderate, though weekends and holiday evenings bring heavy flows towards the theme park, so it is better to avoid the main routes and use the lanes along the Marne. The towpath by the river is popular with walkers and cyclists, and the villages along the bank have small quays and old houses.

Coupvray's church holds the grave of the man who invented the six-dot reading system, and the small village around it has changed little since his time. The Marne valley was once the scene of fierce fighting in the First World War, and the battle of the Marne in 1914, which halted the German advance on Paris, was fought not far to the east. Memorials and cemeteries are scattered along the roads.

Esbly has a railway station with direct trains to Paris Gare de l'Est, and a small centre with shops, a baker and cafes. Fuel is available in town, and a larger shopping area is closer to Marne-la-Vallée. The riverside is a good spot for a rest, with shade and benches, and in summer fishermen sit on the bank.

As the final point of a long forest loop, it is a calm place for the day to end, and well suited to a slow walk by the water.
t.lyons la foret@49.4,1.5:
Beech trees are the point. The forest of Lyons, a few kilometres from the village, is one of the largest and finest beech woods in Europe, about ten thousand hectares of tall, silver-trunked trees that stand in cathedral rows, and in spring, when the leaves are just out, the light under them is green and gold. In autumn it turns copper. The roads that cross it are some of the best in Normandy for easy riding, with long, smooth curves, a good surface and little traffic, and the sense of riding through a vast, quiet hall is hard to beat.

The village of Lyons-la-Forêt sits in a clearing at about 150 metres, and it is one of the prettiest in Normandy, with half-timbered houses, brick and flint walls and an old covered market hall dating from the eighteenth century, in the middle of the square. The film director Claude Chabrol used it as the setting for his Madame Bovary in 1991, because it looks so much like the Normandy of Flaubert's novel. A few kilometres away, the abbey of Mortemer, with its ruins and small museum, is a quiet place to stop. The village is listed among the most beautiful in France, and in summer and on fine weekends it fills with visitors from Paris, so it is better on a weekday.

Lunch here is a pleasure. Normandy is dairy country, and the food is rich: Neufchâtel cheese, a soft, white-rinded cheese in a heart shape, cream sauces, apple tart and cider or the apple brandy called Calvados. Restaurants and tea rooms around the square serve lunch until about two, and you should book on Sundays.

The forest is also home to deer and wild boar, so be careful at dusk, and in wet weather the leaves can make bends slippery. The nights are cool and the air smells of damp wood. It is a very good place to turn for home.
t.milly forest@48.6,2.7:
Fouquet's château is on your doorstep here. Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister, built it from 1656, with Le Vau as architect, Le Nôtre as garden designer and Le Brun as decorator, and in August 1661 he gave a lavish party there for the young king. Within weeks, Fouquet was arrested, and the king took the same team to build Versailles.

Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun are close, and Fontainebleau forest begins to the south.

The ride that ends here has come out of the Milly forest and the Nemours area, so it is a gentle return. Roads are good, with long straights across the open plateau and a few twists as they enter the woods around Maincy. Traffic is light on weekdays but can be heavy near the château in summer, and early morning is the best time to see the building in soft light, when the moat is still and the gardens look their best. The grounds are open to visitors, and the garden cascade and grotto are worth the entry fee if you have the time.

Fuel is available in Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun, where there are stations and supermarkets, and a few cafes in Maincy and the neighbouring villages serve simple lunches. For a more elegant ending, the château has a restaurant, though it is expensive, and the lawns offer a place for a picnic.

The Seine is not far, and a short ride brings you to its banks at Melun for a final view. It is a worthy end to a ride that began in forest and rock.
t.lac@45.7,4.5:
Saint-Martin-en-Haut lives up to its name, which means St Martin on the heights. Aveize and the old hamlets of the area sit among meadows and orchards, and the whole region is unexpectedly rural, though it lies less than an hour from the city.

The ride here began at Lac du Bourget, far to the east, so it ends on a different note. These hills have no famous passes, but the roads are among the best in the region: they climb and dip in long, steady bends, crossing ridges that give wide views, and the surface is generally smooth. Traffic is light, except on summer Sundays when Lyonnais cyclists take over. In winter the heights can be cold and icy, and fog is frequent, so the best seasons are late spring and early autumn.

The Monts du Lyonnais are known for farming. Orchards of cherries, apricots and apples cover the slopes, and goat cheese and charcuterie are sold at village shops. The area was once a centre for weaving silk at home, and a number of old stone houses with large windows, built for looms, survive. Old chapels and calvaries stand on many hilltops.

The nearest large town is Mornant, eleven kilometres away, with a market and stations, though Saint-Martin itself has a small centre with a baker and a bar. Fuel should be taken in Mornant or Lyon before climbing into the hills. For rest, the village has a pleasant square and some benches, and several viewpoints along the road offer a place to sit.

As the finishing point of a Bourget loop, it is a calm and pastoral one, with a good view back over the Rhône valley as the light fades.
t.maumere@-8.6,122.2:
Maumere is where the Trans-Flores road runs out of island, or begins, depending on which way you ride. It is the biggest town in the east of Flores, a trading port with a Catholic cathedral, a busy market and a long waterfront, and the heat and humidity here hit you the moment you stop.

Coming in from Bajawa, you have ridden a long day of mountain road, with endless bends, fast descents through rice terraces and coffee plantations, and the occasional landslide patch where rain has taken a bite out of the tarmac. The surface can be rough, with potholes, loose gravel and livestock on the road, so speed is never your friend. Maumere itself is flat and chaotic, full of motorbikes, minibuses and bemos, and the last few kilometres are slower than the rest of the day.

The town is also known for a disaster. In December 1992 an earthquake and tsunami devastated the north coast of Flores, killing thousands and wiping out villages along the shore, and the memory is still strong. The area is known for its weaving, too. Sikka, a village a short ride east, is famous for its ikat cloth, hand-dyed in rich reds and browns with patterns that vary from village to village, and weavers will often show their work if you stop. Catholicism arrived with the Portuguese, and the Easter processions in Larantuka, further east, are among the most important in Indonesia.

Fuel is no problem in Maumere, with several stations, and it is wise to fill up before heading anywhere else, as villages along the road may only sell petrol from bottles. Warungs along the waterfront serve grilled fish, rice and vegetables at low prices, and fresh coconut water is available on nearly every corner. The coast around the town has beaches with coral reefs, popular with divers, and the sunset over the water is reliable.

Keep an eye on the weather. The wet season, roughly December to March, can bring heavy rain and landslides, and the dry months are far better for riding.
t.bugey lakes@45.3,4.9:
This stretch of country belongs to the border between the Drôme and the Isère, on a flat, fertile plain called the Valloire. It is a sleepy farming region, a land of walnut orchards, maize fields and low villages like Épinouze and Saint-Sorlin-en-Valloire, about fifty kilometres south of Lyon. The roads here are quiet, straight and bordered by hedges and poplars, and the air in late summer smells of cut hay and ripening fruit. It is not the Bugey, which lies far to the north-east, but the end of a long ride has a way of dropping you somewhere unexpected.

The area has one genuine marvel hidden nearby. At Hauterives, a few kilometres to the east, a country postman named Ferdinand Cheval spent thirty-three years, from 1879 onward, collecting stones on his rounds and building a fantastical palace in his garden, a riot of towers, grottoes and carved animals that he called the Palais Idéal. The surrealists admired it, and in 1969 the French state listed it as a historic monument. It is a short run from here and well worth ten minutes if you are not too tired.

For a rider, the Valloire is a restful finish. The roads are flat and fast, with long straights and gentle bends, though there are occasional tractors, so keep your eyes open. Small towns here have a bakery and a bar but not always a petrol station, so for a reliable fuel stop use Roussillon, about twelve kilometres away, or the bigger towns along the Rhône valley. Wind can pick up along the open plain, particularly in spring, and there is the odd smell of manure from the fields, a reminder that this is working land.

In September the walnut harvest begins, and you will see nets laid under the trees and trailers heaped with nuts. Local walnut oil and walnut cake are good things to buy and carry home. The landscape feels unhurried, and after a day of climbing, that is exactly what you want.
t.perche quiet@48.7,2.3:
This is a landscape of big fields, wheat and sugar beet, cut through by motorways and dotted with research laboratories and business parks. The plateau is one of France's main scientific clusters, with universities and institutes that grew up around the old agricultural land, so you will see low modern campuses sitting beside barns and farm tracks.

The name Saulx-les-Chartreux hints at an older story. The Carthusians, a strict order of contemplative monks, once owned land here, and the village remembers them in its name. Many villages in this part of the Essonne grew up around a church and a few farms, and some of the old stone houses and farm courtyards can still be found down side streets. Villebon-sur-Yvette lies in the valley of the Yvette, a small river that runs through woods and meadows toward the Seine, and it still has a pleasant green corner or two.

From the plateau, the road toward the Perche runs west past Chevreuse and Rambouillet, onto smaller lanes. The ride's quiet reputation depends on avoiding the main roads, which can be badly congested at commuting hours, especially on the roads around Courtaboeuf and the A10. Use the smaller departmental roads on the plateau, where the surface is good and the bends are gentle. Fuel is not a problem: Saulx-les-Chartreux has about five thousand people, Villebon-sur-Yvette about ten thousand, and there are supermarkets with cheap petrol nearby.

The best time to ride this area is early on a weekend morning, before traffic builds, or in the evening after the commute. Autumn is gorgeous, with fields turning gold and then brown, while spring brings the bright yellow of oilseed rape. In winter, fog can lie in the valley and ice can form on shaded bends, so be careful.
t.reims@49.3,4.0:
For over a thousand years the kings of France came to Reims to be crowned, and the cathedral that still dominates the city shows why. The tradition goes back to Clovis, baptised here around the year 500 by Bishop Remigius, and some thirty-odd monarchs followed, ending with Charles X in 1825. The present Gothic building dates from the thirteenth century, its west front crowded with statues, among them the Smiling Angel, and it was damaged badly by German shelling in the First World War before being painstakingly restored. Inside, stained glass by Marc Chagall glows blue behind the apse, installed in the 1970s.

Reims is also a champagne capital, and it wears this lightly. Beneath the streets lie kilometres of chalk cellars, some of them Roman quarries called crayères, in which the great houses age millions of bottles at a steady cold temperature, and the cellars and the hillsides around them were added to the UNESCO list in 2015. Houses such as Pommery, Taittinger and Veuve Clicquot are all in town, and most offer guided tours that end, naturally, with a glass. The city also has a nice, odd claim to history: Germany's unconditional surrender in the Second World War was signed here, in a school building, on 7 May 1945. And do not miss the biscuits roses, pink sponge fingers that have been dunked in champagne since the eighteenth century.

For a ride called the Champagne Tourist Route, Reims is the right place to begin. The city is flat and busy, with a wide central square, tram lines to watch, and one-way streets, so park the bike in an underground garage if you stay. Fuel is easy, with stations on every ring road and supermarkets around the edge, and cafés open early. Leaving town, you climb quickly onto the Montagne de Reims, a forested ridge covered in vines on its flanks, where the roads wind between villages with names that appear on bottle labels.

Mornings are the best time to ride, before the day-trippers appear. The vineyards are most beautiful in autumn, when the leaves go gold and red, though harvest brings tractors and slippery grape juice on the tarmac. Spring can bring frost warnings, and night cold in the open chalk country. Wear a layer.
t.epernay@49.0,4.0:
Épernay is the sort of town that makes a bubble feel like an institution. It sits on the Marne river, in the heart of Champagne, and its main street, the Avenue de Champagne, is lined with the grand houses of famous producers: Moët and Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger, Mercier and others, in mansions of stone, brick and wrought iron, set behind gardens and gates. The avenue is sometimes called the most expensive street in the world, a joke based on the value of the bottles stored beneath it.

That is the real secret of Épernay: the cellars. Under the town, chalk galleries stretch for tens of kilometres, cool and damp, where millions of bottles lie on their sides, slowly developing the fine bubbles that give the wine its character. Several houses offer tours, which include a descent into the dark, a lecture on the méthode champenoise and, naturally, a glass at the end. It is best to book ahead in summer, and remember that tasting and riding do not mix.

The hills around, planted with chardonnay and pinot noir and pinot meunier, form the landscape that was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015 for its vineyards, houses and cellars. A few kilometres to the north, in the village of Hautvillers, the monk Dom Pérignon is traditionally credited with refining the techniques of champagne production in the late seventeenth century, though the myth that he invented the wine is just that. His grave lies in the abbey church.

The riding here is a pleasure. The scenic route through the vineyards winds along the slopes of the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Blancs, with good roads, gentle gradients, and long views over rows of vines. The best time is autumn, when the harvest is under way and the vineyards turn red and gold, but spring, with its fresh green growth, is just as good. During the harvest, expect tractors and workers on the roads.

Épernay is a town of twenty-seven thousand, with fuel stations, restaurants and parking, and the centre is compact enough to explore on foot. The suburb of Magenta is named after the battle of 1859, a small piece of Franco-Italian history in a very French town.
t.chateau thierry@49.0,3.4:
Château-Thierry lies along the Marne at a point where the river valley narrows and the hills close in, and it is the town where the poet Jean de La Fontaine was born in 1621. His house is now a museum, and the fables he spun about foxes, crows and cunning grasshoppers are still learned by schoolchildren across France. Above the river, the ruins of a medieval castle crown the hillside, with walls and towers that once guarded the road to Paris, and they give a good view over the roofs and the water.

The town has a solemn side as well. In 1918, the area saw heavy fighting in the Second Battle of the Marne, in which American troops played a significant part, defending the river crossing here and fighting at nearby Belleau Wood, to the north-west. A cemetery and memorial in the woods commemorate them, and there are other monuments around the district. The farmland near the town is rich and rolling, with fields of wheat and rapeseed, and the western edge of the Champagne vineyards begins in the hills around, making this a quiet end to the route.

On a motorcycle, the road along the Marne valley is a pleasure. It is smooth, bendy and gentle, with the river on one side and vines or woodland on the other, and it passes through villages with stone houses and old wash-houses. Traffic is light outside the commute, though lorries use the main road, so choose the smaller departmental roads when you can. The town has nearly sixteen thousand people, so fuel stations, bakeries and cafés are never far, and the riverside is a nice place for a sandwich in the sun.

Autumn brings mist on the river in the morning and the smell of woodsmoke by evening. In summer the shaded lanes are a relief from the heat. If you have time, taste a regional cheese such as Brie de Meaux from a local market, and think of La Fontaine's crow dropping hers.
t.loire castle edge@49.3,2.3:
A modest town on the little river Thérain, in the Oise département, Mouy lies about fifty kilometres north of Paris, among the low chalk hills and wooded ridges of the Picardy edge. The landscape is quiet: wheat fields, hedgerows, woodland and neat red-roofed villages, with the occasional church spire poking up on the skyline. It does not shout about itself, and there is something restful in that after the big roads of the capital.

The area is on the doorstep of two famous places. To the east, Chantilly has a grand château with a collection of paintings in the Musée Condé, a racecourse and the great stables that house horses and a museum of the horse, and the town is also known for its whipped cream. Not far away, the old town of Senlis has medieval walls, a cathedral and a cluster of narrow streets, and the forests of the Oise are full of deer. Together they make the case for ending a day here, on the edge of the château country that gives the ride its name, rather than at the far end of the Loire valley.

The riding is easy and pleasant. Roads in the Thérain valley and the surrounding plateau are smooth and lightly trafficked, with gentle bends, long views over farmland, and a pleasant rhythm of fields and woods. On weekends, cyclists and families are out in numbers. Fuel and food are no problem, because Mouy has about five and a half thousand people, with a supermarket, bakeries and a few cafés. The larger town of Creil is not far away, and has more stations. In winter, mist and ice can build in the valley, so take care on shaded bends and bridges.

In autumn, the beech woods turn deep copper, and mushrooms appear along the verges, and by evening there is a smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke. Park near the church, take a deep breath, and let the day settle. After a long ride, the peace of a small French town is hard to beat.
t.vercors@45.9,4.9:
North-east of Lyon, the land flattens into the Dombes, a plateau of glacial clay that is dotted with a thousand or more man-made ponds. Civrieux, Saint-André-de-Corcy and Mionnay sit on its southern edge, where the ponds, called étangs, glimmer among fields and woods, and herons and egrets stand in the reeds. Since the Middle Ages, the people of the Dombes have farmed fish in these ponds, draining each one every few years to harvest carp and then growing crops in the dry bed before refilling it, a rhythm that has shaped the landscape and the local menu.

It is an unusual and rather lovely part of France. Birds are the main attraction, and a large park at Villars-les-Dombes, a short way north, keeps thousands of them, while migrating species stop on the ponds in spring and autumn. Mionnay, a village of two thousand, has a place in French culinary history, because a famous restaurant here once earned three Michelin stars and drew gourmets from Lyon and further away. The local dishes include frogs' legs, carp and chicken from Bresse, the region just to the north.

For a rider, the Dombes is a calm place to end a day. The roads are flat and straight, with long lines of poplars and a lot of agricultural traffic, and it is a good area to unwind. Fuel is available in Saint-André-de-Corcy, a village of three thousand, and in the larger town of Neuville-sur-Saône, which is a bit further, so you will not run short. Bakeries and cafés are scattered through the villages, and a lunch in a village inn can be a pleasure. In mist and evening light, the ponds seem to glow, and the sky is large.

After the cliffs and balconies of the Vercors, the contrast is considerable. The ride has taken you from stone and precipice to reed and water, and the land has the quiet of a place that has been farmed for centuries. Mosquitoes can be bothersome near the ponds in summer, so carry repellent, and in autumn, fog can lie thick on the lanes in the early morning, so use your lights.
t.fontainebleau forest@48.4,2.7:
The Forest of Fontainebleau is a strange and beautiful place, a woodland of oak, beech and pine growing on a bed of sandstone that has weathered into huge grey boulders, scattered across the hillsides like the playthings of giants. It covers some twenty-five thousand hectares south of Paris, and it was a royal hunting ground for centuries before it became a place of refuge for city dwellers, climbers and painters. UNESCO designated it a biosphere reserve in the late twentieth century, recognising its rare mix of habitats.

The sandstone is the thing. Over millions of years, wind and water have carved it into rounded blocks, ledges and overhangs, and in the forest these blocks have become the world's best-known bouldering ground, with climbers from every country working the problems marked with coloured arrows. The sand itself is pale and fine, and the heaths and gorges of Franchard have an almost desert feel in dry weather. The forest also has the Mare aux Fées, a pond named for the fairies said to bathe in it.

In the nineteenth century, painters of the Barbizon school, among them Rousseau and Millet, came to the village of Barbizon on the edge of the forest to paint nature directly, working outdoors and rejecting the studio tradition, and in doing so they helped pave the way for the Impressionists. The château of Fontainebleau, a vast palace beside the forest, was a favourite of François I and Napoleon, who said farewell to his Guard in its courtyard in 1814 before going into exile on Elba.

The riding here is a very mixed pleasure. The main roads through the forest are smooth and fast, with long avenues of tall trees and dappled light, but many smaller roads are narrow, patched and strewn with leaves and sand, and sudden bends hide in the shade. Speed limits are low and enforced, and some tracks are closed to motor vehicles. Weekends bring heavy traffic, with cyclists, climbers and walkers, so go on a weekday if you can. After rain the surface can be treacherous.

Fontainebleau, a town of nearly twenty thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and parking, and is the best place to stock up. The smell of the forest, resin and leaf mould, is intoxicating on a warm morning.
t.nemours@48.3,2.7:
Nemours lies on the Loing river, in the southern corner of Seine-et-Marne, where the landscape changes from the forests of Fontainebleau to the gentler farmland of the Gâtinais. It is a town of about fourteen thousand people, with a grey-stone centre, a canal beside the river and a medieval castle that still stands guard over the bridge. A good place for lunch, in other words, with enough to look at between courses.

The castle, built in the twelfth century and extended in the fifteenth, is a solid, square fortress with round corner towers, and it houses a museum on the prehistory of the Île-de-France, as well as exhibits about the history of the town. The surrounding area is rich in prehistoric remains, thanks to the rock shelters and caves in the sandstone ridges, and the museum explains how people have lived in the region for tens of thousands of years. The duchy of Nemours, once a royal title, gave its name to a series of notable French nobles.

The Canal du Loing runs through the town, a modest waterway used for centuries to carry goods toward Paris, now mostly frequented by pleasure boats and walkers on the towpath. A seat on a terrace by the canal in summer, with a plate of simple French cooking, is hard to beat. Expect good, uncomplicated fare: a plat du jour, a steak with chips, a goat cheese salad, a tarte aux pommes, and a carafe of house wine. The brasseries around the centre are generally open for lunch from noon until two, and a lot of them are closed on Monday.

The riding to Nemours from the north runs along quiet forest roads and then across open farmland, a good mix of shaded bends and straight sections. The surface is generally good, the traffic light, and the sandstone cliffs on the edge of town give a hint of the scenery in the forest. In autumn, the leaves along the roads can be slippery, especially after rain.

Fuel is easy in Nemours and neighbouring Saint-Pierre-lès-Nemours, both of which have stations and supermarkets, and the town is a convenient base for exploring the area. If you have time after lunch, take a walk along the canal and watch the boats pass through the lock.
t.fontainebleau@48.4,2.7:
Fontainebleau is a royal town in a forest, and the combination is irresistible. The château grew over seven centuries from a medieval hunting lodge into a palace of great beauty, and François I turned it into a showpiece of the Renaissance, importing Italian artists to decorate its galleries. Napoleon was fond of it, too, and it was in the horseshoe staircase courtyard that he said farewell to his Old Guard in April 1814, before leaving for exile on Elba. The courtyard is called the Cour des Adieux, and visitors still stand on those steps for photos.

The forest surrounding the town is enormous, more than twenty thousand hectares of oak, beech and pine, with great grey sandstone boulders scattered through the trees like toys left by a giant. Climbers love it, and a local style of bouldering began here, so you will see people with crash pads and chalk-white hands. In the nineteenth century, painters lived in the village of Barbizon, on the edge of the forest, and worked outdoors, a precursor to the Impressionists. The ride's backroads through the Brie countryside and the coffee stop at Meaux set up a day of gentle riding in the cheese country east of Paris, so arriving at Fontainebleau at the end gives a fine finish.

For a rider, Fontainebleau is a good, easy place to rest. The town has nearly twenty thousand people, and Avon next door has more, so fuel, food and coffee are all easy, with bakeries open from early in the morning. Roads in the forest are smooth and gently curving, with big trees on both sides, but in places they are narrow, and the speed limits are low. Cyclists and walkers are everywhere on weekends, and deer and wild boar can cross at dusk. Leaves can lie thick on the road in autumn and make the bends slippery, so take it slowly.

The town centre fills with visitors in summer and the palace queues are long, but the forest is big enough to absorb everyone. Walk along a sandy track among the boulders for a few minutes, and you will see why the kings chose to hunt here, and why they never left.
t.chevreuse@49.0,2.4:
It is a long way from the valley of Chevreuse, which lies south-west of the capital, and it tells you how a ride that starts with soft forest can end up on the opposite side of the city. Here the landscape is open and slightly bleak, big fields of wheat and sugar beet giving way to housing estates, warehouses and the giant, humming presence of Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport to the north-east.

There is a surprising jewel on the ridge above Écouen. The château, built in the sixteenth century for Anne de Montmorency, Constable of France and one of the most powerful men of his age, is a robust Renaissance building with a moat, grand chimneys and rooms that still hold painted ceilings and monumental fireplaces. It now houses the national museum of the Renaissance, with tapestries, ceramics and weapons from the period, and from its terrace you can look out over the plain you have just crossed. The town around it has steep, quiet streets and a village feel that is hard to square with the surrounding sprawl.

Goussainville has a more haunting story. The old village centre, with its church and a few streets, was gradually abandoned in the decades after the airport opened, as aircraft noise made life unbearable, and parts of it stood empty for years, a ghost village on the edge of a major airport. Now some of it is being restored, and the church of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul stands solitary behind a fence. It is an odd, melancholy place for photographers, though you should be respectful of the houses that are still lived in.

Riding here is mostly practical. Roads are wide, with big roundabouts and trucks, and the evening queues on the A1 and the N16 can be long, but the surfaces are good and there is no shortage of fuel, with Villiers-le-Bel, Goussainville and neighbouring towns all offering several stations and supermarkets. Early mornings on weekends are the quiet time, when the sun comes up golden over the fields and the planes glitter as they climb out of Roissy.
t.romans and@45.6,4.7:
The land here belongs to the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded hills south-west of Lyon that rise to about nine hundred metres at their highest and are made of old crystalline rock. Mornant, Chassagny and Taluyers sit on the eastern flank, where the slope falls toward the Rhône and the soil supports orchards, pasture and, in places, vineyards. The wines of the Coteaux du Lyonnais, mostly light, fruity Gamay reds, come from these hills, and there are small producers who will sell you a bottle in a cellar with a hand-painted sign.

Mornant is a lively little market town of about five thousand people, with a church, a main street of bakeries and a Saturday morning crowd, and it is known as the centre of its own small region. Villages like Chassagny and Taluyers are quieter, with stone houses, a church and a bar. It is a landscape that does not demand attention, which is part of its charm: tiny roads between fields of maize and fruit trees, a view of far-off ridges, the sound of cowbells and tractors.

As an end point for a ride called Romans and Royans, it is a long way from the dramatic limestone cliffs of the Vercors, but a good place to finish. The roads here are narrow and bendy, rising and falling over small hills, and traffic is light except around Mornant itself. Surfaces are generally good, but cyclists are out in force, especially at weekends, and manure and gravel can lie on the bends. A little care pays off. There is fuel in Mornant, as well as bakeries and a small supermarket, and Givors, a larger town, is a short run to the east.

In the evening, the light turns the hills a soft blue and the first mist settles in the hollows. After a day on the cliffs, the gentle lanes are a welcome change. Stop for a coffee at a village bar, and chat to the regulars about the harvest. They will have an opinion, and they will be delighted to share it.
t.chevreuse valley road@48.7,2.0:
The Chevreuse valley owes its fame partly to a duchess. Marie de Rohan, Duchess of Chevreuse, was a leading figure in the plots and intrigues of seventeenth-century France, a friend and rival of cardinals and queens, who was exiled several times for her part in conspiracies against Richelieu and Mazarin. The town's name is forever linked with her, and above the roofs the ruins of the medieval castle, called the Château de la Madeleine, still stand on their rock, the remains of a fortress that guarded the valley for centuries.

The Yvette river runs through the town, a quiet stream with weirs and mill races, and the valley is lined with wooded slopes. At about a hundred metres above sea level, it is a green and sheltered trough, and the effect of being in a deep, quiet valley, only half an hour from Paris, is part of the charm. Chevreuse itself has about five thousand people, a pleasant main street, a few cafes and a market, and is an easy place to stop.

A little further east lies the abbey of Port-Royal-des-Champs, near Magny-les-Hameaux, one of the great places of French religious and intellectual history. In the seventeenth century it was the centre of Jansenism, a strict Catholic movement that attracted thinkers such as Blaise Pascal and the playwright Jean Racine, and was bitterly opposed by Louis XIV, who had the abbey destroyed in 1710. The ruins and a museum on the site give a sense of the drama.
