Fuel is available at stations around the ring road, but there are few in the centre, so fill up before you enter. Cafés and bakeries are everywhere.
t.the garden of cultivation@31.3,120.6:
Suzhou is a city of canals and gardens, and the Garden of Cultivation is one of the smaller and quieter examples of an art that the Chinese took to extraordinary lengths. A scholar's garden here was not simply a plot of flowers. It was a miniature world, a landscape of rocks, water, trees, pavilions and walls, arranged to suggest mountains and rivers and to make a visitor feel they had stepped out of the city. UNESCO listed the classical gardens of Suzhou in 1997, adding more in 2000.

The Ming dynasty, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, saw many of these gardens built by retired officials and wealthy merchants, who used them for poetry, painting, music, tea and conversation. Their design follows careful principles: no single view should be seen all at once, paths twist, windows frame scenes, and pools reflect the sky. Walking through, you pass through moon gates, zigzag bridges and covered corridors, and every turn is a new composition.

The city around the gardens is large, with over five million people, and Suzhou has a long history as a centre of silk production and scholarship. Old canals still run through the centre, with white-walled houses and stone bridges, and boats glide past in the early morning mist. The old saying is that there is heaven above and Suzhou and Hangzhou below.

A word of honesty about riding. In Chinese cities, motorcycles are heavily restricted, and many cities ban them in central areas. Foreign riders usually need special permits and licensing, so riding here is not a casual matter. Most visitors get around by metro, bus or taxi, and the gardens are best explored on foot in any case. Fuel and food are plentiful in the city, and local dishes include sweet and sour mandarin fish and noodles with a clear, delicate broth. Come early in the morning to enjoy a garden before the tour groups arrive, and in spring or autumn, when the weather is mild. Take your time, and sit for a while in a pavilion.
t.the humble administrator s garden@31.3,1:
Wang Xianchen was a retired imperial official who, around 1509, in the Ming dynasty, bought a piece of marshy land in Suzhou and made a garden. He named it after a line in an ancient essay about how a humble man can learn to govern his own small plot, and the name has a modest, ironic ring: the Humble Administrator's Garden is the largest in Suzhou, covering about five hectares, and is regarded as one of the finest in China. It belongs to the group of classical Suzhou gardens that UNESCO inscribed in 1997.

Water is the heart of the design. Pools, streams and lotus ponds cover about three-fifths of the area, and pavilions and covered walkways stand on the edge or on islands, so that you move through a landscape of reflections. A zigzag bridge crosses the water, a hall for viewing lotus faces the central pond, and the surrounding rocks, bamboo and pine trees are arranged like a painting, with views framed by round and hexagonal windows. The effect is of a large country estate shrunk into a city block.

The garden had many owners, passing from the original family to a gambler, then to officials and merchants, and for a time it served as a rebel palace in the nineteenth century. Today it is one of the most visited places in the city, and in peak season, it is crowded, so go early, on a weekday and in spring or autumn. The azaleas in April and the lotus in July are the high points.

Riding is not really part of a visit to Suzhou, since motorcycles are restricted in the city centre, and foreign riders face licensing barriers. The best way to travel is by metro, bus or taxi, and the old centre is compact enough to walk. Fuel and food are no problem, and the city has a rich cuisine, from noodles and dumplings to the sweet, slightly sour flavours of Jiangsu cooking. Bring water and a hat in summer, and allow at least two hours for the garden. Tea is served in a teahouse by the pond, and it is pleasant to sit there for a while.
t.the lion forest garden@31.3,120.6:
If you want to know why Chinese gardens love rocks, go to the Lion Forest Garden. Built in 1342, during the Yuan dynasty, by monks of a Buddhist monastery in Suzhou in honour of their teacher, it is famous for its rockery, a maze of grey limestone from Lake Tai, twisted into peaks, caves and tunnels, some of which are said to resemble lions. The artist Ni Zan, a celebrated painter of the period, is said to have helped with the design. The garden is part of the Suzhou group inscribed by UNESCO in 1997.

The rock maze is the main event. Paths wind through it, rising and falling, passing through tunnels and over little bridges, so that in a small area you can walk quite a distance and get pleasantly lost. Children love it. The best way to see it is without hurrying, pausing to notice the shapes. Seeing the lions depends on your imagination, and the guides will be glad to help.

The garden later passed into private hands, and in the twentieth century, it belonged to the family of the architect I. M. Pei, who was born in China and whose relatives owned the property for a time. It was given to the state in the 1950s and restored. Around it, the buildings are typical of the late imperial period, with whitewashed walls, dark tiles and carved wooden windows, and a pond with a pavilion and a small boat-shaped hall.

Suzhou is a large, prosperous city and its streets are busy. In China, motorcycle use is limited in city centres, and foreign riders face licensing and registration obstacles, so getting around by metro, taxi or on foot is much more practical, and the garden is a short distance from the centre. Fuel, food and rooms are all easy to find. Local specialities include squirrel-shaped mandarin fish and crab roe dumplings, and tea houses offer a quiet place to rest. Visit early on a weekday, in spring or autumn, and give yourself time to explore the rockery. Mist or light rain makes the stones look wonderful.
t.maisons la roche et jeanneret@48.9,2.3:
In the sixteenth arrondissement of Paris, tucked into a quiet cul-de-sac off the Square du Docteur-Blanche, stand two white houses that changed how people thought about living. The Maisons La Roche et Jeanneret were designed by Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret in the mid 1920s, one for a Swiss banker and art collector, Raoul La Roche, and one for Jeanneret's brother, a musician. Today the building houses the Fondation Le Corbusier, and the interiors, with their ramps, flat roofs, ribbon windows and rather austere palette, are open to visitors on certain days, so check the schedule before you go.

This is urban riding at its most stop-and-go: Périphérique access, traffic lights, buses, delivery vans and scooters weaving in every direction. Any bike without an easy clutch will make you regret it by the second kilometre.

You do not come to this place for the riding. You come for the architecture, and for the odd sense of a stage set from a hundred years ago that still looks modern. The quiet of the street, at least on a weekday morning, is a pleasant contrast to the busy avenues around. Auteuil, which surrounds it, is old Paris money, with art nouveau gems by Hector Guimard scattered through the neighbourhood, and the Roland-Garros tennis stadium is a few minutes away if you want to add some sport to your day.

For petrol, food and coffee you are well served in Boulogne-Billancourt, a big town of over a hundred thousand, and in the countless Paris cafés. The best advice is to arrive early before the traffic builds, take a long look at the white façade, and then leave Paris eastbound before the afternoon rush shuts every road in the city.
The Côte de Beaune and the Côte de Nuits are two ridges of gentle limestone, barely a hundred metres above the plain of the Saône, and they hold some of the most expensive agricultural land on earth. The phrase Les Climats du vignoble de Bourgogne refers to the small named vineyard plots, each with its own character of soil and exposure, that Burgundians have mapped and cultivated for centuries; the monks of Cluny and Cîteaux did much of the early work, noticing that wine from one plot tasted different from the next and writing it down. UNESCO recognised the whole system as a cultural landscape, and driving through it you can see why, because the walled vineyards, stone huts and village squares are all part of the same story.

Here, near Ladoix-Serrigny and Savigny-lès-Beaune, you are at the northern end of the Côte de Beaune, a few kilometres from the town of Beaune itself. The riding is the real draw. The D974, the old Route des Grands Crus, runs along the foot of the slope, and the smaller lanes weave up into the villages and between the vines. Nothing is steep, nothing is demanding; it is gentle, slow, and best taken at the speed of someone reading the labels on the wall plaques. Corners are soft, surfaces mostly good, and in September and October the harvest brings tractors and grape pickers onto every road, so you will be patient or you will be stuck.

There are no famous views in the Alpine sense, just the long green or golden stripe of vines on the slope, the red-tiled roofs of the villages and the occasional church spire. Spring brings the first bright green and sometimes frost fires among the vines, and autumn turns the whole hill to rust and copper. Summer is hot and bright; winter is quiet and grey.

Beaune, a town of about twenty-four thousand, has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of restaurants, and the Hospices de Beaune, with its glazed polychrome roof tiles, is one of the sights of eastern France and well worth an hour. The wine auction there each November is famous. The little villages you pass through have cellars that offer tastings, but remember that you are on a bike, and the only sensible approach is a single small glass or a bottle strapped on for later. Burgundy's food is rich and slow: boeuf bourguignon, gougères, poached eggs in red wine sauce, and the local snails.
t.cro de granville@45.0,1.0:
The Cro de Granville is a rock shelter in the Dordogne, near Rouffignac-Saint-Cernin, in the part of south-west France where the limestone plateaus are riddled with caves, shelters and overhangs and where early humans lived and painted for tens of thousands of years.

The nearest places you can count on are Rouffignac, a village of about fifteen hundred people, and Le Bugue, about eleven kilometres away, with a little under three thousand. Both have bakeries, a few cafés and basic supplies, but for proper fuel and supermarkets the larger town is Boulazac, near Périgueux, some twenty kilometres off. If the tank is low, fill it before you wander into the back lanes, because the plateau between the valleys is thinly settled and some of the pumps in the villages are automatic card-only machines.

The riding in this area is lovely in a way that sneaks up on you. The roads are narrow country departmentals, with gentle undulations, tight little bends through chestnut woods, and sudden open views over walnut orchards, maize fields and honey-coloured farmhouses. Surfaces vary, with patched tarmac and the occasional gravel patch on the smaller lanes, and farm vehicles are common, especially in late summer. The Vézère and Dordogne valleys are pretty roads in their own right, flat and fast along the river and busy with canoeists and caravans in July and August.

Food is a major part of the day here. This is duck, goose, walnut and truffle country, with foie gras, confit and cèpes on every menu, and the markets in the small towns are worth a detour on the right day. The Dordogne in high summer can be very crowded around the big cave sites, which often require timed tickets booked in advance, so check Lascaux IV and Rouffignac's own cave, which is visited by little electric train, before you commit to a schedule. May, June and September are the best months, when the light is warm and the roads are clear.
t.bajawa@-8.8,121.0:
Bajawa is a cool highland town in the middle of Flores, and the first thing the body notices is the temperature. You arrive from the sticky coast and climb to around eleven hundred metres, where evenings need a jacket and the air smells of woodsmoke and clove. The town sits in a bowl at the foot of Mount Inerie, a graceful volcano of over two thousand metres whose cone dominates the southern skyline, and its slopes are covered in coffee, vegetables and clove trees. This is the heartland of the Ngada people, whose villages of thatched houses, ancestral shrines and megalithic stones lie within an hour or two of the town.

The Trans-Flores Highway is the reason most people come by motorbike, and it is a great road, though not an easy one. It winds along the spine of the island through rainforest, rice terraces, volcanic craters and fishing villages, hair-pinning up and over ridge after ridge, and you rarely get more than a few hundred metres of straight tarmac. The surface can be broken by landslides, potholes and rain, trucks and buses come round blind corners well over the middle line, and the pace is rarely more than forty kilometres an hour, so a day's progress is shorter than the map suggests. Ride in daylight, as dusk comes fast and the roads are unlit, and expect afternoon rain, especially from November to March.

Bajawa itself is a real town, with petrol stations, markets, small hotels and warungs where you can get rice, grilled chicken and strong local coffee. Flores arabica is well regarded, and the beans are grown at just this kind of altitude. Fill up in town before heading east or west, because the long stretches between villages have only roadside bottles of petrol on sale from small stalls, which are best used only in emergency.

Close by lie traditional villages such as Bena and Luba, where rows of houses face a central yard of stones, with carved poles known as ngadhu and little thatched shrines called bhaga standing for male and female ancestors. They are lived-in places, not museums, so ask before photographing people and expect a small donation to be requested at the entrance. Portuguese traders and Dominican priests left a Catholic imprint, and you will see churches, crosses and rosaries in a country that is mostly Muslim.

Hot springs near Soa and the black-sand beaches of the south coast give good reasons to stay a night or two.
t.moret sur loing@48.4,2.8:
Moret-sur-Loing is what an impressionist painter would have ordered if asked for a small medieval town. It sits on a quiet bend of the river Loing, where an old stone bridge with a mill arches over the water, and the whole composition, with a church tower, reflections and drifting willow, is the one that Alfred Sisley painted again and again after settling here in the 1880s. He is buried in the local cemetery. The town was fortified in the Middle Ages, and two great gates, the Porte de Samois and the Porte de Bourgogne, still stand at the ends of the main street, which runs between them past old houses and tiny courtyards.

It also has a sweet claim to fame. Moret's sugar of the Sisters, a hard, golden barley sugar sold in little twisted sticks, was invented by nuns here in the seventeenth century, and you can still buy it in the town, in tins, with an old-fashioned label. A few hundred metres away at Saint-Mammès, the Loing meets the Seine, and barges laden with grain, sand and containers pass through the locks, so the water stop there is full of working boats rather than pleasure craft.

The surrounding countryside is particularly pleasing. Moret sits on the edge of the Forest of Fontainebleau, a huge royal hunting forest of oak and beech with sandstone boulders scattered through it, and the roads in and out are shady, with gentle bends and not much traffic during the week. The surface is generally good, though forestry lorries and cyclists share the lanes, and weekends are busier. Early morning, with mist on the river, is the best time. In spring the woods are fresh and green, and in autumn they turn copper.

For practicalities, a town with a few thousand inhabitants has bakeries, a supermarket and a couple of cafes beside the river, and the neighbouring Veneux-les-Sablons has fuel and bigger shops. There is a public tap and benches near the bridge, which makes it a convenient water stop. It is also a useful half-day escape from Paris, easily combined with a loop through the forest and the castle at Fontainebleau.
t.paris ile de france escapes@49.5,2.3:
The area is chalk plateau and river valley, with big fields of wheat and sugar beet on the heights and woods and meadows along the water. It lies about eighty kilometres north of Paris, and for people from the capital it is a quiet, flat place to ride out to for lunch.

The cathedral of Saint-Pierre in Beauvais is one of the strangest in France. The medieval builders wanted to make the tallest Gothic choir in the world, and reached almost forty-eight metres in the thirteenth century, but part of it collapsed in 1284 and had to be rebuilt. In 1573 the tall central tower fell as well, and the nave was never finished. The result is a soaring, lopsided building that is still astonishing from the outside, with an astronomical clock inside that is a marvel of nineteenth-century engineering. The town also has a tapestry manufactory, founded in the seventeenth century, that still produces work for the state.

Beauvais has lakes and the Thérain has some quiet stretches, but bathing places in this part of the Oise are limited, so ask locally. Fuel and supermarkets are easy to find in Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, about eleven kilometres away, and in Beauvais itself, with plenty of choice. Bresles is small and quiet, and has a few shops.

The riding is relaxed, with long straight roads and gentle bends, though the plateau can be windy and the farm traffic heavy at harvest. In autumn, mist fills the valleys and the sugar beet lorries leave mud on the road. A spring ride, with yellow rapeseed fields under a blue sky, is lovely, and so is a calm September morning. It is not a place for adrenaline, more a pleasant day with a good lunch and a church or two.
t.milly la foret@48.4,2.5:
Milly-la-Forêt is a small town of just under five thousand people tucked at the western edge of the Fontainebleau sandstone country, at about seventy-five metres above the sea. The town's name tells you what it is: a settlement in a clearing of old forest, with the Gâtinais regional park around it. Its centre is built around a large wooden market hall dating back to the fifteenth century, with a vast timbered roof held on massive oak posts, and in the shade of this structure traders still sell vegetables and cheese. It is one of the finest surviving halles in the Île-de-France, and few visitors know it.

Milly has a long association with herbs. For centuries the surrounding sandy soils have been used to grow medicinal and aromatic plants, the so-called simples, and a fragrant landscape of mint, lavender and chamomile fields is part of the area's identity. The little chapel of Saint-Blaise-des-Simples, a mile or so from the centre, was decorated inside by the poet and artist Jean Cocteau in the early 1960s, and he is buried in the grounds. If you step inside you find delicate line drawings of herbs and flowers and a quiet that feels out of step with the busy world.

On the bike, Milly is a good place to wake up the day. The roads out of the town head into pine and oak forest, with the soft smell of resin on warm days and the odd grey boulder poking out of the heather. Tarmac is mostly smooth, bends are long and gentle, and traffic is light on weekdays but picks up on weekends, when climbers and walkers head for the forest. Not far away in the woods stands the Cyclop, a giant mirrored sculpture by Jean Tinguely and friends, which will make you think you have lost your mind if you come across it by accident.

For coffee and a croissant, the cafés on the market square are the natural choice, and the bakeries around it open early. Fuel is available in the town, so it makes a good place to fill up before going on. Take a seat under the old roof timbers, order a coffee, and look up. It is the kind of ceiling that reminds you how much skill went into everyday buildings before anyone worried about speed.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@46.4,4.8:
You are in the Mâconnais, the southern end of Burgundy, where chardonnay vines cover the limestone hills and the villages are built of honey-coloured stone. Hurigny, La Roche-Vineuse and Sancé are small places within a few kilometres of each other, each with a church and a bakery, and Charnay-lès-Mâcon, with about seven thousand people, offers fuel and a supermarket. Mâcon itself lies a short way to the east on the Saône. The label calls this a swim stop, which is optimistic, but the countryside is lovely for a quiet pause.

The great landmark of the district is the Rock of Solutré, a limestone crag topping out at nearly five hundred metres above sea level that rises abruptly from the vineyards a few kilometres to the south-west, with its neighbour the Rock of Vergisson. At Solutré, archaeologists found a huge prehistoric site where hunters, tens of thousands of years ago, are thought to have driven wild horses over the cliff, and the bones of thousands of animals have been found at the base. The rock gives its name to a whole prehistoric culture, the Solutrean, and is among the best known sites of the Stone Age in Europe. A walk to the top takes about half an hour and offers a vast view.

North-west of here, about twenty-five kilometres off, lies Cluny, where in the Middle Ages the greatest monastery in Christendom stood. Its abbey was the head of a network of over a thousand monasteries across Europe, and its church was the largest in the world until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt. Only fragments remain, but they are impressive. The wines of the Mâconnais, especially Pouilly-Fuissé and Saint-Véran, are the white wines that pair so well with the local goat's cheeses, which come in small cylinders and are sold in every market.

The roads here are made for gentle touring, with rolling hills, vineyard lanes and farm tracks, and the surface is generally good. In September and October the harvest brings tractors and lorries, but also a lovely atmosphere. Spring and autumn are best.
t.fontainebleau forest road@48.4,2.7:
Fontainebleau is a small town that holds a very big place in French history, and the forest around it is one of the finest woods in Europe. The château was a royal residence for eight centuries, from medieval kings to Napoleon III, and each ruler added something, so that the building is a glorious jumble of styles. It was here, in the courtyard known as the Cour des Adieux, that Napoleon said goodbye to his guard in April 1814 before leaving for exile on Elba. The town of nearly twenty thousand people sits at about ninety metres above the sea, and it has every service, including several fuel stations.

The forest covers some twenty-five thousand hectares, and its sandstone boulders, heathland and tall trees make it unlike any other woodland near Paris. The rocks are the remains of ancient dunes, and some of them are the size of houses. In the nineteenth century, painters of the Barbizon school came to work here, leaving the studios of Paris to paint the trees and light directly, and their work helped lead to Impressionism. Today climbers come from around the world to scale the boulders, in a sport that was practised here long before it had a name, and the climbing area is known simply as Bleau.

The forest roads are a joy to ride. They run through beech and oak, with long gentle bends and flickering light, and the tarmac is usually in good shape. However, the speed limit is low, and police and cameras are active, so stay within it. Wild boar and deer cross the road, especially at dawn and dusk, and cyclists and walkers are everywhere on sunny weekends. On wet days, the leaves and pine needles make corners treacherous, so take care.

Spend a little time in the town if you can. The streets around the château have cafés and restaurants, and pastry shops where a slice of something sweet makes a fair reward. A walk in the palace gardens, with their carp pond and formal parterres, is a gentle way to rest between rides.
t.anse@45.9,4.7:
Anse is a small town of just over five thousand people on the Saône, at the point where the little river Azergues joins it, and it is the gateway to the Pierres Dorées, the Golden Stone country of the southern Beaujolais. The villages of this district are built of a soft, honey-coloured limestone that glows in the evening light, and the vineyards that cover the hills produce the lighter Beaujolais wines. As a fuel gate and start and finish of the ride, Anse is a convenient place, with fuel stations, a supermarket, bakeries and cafés, and it is easy to reach from Lyon, about twenty-five kilometres to the south.

The town has a long past. In Roman times it was a staging post called Asa Paulini on the road from Lyon to the north, and its position on the Saône made it a trading centre in the Middle Ages. The Château des Tours, on the edge of town, dates from the thirteenth century and was a residence of the archbishops of Lyon, who held much of the surrounding land. It is a solid fortified building with towers and a moat, and today it hosts events and exhibitions.

Leaving Anse, the road quickly climbs into the hills, with vineyards on the slopes and villages perched on ridges. The bends are gentle to medium, the surface is mostly good, and the views open across the Saône valley to the Dombes plateau and, on a clear day, the Alps. This is a classic day-trip landscape for Lyonnais riders, which means that weekends, especially sunny ones, can be busy, and cyclists share the roads. A weekday ride is calmer.

For a final or first meal, the local restaurants serve the food of Lyon and the Beaujolais, with sausages, andouillette, cervelle de canut, a herb and cream cheese spread, and the local wine, light and fruity and best served slightly cool. Fill the tank before the climb, because the hill villages have few stations, and enjoy a cup of coffee on the terrace before setting off.
t.mantes la jolie@49.0,1.7:
Mantes-la-Jolie carries its pretty name with a straight face, though the town of forty-four thousand is mostly practical rather than pretty, a Seine-side workhorse about fifty kilometres downstream from Paris. Tradition says Henri IV gave it the nickname, and the one thing that truly justifies it is the collegiate church of Notre-Dame, a Gothic building of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries whose façade and proportions echo the cathedral in Paris so closely that architects call it a rehearsal for it. Walk in and the light through the nave is worth five minutes even if you are in leathers.

For a rider, Mantes is the natural place to gather yourself at either end of a day. Fuel is easy, since a town this size has stations all around the ring roads, as well as supermarkets, bakeries and a station with trains to Paris Saint-Lazare if you need to bail out. Across the river lies Limay, with an old humpbacked bridge and a church on the slope, and the cluster of Mantes-la-Ville beside it. The two bridges over the Seine are bottlenecks at rush hour, so a finish here at six in the evening can cost you twenty minutes in a queue.

What makes the area good for riding is what lies on either side. North of the river the Vexin plateau rolls away in wheat and rapeseed, cut by small valleys and strung with villages of pale limestone, while downstream the Seine swings through long loops under white chalk cliffs. The roads that drop to the water tend to be narrow, with blind bends and walls, and they are at their best early on a weekday when the river mist has not yet lifted. Surface quality is generally fine, though farm traffic leaves mud on the corners at harvest and in wet weather.

If you have time at the end of the ride, sit by the Seine and watch the barges. Commercial traffic still moves grain, sand and containers along this stretch, and the slow rhythm of the water is a good way to let the engine cool and the day settle. The cobbled lanes of the old centre are worth a slow walk, with the bike parked near the church.
t.auvers sur oise@49.1,2.2:
Few villages have as much weight on their shoulders as Auvers-sur-Oise. Vincent van Gogh came here in May 1890, lodged in a small room above an inn, and in the seventy days he stayed painted around seventy canvases, among them the church, the wheat fields and the town hall bedecked with flags, before he died of a gunshot wound in July. He and his brother Theo lie side by side in the little cemetery above the fields, under a blanket of ivy. The room he rented at the Auberge Ravoux is preserved almost bare, and it is more moving for being so small.

He was not alone in loving this valley. Daubigny settled here before him and painted from a floating studio on the Oise, and Pissarro, Cézanne and Corot all worked in and around the village. At roughly seventy metres above sea level, the Oise here runs wide and slow between poplars, with low chalk hills behind, and you can understand why painters liked the light. The village has about seven thousand people, enough for a couple of bakeries, restaurants and cafés, which in season fill with day trippers who come to follow the painter's footsteps.

For a rider it is a food stop, and a good one if you arrive before the coach parties or after they leave. The roads in are pleasant, running along the river and climbing a short way to the plateau, with bends that call for attention rather than speed. Traffic can be heavy at weekends in summer, with cars searching for parking, and the lanes around the church are narrow and cobbled in places. Leave the bike on the edge and walk up.

Climb to the church and the cemetery behind it, and the wheat fields that Van Gogh painted stretch out beyond the wall. In June they are green and gold, and the crows that wheel above them are a quiet allusion to his last great painting. Take an hour if you can. The village sells postcards and prints, but the best souvenir is the view from the top of the hill, with the valley and a distant line of trees on a clear afternoon.
t.saint etienne@45.4,4.4:
Saint-Étienne wears its history in layers of coal, iron and cloth, and from the ring roads on the north side you can see how a city spread across a series of ridges, with the hills of the Pilat to the south and the mining basin of the Gier to the east. This is the second time the rides use it as a base, and it makes sense: with nearly a hundred and seventy-six thousand people, it has fuel on every approach, early bakeries and a tram that runs through the centre. The suburbs of Saint-Genest-Lerpt and Saint-Priest-en-Jarez, each with about six thousand people, climb the hills on the north side and make the quickest exit onto quieter roads.

The city's industrial story is still visible, not least in the preserved Puits Couriot, a former pithead with a tall headframe that now forms part of a mining museum. Nearby in Firminy, about ten kilometres west, stands the largest ensemble of buildings designed by Le Corbusier in Europe, including a housing block, a stadium and a church whose concrete cone rises against the sky. These are the places to see if you have a free hour or an interest in modern architecture, and they are no distance from the route.

As a ride start, Saint-Étienne offers an easy exit to the hills. In twenty minutes you can be climbing among beech and fir toward the Pilat, with the ridge road and its views opening out over the Rhône valley, and in an hour you can be in the high country, the air noticeably thinner and cooler. The same roads bring you back at the end of the day, usually in the lower light of evening, with the glow of the city below you and the smell of woodsmoke on the air.

Coming back in the dark, take care at the junctions near the ring road, where trams, buses and delivery vans share narrow streets. The city can be damp and foggy in autumn and winter, while in summer the heat in the valley is a pleasant contrast to the hills. A plate of local sausage with potatoes in a simple restaurant is the right way to end it.
t.etretat cliffs@49.7,0.2:
Étretat is a pebble beach with a view that has been painted, photographed and written about for nearly two centuries. On either side of the town, white chalk cliffs rise out of the Channel, and the sea has carved them into arches and a free-standing needle. The Falaise d'Aval, to the south, ends in a natural arch like an elephant's trunk dipping into the water, and the Aiguille stands off the shore as a spike of chalk, nearly a hundred metres tall. Monet painted these cliffs again and again, trying to catch the way the light changed the colour of the stone, and Courbet and Boudin did the same.

The place also belongs to fiction. The French writer Maurice Leblanc set an adventure of his gentleman thief Arsène Lupin in the hollow needle, and a small museum in the town plays with the legend. On the cliff top above the beach stands a memorial to the aviators Nungesser and Coli, who took off in 1927 in a plane called L'Oiseau Blanc to cross the Atlantic and were never seen again. It is a quiet, odd monument, and the view from it is worth the climb.

Riding here is mostly about the approach across the Pays de Caux, a high, flat plateau of wheat, flax and sugar beet, with farms hidden behind rows of beech trees and hamlets of brick and flint. The roads are straight in places and then dip suddenly toward the sea in short valleys. The surface is generally good, but the plateau is exposed, and wind can be strong, so crosswinds deserve respect. In summer, the town is crowded and parking is tight, so arrive early or late, and leave the bike where signs allow.

Fuel is not in the town itself in any quantity, and Fécamp, about thirteen kilometres to the north, is the nearest bigger town with stations, shops and a harbour. Fécamp is also known for its liqueur, Bénédictine, produced in a flamboyant palace, and for its history in cod fishing. Back in Étretat, cafés and crêperies line the streets near the beach, and fresh seafood is easy to find, though prices reflect the view.

Walk up the cliff path on the south side for the best look. The wind is strong, the gulls hang almost still in the air, and the sea is a pale green far below.
t.vezelay@47.5,3.7:
You see Vézelay from a long way off, a hill crowned with a basilica, with a village strung along the ridge below it. It is one of the great Romanesque churches of France, the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, begun in the early twelfth century to house relics said to be those of Mary Magdalene. Pilgrims came in thousands, and in 1146 Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade here, to a crowd so large that he spoke in the open air. It is also a starting point for one of the Camino de Santiago routes, so you often see walkers with scallop shells on their packs.

Inside the church, the nave is long and pale, and the capitals carry carved scenes, with devils, saints and the occasional joke. On the summer solstice, the sun shines through the windows and lays a line of light spots down the centre of the nave, a detail that draws crowds. The village around the basilica is a steep, cobbled street of galleries and stone houses, and the whole is a World Heritage site, listed in 1979.

The ride into Vézelay is a pleasure in itself. The valley of the Cure river is green and quiet, with the hills of the Morvan to the south, covered with oak and beech. The roads are narrow and full of gentle curves, and the traffic is light outside the summer weekends. Be careful with the last climb into the village, which is steep and cobbled, and find a place to park below the town, then walk up. The hill is a good spot for a sunset, when the light turns the stone honey-coloured.

Avallon, about twelve kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with petrol stations, supermarkets and a handful of restaurants. The area is known for Charolais beef, and for local cheeses and Burgundy wines such as Chablis, which is not far to the north. This is a ride for a slow, unhurried day, and the abbey of Fontenay, which this route links with, is one of the best-preserved Cistercian monasteries, founded by Bernard's followers in 1118.
t.coteaux d hautvillers@49.1,3.9:
On the hill above Hautvillers, the rows of vines run straight down to the Marne, and the colour changes with the season: bare, brown and clipped in winter, green in summer and red-gold in October. This is the cradle of Champagne, or at least one of its most famous corners. The Benedictine abbey of Saint-Pierre, in the village, was home to the monk Dom Pérignon in the late seventeenth century, who did not invent the sparkling wine, as legend says, but improved its making and blending, and whose name now belongs to a prestige cuvée.

The hillsides, houses and cellars of Champagne were added to the UNESCO list in 2015, and the landscape is a working one. Small growers' houses stand cheek by jowl with the great marques, and underneath the chalk, kilometres of cellars hold millions of bottles at a steady cool temperature. The village itself is full of wrought-iron signs, each one representing a grower or a cellar, and it is lovely to walk through.

Riding here is gentle and rewarding. The roads wind between the vines, up and down the slope, with views over the Marne valley and the forested ridge of the Montagne de Reims behind. The surface is generally good, but lorries and tractors are common at harvest time in September, and mud on the road is a hazard. Early morning is peaceful, with mist in the valley and the light slanting through the vines.

The nearest places for fuel, food and a bed are Épernay, a few minutes away, whose Avenue de Champagne is lined with grand houses of the main producers, and the villages of Dizy and Mardeuil. Visits to the cellars often require booking, and since you are on a bike, tastings should be taken with restraint, spitting if you must. Buy a bottle for later and be careful to pack it well. From here the route goes south-west to Fontainebleau, across the plains of Brie, which are fast and flat.
t.couvent sainte marie de la tourette@45.8:
A concrete box on stilts, set on a slope among trees, is not what you expect from a Dominican priory. Le Corbusier designed the convent of La Tourette in the late 1950s for the friars of the order, and it was completed in 1960, with the young composer and architect Iannis Xenakis working on its rhythmic window walls. The church is a bare cube of rough concrete, lit by a few carefully placed openings, and the cells for the friars are small and very quiet, each with a balcony. It is a place where the building is the sermon, and it was added to the UNESCO list in 2016.

It stands in the hills of the Monts du Lyonnais, about twenty-five kilometres from Lyon, near the village of Éveux and the old mining hamlets of Sourcieux-les-Mines and Sain-Bel. The countryside is soft and green, with orchards, pastures and small forests, and the roads are narrow and winding, with farm traffic and cyclists on fine days. Surfaces are generally good, with the odd patch of rough tarmac, and the corners are the kind that reward a relaxed pace.

Visits are usually by guided tour, and the community also takes guests who wish to stay, so check opening times before you ride up, because the friars' schedule is not flexible. The approach is steep and the car park is small. Dress quietly, switch off your phone and keep your voice low inside, since there is a living community here, and silence is part of the building.

The nearest places with fuel and a decent meal are Sain-Bel and the larger town of L'Arbresle, a few minutes down the valley, while Lyon has everything and a rich food culture, with its famous bouchons serving andouillette, quenelles and pink pralines. This ride links Le Corbusier's earlier works, the Maison de la Culture at Firminy, with the Cistercian abbey of Hautecombe on Lac du Bourget, so it is a day for architecture lovers, with a mix of concrete and stone, and a lot of good road in between.
t.chartres cathedral@48.4,1.5:
You see Chartres from miles away across the wheat. The Beauce is a vast, flat plain, one of the great granaries of France, and the cathedral rises out of it with two mismatched spires, like a ship on a green sea. After a fire in 1194 destroyed most of the earlier church, the townspeople rebuilt it in about thirty years, a remarkable pace for the time, and as a result the building has a unity that few Gothic cathedrals can claim. It was one of the first sites to be added to the UNESCO list, in 1979.

What really matters here is the glass. More than a hundred and fifty windows from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries survive, and the deep blue that glows in them, known as Chartres blue, has never been exactly matched. On a sunny morning, the nave fills with coloured light that moves slowly across the floor. Set into the floor of the nave is a stone labyrinth about thirteen metres across, which pilgrims once followed on their knees, and which is usually uncovered on Fridays during the warmer months.

The approach is pleasant riding. The roads across the Beauce are straight, quick and exposed to wind, with fields stretching to the horizon, and the lanes in the river valley of the Eure are gentler and greener. The old town below the cathedral is a tangle of steep, cobbled streets and half-timbered houses, best walked rather than ridden. Park outside the centre, where there are places for bikes, and go up on foot.

Chartres has about forty-four thousand people, so you will find fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafes. The local speciality is the pâté de Chartres, a game pie, and the town has a long tradition of baking. The ride from here continues across the Gâtinais to Fontainebleau, a pleasant run through forest and farmland, and the whole day moves from a cathedral to a royal palace, a good lesson in French ambition. Go early and have the nave almost to yourself.
t.paris@48.9,2.4:
Paris is a good place to start a ride and a bad place to ride in. The Périphérique, the ring road, carries more than a million vehicles a day, scooters thread through the lanes with great confidence, and cobbles, tram rails and painted crossings are slippery in the wet. The city also operates a low-emission zone, so check the rules and get the right sticker for your bike before you arrive. If you can, leave the bike at the hotel, ride the metro and save the machine for the morning when you head out.

Once you are out, the east side of the city opens onto the plains of Brie, with big skies, fields of wheat and rapeseed, and quiet small roads through villages of pale stone. This day's ride leads to Provins, about ninety kilometres away, a medieval town that was once one of the great trading centres of the Champagne fairs. Its upper town still has ramparts, a great tower called the Caesar Tower, and cellars that run under the streets. Provins also grows roses, and the old recipe for rose petal jam is still made.

Paris itself, of course, is full of history. The Seine runs through the middle in a wide curve, with Notre-Dame on its island, the Louvre along the right bank and the Eiffel Tower built for the exhibition of 1889. The city has had its present form since the nineteenth century, when Baron Haussmann cut the wide boulevards through the medieval maze. If you only have an evening, go for a slow walk along the quays at dusk, when the lights come on and the bouquinistes are shutting up their green boxes.

Fuel is plentiful, though there are fewer stations in the centre than in the suburbs, so fill up on the outskirts before you head out. Breakfast on the way out of town in a corner café, with a coffee and a croissant at the bar, is the proper thing, and by the time you reach the Brie, with cheese in its fields, the capital will have faded in the mirrors.
t.laugerie basse@45.0,1.0:
In the nineteenth century, a gentlemanly sort of archaeology took place in the Vézère valley. Édouard Lartet, a French geologist, and Henry Christy, an English banker and ethnologist, came to the cliffs near Les Eyzies in the 1860s and began digging in the rock shelters at the foot of the cliff, the Laugerie sites. They found worked flint and bone, and above all engraved objects: a reindeer carved on an antler, a fish, and a small figure of a naked woman that the finders, with Victorian delicacy, called the Vénus impudique, the immodest Venus. These finds helped to show that people had lived here alongside reindeer, in a cold climate, many thousands of years ago.

Laugerie-Basse is the lower shelter, a long overhang beneath a limestone cliff just beside the river, in the Magdalenian period, about fifteen thousand years ago. The cliff leans out so far that you can imagine the camp: hearths, hide tents, tools and the long dark winter. The reindeer have long gone, but the valley still has a particular quality of light, with the pale rock, the green river and a thin mist in the morning.

The road along the Vézère here is one of the best in the Périgord for an unhurried ride. It follows the river with the cliff on one side, passing farms, walnut trees and the occasional château. In summer, caravans and bicycles slow the pace, so go early or on a weekday. The surface is good and the bends are easy, and on a cool morning the smell of woodsmoke and wet leaves hangs in the valley.

Le Bugue, a few kilometres away, has fuel, and Les Eyzies has food and a few hotels. Try the local walnut oil, cheese and a glass of Bergerac, and leave room for a plate of confit de canard. The ride from here goes west toward the Atlantic coast and the great Vauban fortress at Blaye, on the Gironde, and then the Médoc, so the day trades prehistory for seventeenth-century military engineering, and the vineyards are never far.
t.mont ventoux@45.7,4.4:
The plateau of the Monts du Lyonnais, west of Lyon, is the closest thing the city has to a country backyard, and this spot, near Haute-Rivoire, Saint-Laurent-de-Chamousset and Sainte-Foy-l'Argentière, lies in the middle of it. It is a landscape of rolling pastures, orchards and woodland at around six or seven hundred metres, with small farms, stone villages and long views, and on the clearest winter days the Alps show as a pale line on the eastern horizon. To the west the land drops toward the plain of the Forez and the Loire, with Feurs, a market town of about eight thousand people, in the middle distance.

Ventoux is a very long way from here, and the label merely reflects the ride that ends in this area. What the district offers instead is quiet. The name Sainte-Foy-l'Argentière recalls the silver mines that were worked in the Middle Ages in this part of the hills, a reminder of an industrial past that has left little visible trace. Saint-Laurent-de-Chamousset is a small market town on a crossroads, with a handful of shops, and Haute-Rivoire is a village with a church and a main square.

The roads are good for relaxed riding. They roll across the plateau in a series of gentle bends, past fields of cattle and orchards of apples and cherries, with the occasional steep descent into a stream valley. Traffic is light, apart from the odd tractor, and the surface is generally decent, though patched. In winter the plateau can see snow and ice, with fog in the hollows, and the roads are not always gritted. Spring brings blossom, and in summer the hay is cut and the air is thick with the smell of grass. A good time for a ride is a late September afternoon, with the light low and golden.

Fuel is available in Saint-Laurent-de-Chamousset and other larger villages, but stations are fewer than in the suburbs, so do not let the tank fall too low. Bakeries and small cafes open in the morning, and many close in the middle of the day, for the French lunch. The local cheese, often a small goat's cheese, goes well with the local bread. Take a moment at one of the high points to look east toward the city and west to the distant plain, and consider that you are riding across a ridge between two great river systems.
t.seine loops@49.0,2.6:
East of Paris the land flattens into the Brie plateau's margin, and the towns here run together in a belt of low houses, retail parks and market gardens. Mitry-Mory is the nearest place of any size, with about 18,500 people, and Claye-Souilly and Villeparisis lie a little further along. It is not scenic in a postcard sense, yet it has a quiet logic: this is where Paris has always fed itself, and farmland still survives between the suburbs.

The key to the landscape is water. The Canal de l'Ourcq runs through Claye-Souilly, dug at Napoleon's order in the early nineteenth century to bring fresh water into the capital, and its towpath is now a popular bike route. A little further the Marne winds toward Meaux, home of the famous Brie cheese. The Seine Loops ride that ends here wanders through river bends and wooded hills further west, so this place is a return, a slightly melancholy closing of the circle.

Riding in from the north-east you are rarely far from aircraft. The flight paths into Roissy-Charles-de-Gaulle run overhead, and on a clear day the jets seem to descend directly toward your visor. The roads are mostly flat and fast, with long straights between roundabouts and the occasional unexpected tight bend where a road follows an old field boundary. Surfaces are generally fine, though the heavy lorries serving the logistics depots take their toll on the verges, and rush hour on the main routes into the city is something to avoid.

Fuel is straightforward, and a supermarket at the edge of town will sell you a sandwich and a bottle of water for the last stretch. If you have time, the Parc de Vaujours and the old fort on the ridge give you a glimpse of the green belt that surrounds the capital. It is not the part of France that shows up in glossy brochures, but it is real, and it is a fine place to finish: unfussy, unhurried, and a short hop from your own front door.
t.paris south west@48.8,2.2:
Vélizy-Villacoublay sits on a plateau south-west of Paris, 80 metres above sea level, and from the saddle it feels like a place that exists to be left. It is a business and aeronautics town: the military airfield at Villacoublay lies on one side, aircraft makers have their offices here, and a vast shopping centre brings visitors from a wide area. Over 21,000 people live in it, which means fuel, coffee and food are immediate, and no reason to carry more than a sandwich.

What matters is the direction you go. Head south-west and the road takes you quickly to Versailles, the royal forests and the green valleys beyond. The Rambouillet forest, a great stretch of oak and beech that Louis XIV hunted in and that presidents still use as a retreat, lies half an hour away, with long, quiet roads where the corners come in tidy sequence. A little east the Chevreuse valley opens, a regional natural park since the 1980s, with the ruins of the Port-Royal abbey and the château of Breteuil among its attractions, and a comfortable web of small lanes between villages.

Getting out is the challenge. The N118 and A86 block up on weekday mornings and Friday evenings, and the bridges and junctions near Vélizy can hold you for twenty minutes if you misjudge the hour. Leave before seven or after nine and the exit is easy. The plateau is windy, and early in the day you may find the grass beside the roads crusted with frost well into spring. When the sun comes up behind the planes at Villacoublay the light on the runway is lovely.

On the way back, the Forêt de Meudon and the road past the airfield offer a quieter alternative to the main routes. The ride this place begins and ends is a double loop through Rambouillet and Chevreuse, so you are likely to see this gate twice in a day: once at dawn with a full tank, once at dusk with a tired smile.
t.paris south@48.8,2.4:
There is a rose in L'Haÿ-les-Roses, and a very particular one. In the late nineteenth century a Parisian businessman named Jules Gravereaux planted a rose garden here, with thousands of varieties, and it became a world reference collection. The Roseraie du Val-de-Marne, as it is now called, still draws visitors in May and June, and the name of the town was changed to honour it. So the first thing a rider sees when leaving Paris by the southern gate may be a hedge of petals.

Otherwise the surroundings are humdrum. Near 30,000 people live here, among apartment blocks, ring roads and the buzz of nearby Orly airport, whose planes pass low overhead. The famous Rungis wholesale market, which feeds Paris and much of the region, lies just beyond, and from three or four in the morning the roads around it fill with lorries. Avoid the area at that hour if you can.

The two rides that start and end here point in opposite directions: one heads south-west toward the plains of Chartres, the Perche hills and a return along quiet lanes, the other drifts down into the Gâtinais, a region of sandy forest, pale fields and small villages south of Paris. Both take you out of the sprawl quickly. The N20 and the A6 are the obvious roads, but they are slow at rush hour, so take D-roads through the villages of the Bièvre valley and the Essonne countryside, where the traffic eases and the corners start to appear.

Fuel is no problem here, with stations all around, and the many bakeries open early. Park the bike securely, as theft is a real worry in dense suburbs, and plan to leave before the morning traffic gathers. If you pass by in early summer, a quick detour to the rose garden is worth it, even in a leather jacket, and its scent on a warm evening will linger longer than any petrol fumes.
t.versailles@48.8,2.1:
Versailles is a place that rewards a rider who turns up early. The great château that Louis XIV built, and where French kings lived until 1789, sits at the end of three wide avenues whose scale was designed to impress, and the gilded gates and cobbled courtyard are unforgettable at dawn, before the coaches arrive. At 132 metres above sea level the town lies on a plateau west of Paris, and it makes an elegant starting point for a ride into the countryside.

The history is overwhelming, and well known. The Hall of Mirrors is where the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 and where the treaty that ended the First World War was signed in 1919. The gardens that André Le Nôtre laid out stretch away with canals, fountains and avenues, and the Grand Canal is a cross of water long enough that the king sailed gondolas on it. The château itself is closed on Mondays, which is worth remembering, but the town around it, with its market halls and its cathedral of Saint-Louis, is lively every day.

The riding begins just beyond. With 85,000 people in the town, fuel is simple, and from the south side the roads lead into the forest of Satory and then down into the Chevreuse valley, a green fold of small roads between wooded slopes. The Vallée de l'Eure ride heads south-west into more open farmland, with long fast bends and a distant skyline of church spires. Early in the morning, with mist in the valleys, both routes feel like secrets that the city has forgotten to guard.

Try not to arrive by the main avenue at midday on a weekend, because tour buses and slow-walking crowds make it impossible. The alternative is to park in a side street and walk. Stop at the market at Notre-Dame for fresh bread and cheese, and let the old royal town show its quieter side. A day that begins at these gates has a great deal to live up to, and the countryside tends to deliver.
t.oingt golden village@45.9,4.6:
Oingt looks as though someone has poured honey over a hill. The village stands at the heart of the Pierres Dorées, the Golden Stones country of southern Beaujolais, and its houses are built of a limestone coloured by iron into every shade from butter to rust. Steep cobbled lanes wind up toward a medieval tower and a church, and the whole place is on the list of France's most beautiful villages, a title that here feels earned rather than marketed.

It is also a very small place, and the nearest town with real services is Gleizé, just beside Villefranche-sur-Saône, around ten kilometres away. Theizé, a smaller twin among the vineyards, is closer. So arrive with a full tank, and plan lunch in advance on weekdays, when some of the village's few restaurants are shut. Parking lies outside the walls, and the lanes inside are for feet. Wear boots rather than slick soles, since the stones are smooth and often damp.

Oingt has a literary footnote. Marguerite d'Oingt, born in the village in the thirteenth century, became a Carthusian prioress and wrote some of the earliest known mystical texts in the Franco-Provençal language, a quiet voice from a world of stone and candlelight. From the old tower the view runs across vineyards and orchards toward the Monts du Lyonnais, and on a clear day the Alps hang pale on the eastern horizon.

The roads around the village are some of the nicest in the region. Narrow, winding and well maintained, they loop through gamay vines and cherry orchards, past farmhouses with golden walls and terracotta roofs, and the corners are tight enough to be fun without ever being savage. In spring the hillsides are pink and white with blossom, and in autumn they turn red and gold, the colours of the stone repeated in the leaves. Wine is the thing here: Beaujolais, of course, made from gamay, and often drunk young and a little cool, which suits a warm afternoon on a terrace. It is a good place to begin a day, or to end one with a glass.
t.vienne@45.5,4.9:
Vienne has been a city for two thousand years and it still shows it. On the east bank of the Rhône, about thirty kilometres south of Lyon, the Romans built a prosperous colony here, and the temple of Augustus and Livia still stands in the centre, as complete as when it was built, with its Corinthian columns facing a small square of cafés. Nearby a Roman theatre climbs the hillside, and every July it fills with music for a jazz festival that has become one of the best known in Europe.

For a rider, Vienne is a very practical stop. With over 32,000 people, it has fuel stations on the approaches and a good range of cafés and shops, and it is on the main route between Lyon and the south, so it is a natural place to refill and eat. Be aware that the one-way system in the centre is confusing, and that traffic backs up on the bridges across the Rhône. Park near the river and walk in.

Across the water, on the right bank, the steep terraces of Côte-Rôtie climb from the village of Ampuis, and the wines made from Syrah on those slopes are among the most celebrated in France. A little further south, Condrieu produces its fragrant white Viognier. Behind them, the Pilat massif rises in a long wooded ridge, which is one of the better riding areas in the region, with roads that twist up through chestnut woods to open crests. Vienne is the gateway.

There is a modest Roman pyramid standing alone in a field near the old circus, a curious monument whose purpose is still debated, and the cathedral of Saint-Maurice, a long Gothic building at the foot of the hill, is worth a look if you have the time. Evenings are lively in the centre, with restaurants serving Lyon-style food, and the Rhône at dusk is a pleasant place to unwind.
t.cave thomas underground@49.1,3.9:
The Marne valley at Dizy is where the vineyard slopes begin. A few kilometres from Épernay, this small village of nearly 2,000 people lies at the foot of the hillside, and above it the rows of vines climb in neat stripes to the edge of the forest. In autumn, harvest brings tractors, trailers and pickers, and the lanes are sticky with grape juice and splashed with the dark red of crushed fruit. It is a busy time, and also the best, if you can bear the delays.

Beneath the vines lies something more remarkable still. The chalk of Champagne is soft enough to dig, and over the centuries growers and merchants have carved galleries into it, kilometres upon kilometres of cellars where the bottles rest at a constant cool temperature for years. A wine cave like the one marked here is part of that web, a vaulted, damp tunnel of pale rock where the air smells of cold stone and a little of yeast. In 2015 the hillsides, houses and cellars of Champagne were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, and the cellars are a large part of the reason.

Many producers welcome visitors, though most prefer an appointment, particularly in the busy season, and tastings are typically small and unhurried. Motorcycles are comfortable enough on the road here, but remember that a tasting and a ride do not mix; spit, or hand the keys to someone else.

The riding along the foot of the slope is simple and attractive. The road runs between vines and orchards, with small curves and short climbs into the villages, and the views across the valley are wide. Wind can be strong on the exposed ridge above, and early frost in spring can threaten the buds. The light on the vines in September, when the leaves begin to turn, is one of the finest sights in France.
t.fort chabrol@49.1,3.9:
Fort Chabrol is a name that suggests rampart and cannon, though what you meet on the ground is the green valley of the Marne, a few minutes' ride from Épernay. The village of Mardeuil, with about 1,500 people, sits on the river's edge, with a canal and a railway running alongside it, and the pace is calm.

The Marne runs here between low, wooded slopes, with poplars and willows along the banks and a towpath where cyclists and fishermen share the space. On the southern side, the Côte des Blancs rises, a hillside planted almost entirely with Chardonnay, while north of the river the slopes lead up to Hautvillers and the Montagne de Reims. The fields in between grow wheat and beet, and in spring they are a pure bright green.

For the rider, the roads here are gentle. Small, winding lanes follow the valley, with brief climbs among the vines and quick drops into the villages, and the surfaces are generally good. At harvest the tractors can slow you to a crawl, and in winter fog hangs in the valley until noon. Épernay is a couple of kilometres away, with more than 27,000 people, so there is no shortage of fuel stations, and the town centre offers cafés, bakeries and brasseries.

If you have the time, walk along the river and look at the water. In the days of the Roman road, this valley was a thoroughfare, and the bridges and fords have been fought over since the Middle Ages. Armies have marched through here more than once. Today the only invaders are tourists carrying bottles, and they are mostly well mannered. The village is a good place to park the bike and think about what to eat.
t.champagne hillsides@49.1,3.9:
Hautvillers is the village that Champagne drinkers should visit once. On the hillside north of the Marne, above the little towns of Dizy and Cumières, it keeps its abbey church, where Dom Pérignon, a Benedictine monk who looked after the abbey's cellars and vineyards in the late seventeenth century, is buried. The legend that he invented champagne is only a legend, as he spent much of his energy trying to stop the wine from fizzing, but he did a great deal for blending and viticulture, and the name now belongs to a famous bottle.

The slopes of Champagne are the part of the world that this stop is really about. They are now a World Heritage landscape, with villages, wineries and cellars all part of the listing, and the view from the vineyards above Hautvillers is one of the best in the region, with the Marne curling below and Épernay laid out on the far bank. The village itself has wrought-iron signs hanging above its shopfronts, each one showing a grower's craft, and the streets are quiet and neat.

Épernay, four kilometres away with more than 27,000 people, is the place for petrol and supplies. Hautvillers has a few cafés, but little else, and in high season its narrow lanes can be crammed with coaches. Try to arrive in the morning, park outside the centre, and walk. The roads that climb to the village are steep and tight, with hairpins through the vines, and they are some of the most enjoyable riding in the Marne, as long as you take them gently and expect the odd tractor.

The best time is early autumn, when the grapes are ripe and the vines turn yellow and red, but spring has its charms too, with white blossom and fresh grass. In winter, the hillside is bare and the village feels deserted. Wherever you come from, a quiet hour here, with the vines below and a coffee in hand, makes a good break from the saddle.
t.avenue de champagne@49.0,4.0:
Avenue de Champagne is the grand boulevard of Épernay, and its fame is out of all proportion to its length. Along it stand the great champagne houses, Moët & Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger and others, in mansions built with the profits of the nineteenth century, with wrought-iron gates, tall windows and manicured lawns. Napoleon was a friend of the Moët family, and the story goes that he stopped here on his way to war. Whatever the truth, the street has the air of a place where money has always been well spent.

What you cannot see is more impressive. Under the pavements run cellars carved into chalk, a labyrinth of galleries that reaches many kilometres in total, and the avenue is, in a sense, the roof of an enormous cold, dark warehouse where millions of bottles lie waiting. It is no accident that the area is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars.

Épernay, with more than 27,000 people, is a perfectly sensible place to stop. Fuel is easy at the edge of town, and the centre has bakeries, brasseries and shops, though the quality of food in this town is in keeping with the price of the wine. If you want a tour, book ahead, because the major houses fill up quickly, especially at weekends and in autumn. Remember, too, that tasting and riding are a poor pair. Choose a designated driver, or take the train back.

On the bike, the avenue itself is slow and flat, lined with plane trees and parked cars, with strict speed limits and cameras. It is a place for strolling more than racing. The real riding lies beyond the town, where the roads wind up through the vines to Hautvillers and the Montagne de Reims. Come back in the evening, when the lamps come on along the avenue and the mansions glow, and you will see why the town takes such pride in itself.
t.caves de l avenue de champagne undergrou:
The caves under Épernay are older than most visitors imagine. Long before anyone thought of sparkling wine, the chalk here had been quarried for building stone, and the old quarries, known as crayères, were later turned to storage. Merchants of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries enlarged them into whole networks of galleries, and the cellars along the avenue still hold the wine at a steady, cool temperature of about ten degrees, whatever the weather above. In summer the contrast is dramatic, and visitors step out after a tour blinking in the heat, with their teeth chattering.

The thing to know is that the temperature drop is real: even on a warm day, a jacket is welcome below ground. Tours are usually guided and typically last about an hour, with a tasting at the end, and booking ahead is wise in high season. Some of the big houses run small trains through their galleries, a surprisingly cheerful way to see them. Nothing underground is suitable for bikes, of course, and you will need somewhere safe to park your machine and kit.

The town above, with its 27,000 people, is a plain working place with a long wine trade. There is fuel at the edge, a market hall in the centre, and a handful of decent places to eat. A Champagne lunch is a very particular pleasure, with fish, cheese and a glass of something dry, but it does not suit the afternoon ride. If you have to ride on, order a coffee, and take your time.

The UNESCO listing that includes the cellars recognises more than the wine. It recognises a whole way of life, from the growers' villages to the merchants' houses, and the infrastructure of cellars that made the trade possible. Standing in one of those cool galleries, with the rows of bottles stretching away into the dark, you understand how much patience the region has needed. It is a good place to slow down.
t.maison de la culture de firminy@45.4,4.3:
Firminy is a coal-and-steel town in the Loire valley that happens to hold the largest group of Le Corbusier buildings in Europe. The architect was invited here in the 1950s to plan a new neighbourhood, Firminy-Vert, for workers whose old houses were crumbling, and over the next decades several of his designs went up: a housing block, a stadium, a youth and culture centre and, finished long after his death, a great concrete church. The Maison de la Culture is the long, bold building with a sagging roof that looks as if it had been poured from a jug, and it is part of the UNESCO listing given to his work in 2016.

Firminy itself, with about 18,000 people, is a modest place, and the neighbouring city of Saint-Étienne is bigger, rougher and more interesting than its reputation. The whole valley was built on mining and metalworking, with slag heaps now grassed over and old pit-heads standing like monuments. The Gier and Ondaine valleys have been quietly reinventing themselves for decades, and the contrast between Le Corbusier's utopia and the humble brick terraces nearby tells a good deal about twentieth-century France.

For a rider, the pleasure lies in what surrounds it. To the east the Pilat massif rises in a long wooded ridge, with small twisting roads climbing from the valley to open crests. To the south and west the Velay hills spread out in a rolling plateau of pasture and basalt, where the roads are quiet and the views are wide. Fuel is plentiful in Firminy and Saint-Étienne, and the old centre has cafés and brasseries. The building is easy to find, with parking nearby, and the inside is usually open to visitors on set days, so check the schedule before you go.

Concrete is not everyone's idea of beauty, and the weather in the Loire valley is often grey. But on a clear day, with the shadows sharp and the sky blue behind the sloping roof, the structure has a clarity that stays with you. Stand a while on the terrace, then ride up into the hills.
t.caves cooperatives d hautvillers undergr:
Hautvillers has grown a number of cooperative cellars that suit the independent grower. Many of the families who farm the vineyards here own only a few hectares, too little to run a press house and a cellar of their own, so they join forces, pressing their grapes together and sharing the equipment. Cooperatives like this have kept village winemaking alive in Champagne, alongside the big houses, and their bottles are often good value.

Dizy, about two kilometres away, is the nearest village, with fewer than 2,000 people, and Épernay, four kilometres off, is the place for petrol and a proper meal. The area is part of the UNESCO listing for the hillsides, houses and cellars of Champagne, and the landscape of vines is its own monument. Nothing here is grand or showy. The buildings are plain, and the interest is in the working life of the vineyard.

September is the time to see it. The harvest brings pickers from all over France and beyond, who work in lines along the vines, filling baskets and crates by hand, as the law requires for Champagne. Trucks and tractors crowd the lanes, and the smell of pressed grapes drifts over the villages. If you ride through, take it slowly and give the vehicles space, since drivers are tired and the roads are narrow. At other times of year the vineyards are quiet, and the pruning of the vines in winter has its own stark beauty.

The roads that climb to Hautvillers are tight and steep, with hairpins through the vines, and the views at the top reach across the Marne to the hills opposite. In spring the grass between the rows is bright green, and in autumn the leaves turn red and gold. It is a comfortable place to end a ride, with a glass of something local, and a sense that the wine you are drinking was made by the family in the next house.
t.clermont ferrand@45.8,3.1:
Clermont-Ferrand is a city of black stone. Its cathedral, built of dark volcanic lava from nearby Volvic, rises over the old centre like a ship in a storm, and the Romanesque church of Notre-Dame-du-Port, one of the finest in the Auvergne, stands nearby, with a carved doorway and a warm, honey-coloured interior. The city's other great monument is rubber: the Michelin tyre company was founded here in the nineteenth century, and its headquarters and its small museum still shape the town. Blaise Pascal, the mathematician and philosopher, was born here in 1623.

What makes it a place for riders is the landscape just west of the city. The Chaîne des Puys is a line of dormant volcanoes, about eighty of them, which rise from the plateau in neat green cones, some with craters you can walk around, and the whole chain has been listed by UNESCO. The tallest of them, the Puy de Dôme, stands at 1,465 metres, and its summit is reached today by a cog railway or on foot rather than by road. The roads around its base are among the best in central France, with long sweeps, tight bends and views of cones in all directions.

Clermont-Ferrand has about 139,000 people, and fuel and food are easy to find. The centre is dense, with one-way streets, tram lines and cobbles, and it is best to park outside and walk. The weather can change quickly on the high ground, and a warm morning may turn cold and windy by noon, so carry a layer. Winters bring snow to the volcanoes, and some roads may be icy.

The food of the Auvergne is hearty, built on cheese, sausage, lentils and potatoes. Saint-Nectaire, Cantal and the blue Fourme d'Ambert are the classics, and a dish of aligot, mashed potato stretched with cheese until it hangs in ribbons, is a fine reward after a day on the volcanic roads.
t.alpe@45.6,4.6:
Saint-Martin-en-Haut and Saint-Didier-sous-Riverie lie in the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded, wooded hills about thirty kilometres west of Lyon, where the city's suburbs give way to orchards, cattle and small farms. It is gentle country, the sort of place where Lyonnais go for a Sunday drive, and for a rider, the roads are fun and quiet, with lots of small curves, short climbs and pretty views toward the Alps on clear days. The dot marks a point on the long ride home after a day in the high mountains.

The route has covered a lot of ground. Alpe d'Huez, in the Oisans, is one of the most famous climbs in cycling, with twenty-one numbered hairpins that rise about a thousand metres in thirteen kilometres, and the stage finish has become a place of pilgrimage for Tour de France fans, particularly the Dutch, who have a corner named after them. The road is wide and well surfaced, and on a motorcycle it is more fun than hard. The valley below, with its glaciers and high passes, includes the Col du Lautaret and the Galibier, two of the great Alpine crossings, which are closed in winter.

Mont Ventoux, in Provence, is another cycling legend. Its summit, at 1,912 metres, is a bare, white crown of limestone that looks like snow even in July, and the road up from Bédoin is long and exposed, with a strong wind called the mistral often blowing from the north. A memorial near the top marks the spot where the British cyclist Tom Simpson died in 1967 during the Tour. The view from the top, over the Rhône valley and the Alps, can stretch for a hundred kilometres.

By contrast, the Monts du Lyonnais are soft and green. The roads wander through villages built of golden stone, past cherry and apple orchards, and the local cuisine is simple and hearty, with sausages, cheese and fruit tarts. Traffic is light, but cyclists are common, especially at weekends.

Fuel is easy in Saint-Martin-en-Haut, with a station and a bakery, and larger supermarkets can be found in Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise. In the evening, the light over the hills is warm, and you can sometimes see the white line of Mont Blanc on the horizon, a last reminder of the day.
t.dombes lakes easy@45.9,4.9:
Saint-André-de-Corcy is a village on the southern edge of the Dombes, a flat plateau of clay and water north of Lyon that is unlike anywhere else in France. Over the centuries, monks and landowners dug a thousand or so shallow ponds, called étangs, across the clay to raise fish, and the whole landscape is a patchwork of water, reeds, meadows and little woods, with farmhouses built of brick and timber. The dot lies at the southern edge of this strange country, with Mionnay just beside it.

The ponds work on a long cycle. In the autumn or winter the farmers drain the water through a sluice, harvest the carp, tench and pike that have grown there for several years, and leave the bed dry for a season to grow oats or to rest. Then the pond is flooded again, and the cycle repeats. The result is a landscape that looks wild but is in fact tended by hand, and it is rich in wildlife. Herons, black-necked grebes, kingfishers and migrating waders find food here, and the Parc des Oiseaux at Villars-les-Dombes, a few kilometres north, has a large collection of birds from around the world.

For a rider, the Dombes are an easy day. The roads are flat and straight, running between ponds and woods, with long views and little traffic. They are best taken slowly, with a stop to watch the birds, and the light is lovely at dawn and dusk, when mist rises from the water. Sandy patches and fallen leaves can make the surface slippery in autumn. In summer, mosquitoes and heat make the afternoon less pleasant, and the high season is spring and early autumn.

The local cooking reflects the landscape. Carp, fried or in a stew, and frogs' legs are the classic dishes, and the village restaurants serve them with butter, garlic and parsley. Mionnay is known to food lovers as a place with a long tradition of excellent restaurants, and a table here is worth booking in advance.

Fuel is easy in Saint-André-de-Corcy, with stations on the main road and a small supermarket. Lyon is half an hour away.
t.provins@48.4,2.5:
Milly-la-Forêt lies south of Paris on the edge of the Gâtinais, a region of gentle hills, sandy soil and woods that has long been associated with herbs and healing plants. For centuries, the villages here grew medicinal herbs, called simples, such as chamomile, mint and verbena, and the tradition is still celebrated in the town's herb market and in a small conservatory of herbs. The village is quiet and handsome, with a medieval covered market hall of heavy timber that dates from the fifteenth century and still stands in the centre.

Milly has a surprising artistic connection. The writer and artist Jean Cocteau lived nearby and, in the 1950s, decorated the small chapel of Saint-Blaise-des-Simples, a tiny twelfth-century building, with delicate drawings of plants and figures in his light, clear line. He is buried there, under a plain stone, and the chapel is a quiet, strange and lovely place, open to visitors in season. The nearby Moigny-sur-École is a village of old stone houses beside a small river, with a calm, forgotten feel.

The ride heads east to Provins, a medieval town in the Brie, where merchants once gathered for the great fairs of Champagne.
