Its fortified upper town, with Caesar's Tower, a twelfth-century keep, and its ramparts, remain remarkably intact, and a tour of the underground tunnels gives a sense of the town's past. The road there crosses open farmland, with big skies and long straight stretches, before climbing to the old town on its hill.

The riding near Milly is gentle, with narrow roads between wheat fields and woods, and the occasional sandstone boulder beside the road. The roads are well surfaced, and traffic is light on weekdays. At weekends, the Fontainebleau forest, just to the south, fills with cyclists and climbers, so ride with care. In spring, the rape fields turn the landscape bright yellow.

Fuel is easy in Milly-la-Forêt, with a station on the main road and bakeries in the centre. Restaurants serve simple French food, and a plate of local cheese and a glass of wine is the natural lunch. Paris is about an hour to the north.
t.vexin limestone@49.0,2.6:
Roissy airport is close enough here that you will see aircraft sliding down the sky at a low angle, a strange companion for a ride that began among limestone villages and river cliffs.

It is honest to say that the riding here is a transition. You are crossing a landscape that has been squeezed between logistics warehouses, the runways of Charles de Gaulle and the cereal fields that still survive between them. Roads are fast and straight, roundabouts are frequent, and heavy lorries use the same lanes as you. The pleasure is in the moments between: a line of poplars, a small village church, a farm track that lets you slow down. If you have any choice, avoid rush hour on the N2 and the roads around the airport, because the traffic here can turn a good day sour in minutes.

The land itself has a long history of feeding Paris. This plain once supplied grain and vegetables to the capital, and the villages kept their old centres even as everything around them became industrial. Goële, the old name for the area east of here, still turns up on signposts and in the names of local products. The clay soil explains why the fields are so heavy and productive, and also why they turn into a sticky mess after winter rain.

Practically, Mitry-Mory has everything: fuel, supermarkets, a handful of cafes, and a railway line into Paris if the bike or the rider needs to call it a day. The smaller Moussy villages are quieter and good for a last coffee if you find an open bar, though in this part of the Paris region many village cafes close on Sunday afternoons and Mondays. Fill the tank before you head into the city, because station prices drop noticeably once you leave the autoroute and its service areas behind.

For a finish, it works in its way: you are close to the Paris ring and the northern road network, with the long limestone day behind you. Take a minute to look out over the stubble or the green crops, and notice how large the sky is.
t.chantilly to@48.9,2.8:
Mickey Mouse is the unavoidable neighbour here. On a summer afternoon the roads around this part of the Seine-et-Marne are full of coaches and rental cars, and the air in the car parks smells of fried food and hot tarmac.

Riding here is mostly a matter of survival and patience. Roundabouts follow one another, the surface is smooth because everything is new, and the road layout is designed around cars and buses, not around anyone who wants to enjoy a corner. If you reach this point on a weekday morning or after dark, it is far easier. A Sunday evening, when the day trippers all head home at once, is the worst time to be on the roads around Esbly or Val d'Europe.

Even so, the place has a history you can feel if you look. Before it was a new town, the Brie plateau here was farmland and small villages, and a few old centres survive among the housing estates, with a stone church and a lane of old houses. Esbly, to the north, sits on the Marne and has a railway line into Paris and a pleasant riverside, so if you want to stretch before the last section it is a good place to do it. The Marne itself winds through meadows and poplars, and is the nicest corner of the area.

Fuel and food are easy, almost too easy. Val d'Europe has a shopping centre and plenty of chain restaurants, and the larger stations stay open late. Esbly, about five kilometres away, has a more human scale, with a baker, a small supermarket and a station. Parking is rarely a problem unless you are heading into the theme park itself, in which case you will need to follow the signs and pay.

As a finish to a day on the Chantilly forest roads, this is the moment when the quiet ends and the capital's gravity pulls you in. The best advice is to take a last look at the green behind you, and then commit to the final stretch.
t.route napoleon@46.1,4.5:
The Azergues valley is the quiet back door into the Beaujolais, and this is where the day ends. Mont Saint-Rigaud, the highest point of the Beaujolais, rises to the north.

The riding is a pleasure in a low-key way. The valley road follows the little river between wooded slopes, with bends that tighten as the valley narrows and then open again, and a surface that varies from good to patchy. Traffic is light, and you will meet more cyclists and tractors than cars. The side roads climbing out of the valley are narrower and steeper, with hairpins and short, sharp gradients, and a few have views over a patchwork of fields and woods that deserve a stop. Early autumn is the best time, when the vineyards turn red and gold and the air smells of crushed grapes.

The area has a long working history. The Azergues valley was a centre for textile weaving in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the old mills and weavers' houses still stand in some villages. Lamure itself was a small industrial town for a while, and a former railway line along the valley now provides a quiet walking and cycling route. The granite and pink sandstone buildings give the villages a warm look in the evening sun.

Fuel is not guaranteed in the valley, so plan on Gleizé, which is nineteen kilometres away and has a full range of stations and shops. Lamure and Grandris have a bakery and perhaps a bar, which is enough for a coffee or a bite, and the local farms sell cheeses, sausages and wine if you are lucky enough to find one open.

Because the ride is a weekend loop that ends here, take your time over the last kilometres. The descent into the Saône valley is quick and easy, and it is worth lingering over the last of the Beaujolais light before you leave the hills.
t.vallee de@48.8,2.0:
Planned in the 1960s and built over the following decades, it is a district of roundabouts, cycle paths, office parks and lakes, sitting on the plateau west of the Chevreuse valley, and the people who live here are mostly commuters to Paris and La Défense.

The ride to this point has come out of the Chevreuse valley, so the contrast is sharp. Here the roads are wide, smooth and well signed, which makes them easy but not exciting, and the many roundabouts are best taken with care, especially in wet weather. But a short ride south brings you into old Trappes and the forested side valleys, where the lanes narrow and the villages have kept their stone churches and farms.

The most interesting thing nearby is natural. The Étang de Saint-Quentin, a large artificial lake on the town's edge, is a nature reserve for birds, with reedbeds that attract herons, grebes and, in winter, many wintering ducks. A cycle path runs round the water, and benches along the bank give you a good view. The national velodrome, built for track cycling and used in the 2024 Olympic Games, is also just beside the lake, and visitors can sometimes watch training sessions.

Versailles, with its famous palace and gardens, is only a few kilometres to the north-east, and it is easy to visit if you have time and energy. Fuel and food are no problem: the town has large stations and shopping centres, and many chain cafes and restaurants. A bakery in the old village of Voisins offers a sandwich and a coffee, and the lake is a pleasant place to eat it.

At the end of a dawn loop, this is a quiet and orderly place to finish, with a little nature and a hint of history to round off the morning.
t.annecy bauges@45.9,4.4:
Tarare is a textile town that grew rich on muslin, and its big, grey nineteenth-century factories still stand along the river Turdine.

This is not an Annecy or a Bauges, as the ride name suggests, but it has its own appeal. The roads climb out of the town in long, steady bends through pine woods and rough pasture, reaching ridges that give broad views to the east over the Beaujolais and sometimes to the Alps. The surface is generally good, though patchy near the top, and the weather can turn quickly: mist and strong wind are common, and in winter snow can close the higher roads. The A89 motorway tunnels under the main ridge, so the old road over the Col des Sauvages is quiet, which makes it a good ride.

Tarare's history is all about cloth. In the nineteenth century, thousands of people worked in its mills, making fine muslin, velvet and embroidered cloth that was sold across Europe. The town is also known for its brioche, which locals bake with pink pralines, a sweet tradition shared with Lyon. Violay and the villages around it are quieter, with farms, old churches and a handful of wayside crosses.

For fuel, Tarare, with over ten thousand people, has stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and is the sensible place to fill up before the hills. A pastry shop in the centre sells the local brioche, and cafes along the main street are cheap and friendly. If you want to rest, the valley by the river has a few benches, though the hills are better.

As a final point on a long loop, it is a good place to be high and quiet before the descent to Lyon, and to look back at the hills you have crossed.
t.baker city@44.8,-117.8:
Baker City looks across a wide, dry valley at the Elkhorn Mountains, a jagged line of peaks that stay snowy well into the summer, and the contrast between sage-covered flats and white summits is the first thing you notice. It is a town of about ten thousand people in the far east of Oregon, on the old Oregon Trail, and its brick downtown is better preserved than most in the West. The Geiser Grand Hotel, a grand 1889 building with a stained-glass ceiling in the dining room, recalls the gold boom that made the town rich.

Gold was found in the Blue Mountains in 1861, and Baker became the commercial hub of the region, with miners spending their dust in its saloons and shops. Many of the old mining sites still lie in the surrounding hills, including the ghostly remains of dredges in the Sumpter Valley. On the ridge above town, the National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center tells the story of the emigrants who walked this route in the mid nineteenth century, and from its viewpoint you can see wagon ruts still faintly scarring the land.

From Baker, the Hells Canyon Scenic Byway runs east and north toward the Snake River, which forms the border with Idaho. Hells Canyon, carved by the Snake, is the deepest river gorge in North America, about 2,400 metres from the rim of the Seven Devils Mountains to the water, deeper than the Grand Canyon. The road follows reservoirs behind the Brownlee and Oxbow dams, with long, easy bends and views over the water, and the canyon only reveals its depth when you reach the viewpoints near the far end. It is a remote road, with very little traffic.

Services are thin once you leave town. Fuel in Baker City, and fill up, because gas stations along the byway are few and far apart, and mobile coverage drops out in the canyons. Pack water, since summer temperatures in the valley bottom can be fierce.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons. In June the hills are green and the wildflowers are out, and in September the cottonwoods turn gold. Winter brings ice and snow, and the high roads often close. Watch for wildlife, particularly deer and elk at dusk, and for cattle on open range roads.
t.shanghai@31.2,121.5:
Shanghai is a city of superlatives that does not seem to mind. It is the biggest city in China by population, with more than twenty million people, and it sprawls across the delta of the Yangtze, a flat, humid plain cut by creeks and canals. Until the nineteenth century it was a fishing and trading town, and then, after the British forced China to open the port in the 1840s, it grew into the most cosmopolitan city in Asia, with foreign concessions, banks, department stores and nightclubs along the Bund, the riverside street lined with grand stone buildings that still stand.

Across the Huangpu river from the Bund, Pudong was rice fields thirty years ago, and now the glass towers there, including the twisting Shanghai Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the world, form one of the most famous skylines on earth. The old city, the French Concession and the quiet lanes of lilong housing hold a more intimate Shanghai of plane trees, cafés and small shops, and a morning walk on a back street is often the best way to get a feel for the place.

The afternoon trip described here heads north-east to the Chongming Dongtan wetland on the island of Chongming, at the mouth of the Yangtze, an important stopover for migrating birds. The trip uses the Yangtze River Tunnel and Bridge, which opened in 2009 and carries a long, fast expressway across the water. The road is smooth, but traffic can be heavy at weekends, and speed cameras are everywhere.

Shanghai restricts motorcycles in the city, plates are expensive and tightly controlled, and a foreign licence is not valid for riding. The metro, taxis and the high-speed railways are the practical alternatives, and an organised tour is the way to reach the wetlands.

Fuel, food and everything else are in endless supply. Try xiaolongbao, soup dumplings, and the sweet braised dishes of the local cuisine, and finish the evening on the Bund with the lights of Pudong across the water.
t.migratory bird sanctuaries along the coa:
This is Chongming Dongtan, a wetland of international importance, and it is a different world from the endless city, a good hundred kilometres away. The sky is wide, the horizon is flat, and the only sounds are wind in the reeds and the calls of birds.

Chongming is the largest alluvial island in the world, built up over centuries from the silt that the Yangtze carries down from the interior. The land is still growing at its eastern end, as sediment builds new mudflats, and the wetlands that form there are among the most important stopover sites on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, one of the great bird migration routes. Each spring and autumn, hundreds of thousands of waders, ducks, geese and gulls pass through, resting and feeding on the mud before flying on to Siberia or Australia. Rare species, such as the black-faced spoonbill and the Far Eastern curlew, can be seen, and winter brings flocks of swans and geese.

The reed beds, mostly common reed and bulrush, are the habitat for smaller birds and, on the margins, for an invasive cordgrass from North America, which conservationists have been working to control. A boardwalk and observation towers at the park allow visitors to get close, and the best time is in the early morning at high tide, when the birds are pushed up to the edge. Bring binoculars and a windproof jacket, because the wind off the sea is strong.

Getting here from Shanghai is straightforward by car or bus, over the Yangtze Tunnel and Bridge, and then along the island's main road, which runs straight and flat between rice fields and greenhouses. Riding your own motorcycle in China requires special permits and is rarely available to visitors, so most travellers come by tour or taxi. Services on the island are limited, with some small restaurants and shops, but fuel and food are available in Chengqiao, the main town.

The island is known for its crabs, especially in autumn, and for a sweet rice cake sold in local shops. Try both.
t.lyon@45.7,4.8:
Two rivers meet in Lyon, and the whole city arranges itself around them. The Saône comes in from the north, slow and green, under the hill of Fourvière with its white basilica; the Rhône rushes down from Switzerland, wide and fast; and between them lies the Presqu'île, a long peninsula of squares and grand streets that ends at the modern Confluence district. For riders, Lyon is a start and finish more than a destination, but it is a fine one, especially if you arrive hungry.

The Romans founded Lugdunum on Fourvière and made it the capital of Gaul; two Roman theatres still sit on the slope below the basilica. Down by the Saône, Vieux Lyon is one of the largest Renaissance quarters in Europe, built when Lyon was a banking and printing city, and riddled with traboules, covered passages that cut through courtyards from one street to the next. Later the silk workers, the canuts, filled the tall workshops of the Croix-Rousse hill and rose in famous revolts in the 1830s. The Lumière brothers made their first films here, and every December the Fête des Lumières fills the city with light shows.

Food is the city's religion. The bouchons serve heavy, wonderful dishes such as quenelles, andouillette and cervelle de canut, a soft herb cheese whose name means silk weaver's brains, and Lyon has long claimed to be France's gastronomic capital. Beaujolais lies just to the north and the Côtes du Rhône to the south, so the wine is never far away either.

Getting in and out by bike is the less charming part. The ring roads and the tunnels under Fourvière are congested at rush hour, and the city has a low-emission zone, so check the current rules and stickers for your bike before you arrive. Once you escape, the reward is quick. The Annecy and Bauges rides head east over the plain and into the pre-Alps, where the Bauges massif is all limestone cliffs, pasture and quiet D-roads. The Vercors rides go southeast toward Grenoble and the dramatic balcony roads such as the Col de la Machine, where the road is cut into the cliff above the gorges.

Fuel, food and accommodation are plentiful everywhere. Fill up on the outskirts rather than in the centre, where stations are scarce and parking is tight, and save the bouchon dinner for the evening you return.
t.near lentilly@45.8,4.7:
West of Lyon, the land rises into soft hills, and the city's suburbs dissolve into villages, orchards and woods. To the north lie the vineyards of the Beaujolais, and on clear days you can see the Alps, even Mont Blanc, far to the east across the plain.

The Monts du Lyonnais are farming country, with dairy cattle, fruit orchards and small fields divided by hedges and woods. The villages have stone churches and old farmhouses, and the roads wind gently through them, climbing to small cols with views over the hills. The Col de la Luère, above Pollionnay, is well known to Lyon's cyclists and is a pleasant climb on a bike with an engine, with tight bends through the forest and a view over the city from the top. To the north, the Pierres Dorées area of the southern Beaujolais has villages built of golden limestone that glow in the evening sun, such as Oingt, perched on a hill above the vines.

This point serves as a finish for two long rides. The Alpe d'Huez and Mont Ventoux day is a huge undertaking, combining the twenty-one hairpins of the Alpe d'Huez with the bare, windswept summit of the Giant of Provence, and returning here after such a day feels like a homecoming. The Route Napoléon weekend follows the road taken by Napoleon on his return from Elba in 1815, from the Riviera through Grasse, Castellane and Digne to Grenoble. Both are long and demanding, and the gentle hills around Lentilly are a fine place to wind down.

The roads near Lyon can be busy at rush hour, especially the routes leading into the city, and the A89 and the N7 carry heavy traffic. The country roads, however, are quieter and pleasant, though narrow and sometimes bumpy, with farm traffic and cyclists. In summer the heat can be intense, while autumn brings fog in the valleys and colourful woods.

Lentilly has fuel, shops and a few places to eat, and there are larger supermarkets and services in the western suburbs of Lyon. After a long ride, a glass of Beaujolais and a plate of local charcuterie in a village bistro is a fitting reward.
t.chevilly@48.0,1.9:
Flat does not begin to describe the Beauce. North of Orléans the land opens into an enormous plain of wheat, barley and rapeseed, so level and so open that grain silos and church steeples stand out like lighthouses, and the sky takes up most of the view. Chevilly is a small village on that plain, beside the old road from Paris to Orléans, with a church, a few streets and an eighteenth-century château set in a park on the edge of the village.

Look out across the fields near Chevilly and you may spot something odd: a long concrete track raised on pillars, running dead straight toward the horizon. This is the test line of the Aérotrain, a hovercraft train developed by the engineer Jean Bertin in the late 1960s. Prototypes floated on a cushion of air along this track at speeds of over 400 km/h, but the project was abandoned in favour of the TGV, and the track was left standing in the fields, a strange monument to a future that never came.

The Beauce has long been called the granary of France, and its soil is among the most fertile in the country. In summer the wheat ripens to gold, and the harvest fills the roads with combines and grain trucks. The wind blows freely across the plain, and dozens of wind turbines now turn above the fields. On a clear day you can see the spires of Chartres Cathedral rising from the plain further northwest, as pilgrims did for centuries.

The riding is straight and simple. The roads are long, flat and mostly well surfaced, and the wind is often the only challenge, especially for lighter bikes. The N20 and the A10 motorway carry heavy traffic between Paris and Orléans, but the side roads through the villages are quiet. This is a place to make good time, to enjoy the space and the light, and to watch the weather move across the sky, rather than to look for curves.

Chevilly has a few shops, and fuel is easy to find in Artenay to the north or in Saran and the northern suburbs of Orléans, a short ride south. Orléans itself, with its cathedral and its memories of Joan of Arc, who lifted the English siege of the city in 1429, makes a good stop for lunch or a coffee. In summer, carry water and sun protection: there is little shade on the plain.
t.saint aignan@47.3,1.4:
Saint-Aignan rises from the south bank of the Cher in tiers: a stone bridge, a riverside quay, steep streets of white tufa houses, a Romanesque collegiate church, and above it all a Renaissance château on its rocky terrace. It is a small town in the southern Loire valley, surrounded by vineyards, woods and fields, and it has the soft, unhurried feel of the Touraine.

The collegiate church is the town's treasure. Built in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, it has a fine bell tower, carved capitals and, in the crypt, a set of medieval wall paintings in remarkably fresh colours. The château, rebuilt in the Renaissance style, overlooks the river and the town, and the view from its terrace across the Cher is lovely. Downstream lies Chenonceau, the château that spans the river on arches, one of the most famous in France, and Montrichard with its keep.

Many visitors come to Saint-Aignan for something completely different: the ZooParc de Beauval, just outside the town, one of the largest and most visited zoos in Europe, famous for its giant pandas. On summer weekends the roads around the town are busy with families heading there, so plan accordingly.

The riding in the area is gentle and pleasant. The roads follow the Cher valley through vineyards and meadows, with long, smooth bends and views of the river, and climb onto low plateaus of woods and fields. Small lanes wind between villages, with little traffic outside the tourist season. To the east lies the Sologne, a flat land of forests, ponds and hunting estates, while to the south the land rises gently toward the Berry. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with green fields, mild weather and fewer tourists.

The local wines are Touraine whites and reds, especially sauvignon blanc and gamay, and the region produces goat's cheeses, including the ash-coated Selles-sur-Cher made just a few kilometres away. There are cafés and restaurants in the town centre, as well as supermarkets with fuel around Saint-Aignan and Noyers-sur-Cher across the river. For a bigger town with every service, Romorantin-Lanthenay is about half an hour east. A walk along the river at sunset, with the château lit above you, is a lovely end to the day.
t.chauvigny@46.6,0.6:
Five castles on one rocky spur is an unusual sight anywhere, and Chauvigny wears them well. The upper town stands on a limestone ridge above the Vienne river, east of Poitiers, with the ruins of medieval fortresses, a Romanesque church and narrow lanes packed onto the hilltop, while the lower town spreads along the river below. Approaching from the west, the skyline of towers and walls above the trees is a surprise.

The castles were built by different lords between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, the most important being the baronial castle of the bishops of Poitiers, who held the town. Its ruins host a falconry show in summer, with eagles, vultures and hawks flying over the battlements. The Collégiale Saint-Pierre, at the top of the town, is famous for its carved capitals, with monsters, demons and biblical scenes in vivid detail, some of the finest Romanesque sculpture in the region. The surrounding hills were quarried for limestone for centuries, and the town has a long history of stone working and porcelain making.

The wider area is rich in Romanesque art. About twenty kilometres east, the abbey church of Saint-Savin-sur-Gartempe has one of the most complete sets of medieval wall paintings in Europe and is on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Poitiers, to the west, has its own Romanesque churches and the site of the famous battle of 732, and the Futuroscope theme park lies north of the city.

The riding is easy and pleasant: the roads follow the river valleys and cross low plateaus of fields and woods, with gentle bends and little traffic. The valley of the Vienne and its tributaries, the Gartempe and the Clain, offers some charming routes, with villages, mills and bridges. The climb into the upper town is short but steep, with cobbles and tight corners, so take it slowly. The summer heat can be intense, and spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons.

Chauvigny has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, so it is a convenient place for a break. Local dishes include farci poitevin, a herb and vegetable pie, and goat's cheeses, as well as the macarons of Montmorillon to the south. Park in the lower town or near the top, walk the lanes, admire the carvings and look out over the valley from the castle walls.
t.brie@45.7,0.2:
Do not come here looking for cheese. This Brie is a small village in the Charente, just north of Angoulême, a long way from the famous cheese country east of Paris. It is a quiet place of limestone houses, a church and fields, set in the gentle hills that roll toward the Cognac vineyards to the west and the wooded uplands of the Limousin to the east.

The village sits close to some surprising places. The Touvre, a few kilometres south, rises from one of the largest springs in France, a resurgence of water that has travelled underground through the limestone from the rivers of the plateau, emerging clear, cold and abundant into a short, wide river. At Ruelle-sur-Touvre, a naval foundry was set up in the eighteenth century to cast cannon for the French navy, using the river's power and the region's iron and wood, and the site is still connected with defence manufacturing today.

Angoulême, just to the south, stands on a high rocky promontory above the Charente, surrounded by ramparts that offer views over the valley. The city is famous for its comic strip festival every January, with murals and statues throughout the streets, and for the Circuit des Remparts, a vintage car race held on the streets around the old walls each September. Further west, the Cognac region produces the famous brandy, and the houses of Jarnac and Cognac welcome visitors.

The riding here is relaxed. The roads wind through low hills, woods and fields, with gentle curves, villages and little traffic, though the main roads around Angoulême can be busy at rush hour. The landscape is green and soft, with vineyards and sunflowers in summer and a warm, almost southern light. The roads east toward the Limousin, around La Rochefoucauld and its château, become hillier and more wooded.

For fuel and supplies, the commercial area of Champniers just north of Angoulême has everything, and Ruelle-sur-Touvre has shops too. A glass of Pineau des Charentes, the local aperitif made from grape juice and cognac, is a regional speciality, though best enjoyed once the riding is done. If you have time, take a walk to the springs of the Touvre, where the water wells up from the ground in a quiet, shaded pool.
t.montmorillon@46.4,0.9:
The Gartempe runs right through the middle of Montmorillon, and the town has grown up on both its banks, linked by old bridges, with mills, gardens and steep lanes stepping down to the water. It is a small, quiet market town in the southeast of the Vienne department, surrounded by woods, pastures and the rolling country that leads toward the Limousin.

Montmorillon calls itself the city of writing and books. In the medieval quarter on the left bank, the old streets have been filled with bookshops, bookbinders, calligraphers and artisans working with paper and printing, and wandering among them is a quiet pleasure. The town's other speciality is sweet: the macaron de Montmorillon, an almond biscuit made to a recipe said to go back centuries, which you can buy in the town and even learn about in a small museum. Above the river stands the Maison-Dieu, a medieval hospital complex with an unusual octagonal chapel.

The wider area has some fine sights. The abbey church of Saint-Savin-sur-Gartempe, with its famous Romanesque wall paintings, lies downstream to the north, and the Gartempe valley offers lovely roads and walks, with cliffs, woods and rapids. Lussac-les-Châteaux, to the west, has a prehistoric cave where engraved stones were found, and the area around it is dotted with ponds and woods.

The riding is easygoing and pleasant. The roads around Montmorillon wind through the river valleys and over low plateaus, with gentle bends, good surfaces and very little traffic. It is a peaceful region, far from the motorways, and the roads invite a relaxed pace. The valley roads can be cool and damp in the morning, especially in autumn, when mist lies over the river.

Montmorillon has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, so it makes a convenient break. Local food includes goat's cheeses, lamb and the famous macarons, as well as wines from the nearby Haut-Poitou. For a pause, park near the river, walk across the old bridge into the book quarter and take a coffee on a terrace, with the sound of the water below and the smell of old paper in the air.
t.saint georges sur eure@48.4,1.4:
The Eure is a modest river when it passes Saint-Georges-sur-Eure, winding through meadows, poplars and willows a few kilometres southwest of Chartres. The village sits on the river where the open plain of the Beauce meets the greener, hillier country of the Perche to the west, and it has the calm atmosphere of a commuter village close to a cathedral city, with a church, houses old and new, and fields stretching away on all sides.

On the edge of the village lies a large lake, formed from old gravel pits, which is now a leisure area with walking paths, a beach and water sports in summer, a pleasant place for a break by the water. The Eure valley is dotted with similar lakes, as well as mills and small châteaux, and the river is popular with anglers.

Chartres, just to the northeast, is the reason most people come to this area. Its Gothic cathedral, built mostly in the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, is one of the most perfect in Europe, famous for its stained glass, especially the deep blue known as Chartres blue, and for the labyrinth set into the floor of the nave. On approach across the plain, the two mismatched spires appear on the horizon long before the town itself, as they did for medieval pilgrims. Downstream, at Maintenon, the unfinished aqueduct ordered by Louis XIV to carry water to Versailles still stands in ruins near the château.

The riding around here is gentle. The roads follow the river valley and cross the plain, with long straight stretches, gentle curves and little traffic. To the west, the Perche offers hillier roads, with woods, hedges and manor houses, and the famous Percheron horses. The plain can be windy, and in winter fog often lies over the valley in the morning.

Fuel is easiest to find in Chartres and its suburbs, including Mainvilliers, and there are supermarkets around the city. Saint-Georges-sur-Eure has a few shops, and Chartres has many cafés and restaurants in the old town around the cathedral. If you can, stay for the evening: from spring to autumn, the cathedral and other buildings in the city are lit up with colourful projections after dark, an unforgettable sight.
t.champagne@48.0,0.3:
Champagné has nothing to do with sparkling wine, but it does have a claim to aviation history that most villages would envy. It lies just east of Le Mans in the Sarthe, beside the valley of the Huisne, at the foot of a wooded plateau called Auvours, and in the autumn of 1908 the military ground on that plateau became the stage for one of the great moments of early flight. Wilbur Wright, invited to France to prove that the Wright brothers' machine really worked, moved his demonstrations to the Camp d'Auvours and flew there for weeks, setting records for duration and altitude and carrying passengers in front of astonished crowds. A monument on the plateau remembers it.

Le Mans itself needs no introduction to anyone who rides. Its circuit, south of the city, hosts the 24 Hours car race every June, as well as the 24-hour motorcycle endurance race and the French round of MotoGP. Part of the car circuit uses public roads, including the long Mulsanne straight, the Ligne Droite des Hunaudières, which you can ride on most days of the year at legal speeds, imagining the prototypes thundering past. The old city of Le Mans, the Cité Plantagenêt, has medieval streets, half-timbered houses and Gallo-Roman walls, and the cathedral has a soaring Gothic choir.

The country around Champagné is a mix of woods, fields and pine forest on sandy soil, with the Huisne winding through meadows. The roads are mostly gentle, with long bends through the trees and small villages, and the military camp on the plateau means parts of the woods may be closed to the public. Traffic can be heavy around Le Mans, especially during race weeks, when the whole region fills with fans, so check the calendar before you plan.

The Sarthe is known for rillettes, the slow-cooked shredded pork spread that is the region's pride, best eaten on fresh bread with a glass of Jasnières or Loir valley wine. The Loir valley to the south has troglodyte houses cut into the limestone cliffs, while the Perche lies to the northeast with its rolling hills and manor houses.

For fuel and supplies, Changé, just south, and the eastern suburbs of Le Mans have supermarkets and stations. Champagné itself has a few shops and a bakery. Ride up to the Auvours plateau and look out over the forest, picturing the fragile biplane rising into the air over these trees more than a century ago.
t.sours@48.4,1.6:
Larks sing over the wheat around Sours, and on a still summer morning that and the tick of a cooling engine may be the only sounds. The village sits on the open plain of the Beauce, a few kilometres east of Chartres, with a church, a cluster of houses and farms, and fields that run to the horizon in every direction. It is a place of enormous skies, where the weather can be watched approaching from far away.

The Beauce was immortalised by the poet Charles Péguy, who walked across it to Chartres in 1912 after his son fell seriously ill, and wrote a long poem presenting the plain to the Virgin of Chartres, describing the sea of wheat and the cathedral rising from it like a ship. His pilgrimage inspired a tradition that continues today: every year at Pentecost, thousands of pilgrims walk from Paris to Chartres across these fields. Even on a motorcycle, you can share some of their feeling as the twin spires appear on the horizon long before the city itself.

The plain is not as empty as it looks. The cereal fields are home to birds that nest on the ground, including skylarks, partridges and harriers, which glide low over the crops hunting for voles. Conservation groups work with farmers to protect the nests of Montagu's harriers during the harvest. In winter flocks of lapwings and golden plovers gather in the fields, and the wind turbines that have sprung up across the plain turn steadily in the constant breeze.

The riding is simple and fast: long, straight roads, gentle undulations and wide views, with little traffic outside the main routes. The wind is the main challenge, buffeting the bike on exposed stretches, and the roads can be muddy during the harvest and the sowing seasons, when tractors carry soil onto the tarmac. In summer, with the fields golden and the sky blue, the plain has a stark beauty; in winter, under low grey clouds, it can feel bleak.

Sours has few services, so for fuel, food and supplies, head to Chartres or its suburbs, such as Le Coudray, which have supermarkets and stations. Chartres has many cafés and restaurants around the cathedral, and the old lower town by the Eure, with its bridges, mills and wash houses, is a charming place for a walk. Carry water in summer, as shade is almost nonexistent on the plain.
t.serris@48.8,2.8:
Serris is a town that did not exist in its current form forty years ago. Once a small farming village on the plateau of the Brie, east of Paris, it has grown with the new towns of Marne-la-Vallée and the arrival of Disneyland Paris next door, and today it is a mix of modern housing, shopping streets designed to look like an old French town, and the huge Val d'Europe shopping centre. The old village core, with its church and farm buildings, survives at the edge of the new development.

The scale of change here is remarkable. The decision in the 1980s to build the Disney resort on the plateau transformed the area, bringing a motorway junction, a TGV station, hotels and tens of thousands of new residents. On summer evenings, you can see the fireworks over the castle from the surrounding fields and roads. For many visitors, this is the first glimpse of France outside Paris, and it is a strange introduction.

The real countryside begins just beyond the towns. The Brie plateau is a rich farming region of wheat, sugar beet and woods, cut by the valleys of the Marne and its tributaries, the Grand Morin and the Petit Morin, which wind through meadows, villages and wooded slopes. The Marne valley east of Meaux, with its loops, bridges and riverside villages, offers pleasant riding, and the roads climb gently in and out of the valleys, with views over the fields and the river. Brie de Meaux, the famous soft cheese, comes from this region, and Meaux itself has a cathedral and an old bishop's palace.

The Champagne ride heads east along the Marne valley toward Château-Thierry, Épernay and Reims, entering the vineyards near the border between Île-de-France and Champagne. You can take the A4 motorway for speed, but the river roads are much more interesting, with vineyards appearing on the slopes as you approach the champagne country.

Serris and the surrounding towns have every service, including fuel, supermarkets and fast food, and Lagny-sur-Marne, just to the north, has a pleasant old centre by the river. Traffic around the Disney resort and on the A4 can be very heavy, especially at weekends and during the holidays, so leave early in the morning to avoid the worst of it and to reach the quiet roads of the Brie before the rest of the world wakes up.
t.charly sur marne@49.0,3.3:
Vines on the hillsides tell you where you are: Charly-sur-Marne is in Champagne, even though it lies in the Aisne department, at the western end of the official vineyard area. The town sits on the north bank of the Marne, where the river winds in wide loops through a valley of meadows, poplars and villages, with vineyards and woods climbing the slopes on either side. The champagne made here is mostly from pinot meunier, the grape that thrives in the cooler, clay soils of the western Marne valley.

The valley has known terrible times. In 1914 and again in 1918, the Marne was the scene of decisive battles of the First World War. In the summer of 1918, German forces advanced to the river near Château-Thierry, and American troops, newly arrived in France, fought some of their first major battles nearby, including at Belleau Wood, where the US Marines suffered heavy losses. The American monument on Hill 204 above Château-Thierry, and the cemetery at Belleau, are moving reminders of that summer. Château-Thierry is also the birthplace of Jean de La Fontaine, the seventeenth-century writer of fables, and his house is now a museum.

The riding along the Marne is gentle and lovely. The roads follow the river through vineyards and villages, climbing in places to give views over the valley and its loops, with smooth curves and little traffic outside the main routes. Small champagne houses line the roads, many offering tastings, and the slopes above the river are crossed by lanes that wind between the vines. Spring brings fresh green leaves and blossom, while the harvest in September fills the vineyards with pickers and the air with the smell of crushed grapes.

The Champagne ride continues east toward Épernay and Reims, the heart of the region, where the great houses have their cellars cut into the chalk beneath the towns. Épernay's Avenue de Champagne is lined with grand houses, and Reims has its magnificent Gothic cathedral, where French kings were crowned for centuries.

Charly-sur-Marne has a few shops and cafés, but for a wider choice of services, including fuel, Château-Thierry is the nearest town of any size. Tasting champagne is part of the pleasure here, but France's drink-driving limits are low and strictly enforced, so buy a bottle for the evening rather than sampling too much at the cellar door.
t.lorris@47.9,2.5:
Lorris is a small market town on the southern rim of the Forêt d'Orléans, the largest state forest in mainland France, and it is one of those places whose name carries more weight in history books than its size would suggest. Fewer than three thousand people live here, around a square with a fine old timber market hall and a church whose wooden organ loft is one of the treasures of the Loiret.

The name matters because of a charter. In the twelfth century the Capetian kings granted Lorris a set of customs that fixed taxes, limited forced labour and protected the townsfolk from arbitrary fines. The "coutumes de Lorris" were so admired that dozens of other towns across the royal domain copied them, and historians still cite them when they talk about how medieval France began to give ordinary people rights on paper. The town also gave its name to Guillaume de Lorris, the poet who wrote the first part of the Roman de la Rose, the great love allegory of the Middle Ages. A darker chapter is told in the Resistance museum: the forest hid a maquis in 1944, and the memorial at the crossroads in the woods recalls the young fighters who were killed there that August.

As a fuel stop it does the job. The town has shops, a bakery and a filling station on the edge of town, and if anything is shut, Sully-sur-Loire is about eighteen kilometres south, with its moated castle on the Loire and every service you need. Coffee on the square, under the plane trees, is a civilised pause.

The riding around here is about calm rather than corners. The forest roads run long and straight between oaks and Scots pines, the land is almost flat, and the surface is usually good, so it is a place to settle into a steady pace and listen to the engine. Watch for deer at dusk and for logging trucks on the narrower lanes, and remember that hunting season brings parked cars and people in orange at the forest edges on autumn weekends. South of town the Canal d'Orléans threads through the woods with old locks and lock-keepers' houses, and the ponds of the forest are good for herons and, in spring, for the noise of frogs. It is gentle country, and after the traffic of the Paris ring it feels like someone has turned the volume down.
t.chabris@47.3,1.7:
Chabris sits on the left bank of the Cher where three landscapes meet: the sandy woods and ponds of the Sologne to the north, the open chalky fields of the Berry to the south, and the soft valley of the river itself, wide and slow, lined with poplars. It is a village of around two and a half thousand people, the sort of place you pass through on the way to somewhere else, which is a pity, because it rewards half an hour.

The church of Saint-Phalier is the reason to stop. Phalier was a hermit who lived here in the fifth century, and his tomb in the crypt drew pilgrims for centuries, especially women hoping for children. The building is Romanesque at heart, and the carved stones set into the outer walls, some of them older than the church itself, show strange animals and figures that nobody has ever quite explained. Stand by the south side in the afternoon, when the low sun brings the carving out.

This is goat cheese country. Selles-sur-Cher, a few kilometres downstream, gives its name to a flat round cheese dusted with ash, and Valençay, a short ride south with its grand Renaissance château, has both a cheese, shaped like a truncated pyramid, and a small wine appellation of crisp whites and light reds. Ask for both at a market or a café and you will have eaten the region in one sitting.

The riding is relaxed rather than technical. The road along the Cher follows the valley with long bends and good visibility, and the side lanes into the Sologne are narrow, flat and shaded, with ponds glinting through the trees and the occasional pheasant running out in front of you. South towards Valençay the land rises a little and opens up, and you can see weather coming from a long way off. Spring and autumn are lovely, summer can be hot and still in the valley, and morning mist on the river is common in October.

For anything bigger than a village shop, Romorantin-Lanthenay is about fifteen kilometres north-east, a proper town with supermarkets, fuel and a pleasant old centre on the Sauldre. Chabris itself has a bakery, a café or two and a bridge over the Cher where it is worth pausing to watch the water.
t.pierrefitte sur seine@49.0,2.4:
Pierrefitte-sur-Seine is not where anyone dreams of ending a ride, and that is fine. It is a dense northern suburb of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis, just above Saint-Denis, with tower blocks, small houses, busy junctions and the steady rumble of the routes nationales that carry traffic between the capital and the plain to the north. You arrive here because it is the doorway back into the city after a day in the forests of Chantilly and Ermenonville.

It does have one thing that surprises people. The new home of the Archives nationales is here, a large modern building designed by Massimiliano Fuksas and opened in 2013, where millions of documents of French history are now kept, from royal decrees to revolutionary papers. A couple of kilometres south stands the Basilica of Saint-Denis, the burial place of the kings of France and the building where Gothic architecture was more or less invented in the twelfth century. If you have energy left, it is a far better final image of the day than the ring road.

The last kilometres in are urban riding, plain and simple. Expect traffic lights, buses, delivery vans, filtering scooters and drivers who change lanes with confidence. Arrive in the early afternoon on a Sunday and it is calm; arrive at six on a weekday and you will practise slow-speed balance. Keep an eye on the speed cameras that are common on the approach roads, and on the low-emission rules in and around Paris, which apply to motorcycles too, so carry your Crit'Air sticker.

The contrast with the start of the day is part of the charm. A few kilometres north, the slopes of the Montmorency forest rise above Groslay and Montmagny, and Groslay was famous for centuries for its orchards, especially pears, grown on the sunny hillside for the Paris markets. Beyond that the Plaine de France opens out into big fields, and then the forests of Chantilly begin, with their racecourse, their château and the long straight rides cut for royal hunts.

Fuel, food and everything else are everywhere here, open late, and the RER and metro lines nearby make it an easy place to meet someone or drop the bike for the night. Treat it as a landing strip: put your feet down, take off the helmet and let the day settle.
t.near bresles on the way back@49.5,2.3:
North of Paris, in the Oise, the land flattens into the great chalk plateau of Picardy, all wheat, sugar beet and sky, and Bresles sits on its edge where the small valley of the Thérain drops away towards Beauvais. It is a town of about four thousand people with a solid stone château that once belonged to the bishops of Beauvais, who used it as a country residence and, in the troubled centuries, as a stronghold.

Honesty first, about the swimming. This is not a land of lakes and beaches. What it has instead is water of a quieter kind: the marshes of Bresles, a protected wetland of reed beds, ponds and old peat diggings just outside the town, full of birds in spring, and the gravel-pit ponds of the Thérain valley, some of which are managed for fishing or leisure. Swimming is only allowed where it is signposted, so treat this more as a place to sit by water, cool down and watch the dragonflies than as a plunge.

The riding is open-country riding. Roads cross the plateau in long straight lines between villages, then tip down into the valleys in short bends through beech woods, and the contrast is pleasant. Wind is the real factor: there is nothing to stop it, and on a gusty day the crosswinds across the fields will push you around. Watch for tractors and mud on the road during the beet harvest in autumn, when the lanes can be slick. Summer evenings, with long light over ripe wheat, are the best of it.

Beauvais, about fifteen kilometres away, is worth a detour if time allows. Its cathedral has the tallest Gothic choir ever built, a soaring, unfinished structure whose vaults collapsed in the thirteenth century and were rebuilt with extra supports, and inside is an astronomical clock of remarkable complexity. The town was badly damaged in 1940 but the cathedral survived.

For practical needs, Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, about eleven kilometres away, is the nearest town of over five thousand, with supermarkets and fuel, and Bresles itself has a bakery and small shops. From here the run back towards Paris is quick on the main roads, so it is a good place to stop, drink something cold and let the plateau wind dry you off before the traffic begins.
t.near craponne@45.7,4.7:
West of Lyon, before the city has fully let go, the land starts to buckle into the Monts du Lyonnais, and the villages around Vaugneray, Grézieu-la-Varenne and Brindas sit on that first rise. They are prosperous, leafy places of four or five thousand people each, half suburb and half country, with stone walls, orchards and views back across the Rhône basin to the Alps on clear days. Craponne, a slightly bigger town, is a few kilometres closer to the city.

It is a fitting place to finish because the riding just behind you is some of the best close to Lyon. From here the roads climb west through cherry orchards and small woods towards Yzeron and Saint-Martin-en-Haut, twisting up wooded slopes with tight hairpins and short straights, and then running along open ridges at six or seven hundred metres with views into the Loire basin. Lyon riders use these hills as their evening and Sunday playground, so expect company at weekends, including cyclists who climb the same bends.

The area is full of quiet history. The Romans brought water to Lugdunum, their capital of Gaul, by aqueducts from these hills, and the arches of the Gier aqueduct still stride across fields at Chaponost, a few kilometres south. It is one of the best-preserved Roman aqueduct remains in France, and it is strange and lovely to see it standing among new houses and gardens. The Monts du Lyonnais are also known for their fruit, especially cherries in early summer, sold at roadside stalls, and for small farms that supply the Lyon markets.

The light is often the best part. Late afternoon, the sun drops behind the hills and the whole basin glows below you, with the Fourvière basilica a white speck above the city. In autumn morning fog can sit in the valleys while the hills stand clear above it, a good reason to climb before you descend.

Everything practical is close: fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés in Craponne and the villages around, and the city itself only a short ride away. Traffic thickens fast towards Lyon at rush hour, especially on the main roads through Tassin, so if you can, arrive mid-afternoon or after seven and the last kilometres will be painless.
t.velizy villacoublay@48.8,2.2:
Vélizy-Villacoublay is a modern town on the plateau south-west of Paris, between the forests of Meudon and Verrières, best known for two very different things: one of the biggest shopping centres in the region and a military air base. The base at Villacoublay is where French leaders and foreign heads of state usually land when they come to Paris, and you may hear a government jet coming in low over the trees.

The town itself is mostly office parks, housing estates and wide avenues, and it makes no claim to charm. As a finish point, though, it has real advantages: it sits right on the main road back into Paris, it has every service you could need, and it is surrounded by green. The forest of Meudon, just north, is a large wooded area of oaks and chestnuts with ponds and paths, and the Bièvre valley to the south is a pocket of village houses, mills and meadows that feels far from the city.

The ride in from the Gâtinais and the Milly forest is the reverse of the day's beauty. You come up from the south through farmland and woods, then onto the fast roads around Saclay and Versailles, and finally into the suburbs. The N118 is a quick, busy dual carriageway with speed cameras and a lot of traffic at peak times, so if you have the patience, the back roads through Jouy-en-Josas and Bièvres are slower but much more pleasant, dropping into the little valley and climbing out of it in a few good bends.

It is worth knowing that Versailles is only a few kilometres west. If you finish early, the palace and the park are a short hop, and the long avenues and the scale of the place are a striking last stop. Meudon also has its own history: the observatory on the hill was built on the site of a royal château, and the sculptor Rodin lived and worked there, and his house and garden are now a museum.

Fuel, cafés and food are everywhere, the shopping centre has everything if you need gear or a quick meal, and the tram and train links to Paris are good if you are dropping the bike off. Arrive outside peak hours and the last part of the ride is painless; arrive at six on a weekday and it is a lesson in filtering.
t.near wolowaru@-8.7,121.9:
Wolowaru is a market town in the mountains of central Flores, strung out along the Trans-Flores Highway east of Kelimutu, and on market day the road through it fills with trucks, bemos and people in hand-woven sarongs carrying sacks of rice, coffee and vegetables. It is not a place most travellers stop for long, but it is a good one to pause in: a slice of ordinary life on an island where tourism has only touched a few spots.

The villages around Wolowaru are known for ikat weaving, among the finest on Flores. The Lio people, who live in this part of the island, weave cloth with intricate patterns, dyed with natural colours from roots, bark and leaves, and the designs carry meanings tied to clan, status and ceremony. In villages such as Jopu and Nggela, women sit at backstrap looms on the verandas of their houses, and visitors can watch them work and buy cloth directly. Traditional Lio houses, with steep thatched roofs and carved posts, survive in some villages, along with stone megaliths used in ancestral rituals.

The landscape here is steep and volcanic, with deep valleys, forested ridges and terraces of rice and vegetables carved into the slopes. Kelimutu, the volcano with three coloured crater lakes, lies just to the west, and its slopes rise above the town. The soil is fertile, and coffee, cloves, cacao and candlenut grow in the gardens around the villages. The Flores landscape is dramatic everywhere, but in the centre of the island it is at its most rugged.

The Trans-Flores Highway through Wolowaru is the island's main road, running from Labuan Bajo in the west to Larantuka in the east, and it is a rider's road in the truest sense: endless curves, steep climbs and descents, and constantly changing views. The surface varies, from good asphalt to potholes and landslide damage, and the road is narrow, with trucks and buses taking up most of it. Ende, about twenty-three kilometres away on the south coast, is the nearest large town with full services. Wolowaru has small shops and fuel sold from bottles at roadside stalls, but it is best to fill up properly when you can. The rainy season, from November to March, brings landslides and road closures, so the dry season is better.
t.near detusoko@-8.8,121.8:
The road from Ende up to Moni climbs out of the coastal heat into a world of rice terraces, waterfalls and cloud, and Detusoko sits about halfway along, a quiet village spread across the hillsides with terraced paddies falling away below it and forested ridges rising above. The air is cooler here, the light softer, and in the morning mist hangs in the valleys. A few homestays have opened in recent years, and it makes a peaceful alternative to the busier village of Moni.

Most people on this road are heading for Kelimutu, the volcano whose summit holds three crater lakes, each a different colour. The colours change over time, from turquoise to green to brown, red and black, depending on the minerals dissolved in the water and the volcanic activity below, and no one can predict exactly what you will see. The Lio people believe the lakes are the resting places of souls: one for young people, one for the elderly, and one for those who did wrong. Most visitors ride up from Moni before dawn to watch the sunrise over the lakes, and when the mist clears, the sight is unforgettable.

Ende, the town on the coast below, has its own story. In the 1930s, the Dutch colonial authorities exiled Sukarno, the future first president of Indonesia, to Ende, and he spent several years there. It is said that he developed the ideas behind Pancasila, the founding philosophy of the Indonesian state, while sitting under a breadfruit tree in the town, and the tree, or a successor, is now a monument. His house in Ende has been turned into a small museum.

The road up from Ende is steep and winding, following a river gorge for part of the way, with landslides common in the rainy season and repairs constantly underway. The views are superb, especially of the terraces around Detusoko and the mountains beyond. There are small warungs along the road serving coffee and simple meals, and Ende, about nineteen kilometres back, has fuel and all services. The weather in the mountains can change quickly, with sudden rain and fog, so ride carefully and keep your speed down on the wet surfaces.
t.compiegne@49.4,2.8:
On 11 November 1918, in a railway carriage parked in a clearing in the forest outside Compiègne, the armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War was signed. In June 1940 Hitler insisted that France's surrender be signed in the same carriage, at the same spot. The clearing, now called the Glade of the Armistice near Rethondes, holds a memorial and a replica carriage, and it is one of the places in northern France where history feels uncomfortably close.

The town itself sits at the meeting of the Oise and the Aisne, and its centrepiece is the royal palace, rebuilt for Louis XV and later a favourite residence of Napoleon I and Napoleon III. It is a vast, formal building facing a long park, and inside there is a national museum of cars and carriages, which makes a pleasing change from tapestries if you have a mechanical bent. Compiègne also has a darker medieval footnote: Joan of Arc was captured here in 1430 during a sortie against the Burgundians. Her statue stands in the town, and the old streets around the Gothic town hall are good for a wander.

For riders, though, the forest is the main event. The Forêt de Compiègne is one of the largest forests in France, laid out for royal hunting, and its roads reflect that: long straight avenues between beeches and oaks, meeting at star-shaped junctions where several routes radiate out at once. It is not twisty, but it is beautiful, especially in autumn when the beech leaves turn copper and the light comes down in shafts through the canopy. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, horse riders on the verges and cyclists on weekends, and keep the speed civil.

Compiègne is big enough for everything you need: fuel, cafés, brasseries and bakeries. From here the ride east through the forest to Pierrefonds is short and very pretty, and the roads north into the Oise valley are calm. Expect speed cameras on the approach roads, as in much of France, and on rainy days take care with the cobbled streets in the old centre and slick leaves on the forest roads.
t.pierrefonds@49.3,3.0:
Pierrefonds looks like a fairy-tale castle because, to a large extent, it is one. The original fortress was built at the end of the fourteenth century by Louis d'Orléans, brother of King Charles VI, and was dismantled in the seventeenth century when the crown was taming the great nobles. For two centuries it stood as a romantic ruin above the village. Then Napoleon III, who loved the nearby palace of Compiègne, commissioned the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc to rebuild it, and Viollet-le-Duc did so with more imagination than strict archaeology: towers, battlements, carved beasts, painted halls. Film crews have used it for medieval stories ever since.

The village beneath it is small and charming, with a lake at its foot where the castle reflects on still mornings. A handful of crêperies, cafés and restaurants serve the visitors, and on a sunny day eating outside with the towers above you is a fine way to spend an hour. If you want to see inside the castle, allow time; it is managed as a national monument and the visit is worth it for the sheer theatre of the rooms.

The ride in from Compiègne crosses the eastern side of the great forest, on roads that run straight between ranks of beech and then dip and curve as the land falls towards the Pierrefonds valley. It is easy, scenic riding rather than anything technical. Around the village, the roads wind more, climbing out of the valley through farmland and woods, and on a weekday you will meet very little traffic. Weekends bring day-trippers from Paris, cyclists and horse riders, so take the bends with a little reserve.

Pierrefonds has around two thousand inhabitants, so fuel is not something to count on here; Compiègne, about thirteen kilometres away, is the reliable option. The area is green and damp, with rich clay soils, and after rain the forest roads stay wet longer than you might expect under the trees. In spring and autumn the forest smells of moss and leaf mould, and the castle, catching the late sun, is one of the best photographs in the Île-de-France orbit.
t.selles sur cher@47.3,1.6:
If you like cheese, Selles-sur-Cher needs no introduction. The town gives its name to a small, flat disc of goat's cheese coated in charcoal ash, with a bluish rind and a dense, slightly nutty interior, made under a protected designation in the surrounding area. Buying one from a local shop and eating it with bread on the riverbank is a simple pleasure that justifies the stop all by itself.

Selles itself is a quiet town on the Cher, between the Loire valley and the Sologne, with an abbey church dedicated to Saint Eusice and a château by the river that mixes medieval and Renaissance elements. It is the kind of place where the main square has a bakery, a bar-tabac and a few benches, and where life does not rush. The river here is wide and slow, lined with poplars, and in summer you can watch people fishing in the evening light.

The riding around Selles is gentle. To the north, the Sologne is a flat land of forests, ponds and hunting estates, crossed by straight roads under pines and birches, with misty mornings and the occasional deer bounding across. To the south and west, the Cher valley offers pleasant curving roads through vineyards and fields towards Saint-Aignan and the château country of the Loire. The roads are generally well surfaced and lightly used outside the main tourist season, though tractors are common, and in hunting season you may see gatherings of hunters and dogs at forest edges.

With fewer than five thousand inhabitants, Selles has the everyday basics, cafés and somewhere to eat, but if the tank is low the safer bet is Romorantin-Lanthenay, about eighteen kilometres north, the nearest larger town. Spring, when the Sologne is green and the ponds are full, and early autumn, when the light softens and the vineyards are being harvested, are the most pleasant times. In midsummer the heat can be heavy, but the shade of the riverside trees and a cold drink at a terrace make up for it.
t.pithiviers@48.2,2.3:
Pithiviers gave its name to a pastry before most riders ever heard of the town. The pithiviers is a domed pie of puff pastry filled with almond cream and scored with curving lines on top, and you can still buy a proper one at the bakeries here. It is rich, buttery and almost certainly not what your riding gear needs, but it is the local thing, and that should count for something.

The town lies on the edge of two landscapes. To the west and north stretches the Beauce, the great wheat plain of France, flat to the horizon, where a church spire or a grain silo can be seen from ten kilometres away. To the south and east begins the Gâtinais, a slightly more varied country of small valleys, woods and villages. Historically the Gâtinais was known for saffron, grown on these limestone soils for centuries before the trade died out, and a few growers have revived it in recent years.

Pithiviers has a small but real railway heritage too: a narrow-gauge line, preserved as a tourist railway, runs from the town into the surrounding fields, a reminder of the network of little lines that once carried sugar beet and grain across the plain. In the centre, the Saint-Salomon church and the old streets are pleasant for a short wander, and there are enough cafés to sit and watch the town go about its business.

Riding here is honest work. The Beauce roads are mostly straight and fast, which is fine for covering distance but can be monotonous, and they are exposed: on a windy day, crosswinds across the open fields are tiring. The Gâtinais to the south and east is more interesting, with gentle curves through villages and along small river valleys such as the Essonne. As a town of almost ten thousand people, Pithiviers has fuel, supermarkets and everything else you need. Speed cameras and village speed limits are common, so ride accordingly, and enjoy the sense of space under the big sky.
t.meaux@49.0,2.9:
Meaux sits on a loop of the Marne about forty kilometres east of Paris, and its name is on two famous products: the Brie de Meaux, a soft, creamy cheese with a long history in the markets of Paris, and a grainy mustard sold in stoneware pots sealed with red wax. Either one makes a good souvenir if you have space in a tank bag, though the Brie is better eaten here.

The old episcopal quarter is the heart of the town. The Gothic cathedral of Saint-Étienne rises above the river, and next to it stands the bishops' palace and its garden, laid out in the shape of a mitre. Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, the great preacher of Louis XIV's court known as the Eagle of Meaux, was bishop here, and his study in the garden pavilion is a quiet spot. Walking among these old stones by the Marne gives the town a weight you might not expect.

Meaux is also a gateway to the battlefields of the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914, when French and British forces halted the German advance on Paris; famously, Paris taxis were used to rush reinforcements to the front. On the edge of town, the Musée de la Grande Guerre is one of the most comprehensive museums of the First World War in France, with uniforms, vehicles and life-size trench reconstructions. It is worth a visit if you have even a passing interest in the period.

The surrounding area is the Brie, a plateau of big fields, scattered woods and small villages. The roads are calm once you are out of the urban fringe, with gentle bends through farmland, along the Marne valley and across small rivers like the Grand Morin. The Marne valley itself, especially upstream towards Château-Thierry, gives pleasant, flowing roads with vineyards appearing on the slopes as you approach Champagne. Meaux has fuel, cafés and restaurants, and on a sunny day a coffee by the river under the cathedral is a gentle way to round off the morning.
t.crepy en valois@49.2,2.9:
Crépy-en-Valois was once the capital of the Valois, the old county whose name passed to a whole dynasty of French kings. Today it is a busy market town of some fifteen thousand people on the plateau north-east of Paris, a natural place to refuel before heading on to Laon and the Aisne valley.

The remains of the old castle house a museum of archery and the Valois, a reminder that archery companies were once important social institutions in this part of France, and some still exist. The old town has narrow streets, a few half-timbered and stone houses and the ruined church of Saint-Thomas, its unfinished façade standing on its own like a stage set. It is not a place that demands a long stop, but it rewards a short walk.

The countryside around Crépy is good riding country if you know where to look. To the north lies the Forest of Compiègne, to the east the Forest of Retz around Villers-Cotterêts, and between them a gently rolling landscape of wheat and beet fields, small valleys and villages built of pale stone. Villers-Cotterêts is where Alexandre Dumas was born, and it is also where King Francis I signed the ordinance of 1539 that made French, rather than Latin, the language of official documents. Morienval, a few kilometres from Crépy, has an abbey church with some of the earliest Gothic rib vaults in France, tucked away in a quiet village.

Roads here are generally quiet D-roads, smooth and well signed, with long, open straights across the plateau and more interesting stretches where they drop into valleys and wind through woods. Wind can be a factor on the exposed parts, and the long straights invite speed, but speed cameras are common in this part of France. Crépy has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries in good supply, so fill up, grab something to eat and enjoy the run north towards the Aisne.
t.laon@49.6,3.6:
You see Laon long before you reach it. The town sits on a long, narrow ridge that rises abruptly from the flat plains of Picardy and Champagne, and the five towers of its cathedral stand on top like a crown. Approaching from any direction, the silhouette grows and grows, and it is one of the great arrivals in northern France.

The upper town, enclosed by medieval walls, is a world of its own. Laon was a royal seat under the late Carolingian kings, and the cathedral of Notre-Dame, built in the second half of the twelfth century, is one of the early masterpieces of Gothic architecture. Look up at the towers and you will see stone oxen peering out from the tops, a tribute, legend says, to the animals that hauled the building materials up the hill. The streets around the cathedral are full of old houses, small squares and views over the plains, and walking the ramparts at dusk is pure pleasure.

The climb to the upper town is fun in itself, with several roads winding up the steep slopes in a series of bends. They are short, but they give a sense of drama to the arrival. Once at the top, parking is usually easy, and there are cafés and restaurants around the cathedral and the town hall. The lower town, spread around the base of the hill, has the supermarkets and fuel stations.

South of Laon lies the Chemin des Dames, a ridge road that became one of the bloodiest sectors of the Western Front, above all during the failed French offensive of April 1917. Today it is a quiet road with memorials, cemeteries and the remains of underground quarries, and riding it is a sobering experience. Further south, the Aisne valley offers gentle, flowing roads through woods and farmland towards Soissons. Weather in this region can be changeable; even in summer, a grey day with low cloud can wrap the hill in mist, which is atmospheric, if a little damp.
t.chartres@48.4,1.5:
The spires of Chartres cathedral appear on the horizon while you are still deep in the wheat fields of the Beauce, two mismatched towers, one plain and one flamboyant, rising out of the flat land like a mirage. For pilgrims, for centuries, that first sight was a moment of joy, and it still is if you approach on the quiet roads from the east or south.

The cathedral is one of the great buildings of the world. Most of it dates from the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, after a fire destroyed the earlier church, and it has kept most of its original stained glass, including windows of an intense blue that glassmakers have never quite matched. On the floor of the nave is a large labyrinth, which pilgrims walked as a symbolic journey. Even if you are not a church person, standing inside on a sunny afternoon, with coloured light spilling across the stone, is something you will remember.

Around the cathedral, the old town drops down to the Eure, where old houses, mills and washhouses line the river, and the riverside lanes are made for walking off lunch. Chartres has plenty of restaurants and cafés, from simple crêperies to more refined places, and in the summer evenings the cathedral and other monuments are illuminated with coloured light projections that are surprisingly well done.

The riding around Chartres is a story of contrasts. The Beauce is flat and open, with long straight roads, big skies and, on a windy day, a lot of buffeting. It is not technical, but there is a certain meditative quality to it. To the west, the landscape changes as you head into the Perche, a region of rolling hills, hedgerows, manor houses and the powerful Percheron draught horses. The roads there are narrower and more winding, and the scenery is greener. Chartres has fuel, workshops and all the services you might need, and it is a good base for exploring both landscapes.
t.cannes ecluse@48.4,3.0:
Cannes-Écluse is a small town on the Yonne, just upstream from where that river joins the Seine at Montereau-Fault-Yonne. The name has nothing to do with the film festival on the Riviera; écluse means lock, and the town grew up around the river traffic and the locks that controlled it. Today it is a quiet residential place, and for riders it is mostly a convenient fuel stop on the way south into Burgundy.

The neighbouring town of Montereau carries a heavier load of history. In 1419, on the bridge at the confluence, John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, was assassinated during a meeting with the future Charles VII, an act that pushed Burgundy into alliance with England and prolonged the Hundred Years' War. Nearly four centuries later, in February 1814, Napoleon won one of his last victories here against the Austrians and Württembergers, and there is an equestrian statue of him near the river.

The landscape around Cannes-Écluse is a mix of river valleys, gravel pits, farmland and woods. The Yonne valley road south towards Pont-sur-Yonne and Sens is pleasant, with gentle curves following the river and views of barges and willows. To the east and west, the plateaus are more open, with big fields and straight roads. The surface is generally good, though some minor roads can be patched and bumpy, and the valley can collect morning fog in autumn.

Cannes-Écluse itself has fewer than three thousand inhabitants, so services are limited, but Montereau, a few minutes away, has supermarkets, fuel stations and plenty of food options. This is not a place to linger long, but it is a useful hinge in the ride: behind you lie the woods and plains of the Île-de-France, ahead the long sweep into Burgundy towards Auxerre. If the weather is warm, a few minutes by the river, watching the water slide past, is a pleasant pause before the next stretch.
t.auxerre@47.8,3.6:
Auxerre is best seen first from the bridge over the Yonne. The old town climbs the west bank in a jumble of rooftops, crowned by the Gothic cathedral of Saint-Étienne and the abbey of Saint-Germain, with the river sliding past below. It is one of the classic views of Burgundy, and it sets the tone for a town that wears its history lightly.

The abbey of Saint-Germain is particularly remarkable. Beneath it lies a Carolingian crypt with wall paintings that are among the oldest surviving in France, some dating back to the ninth century. The cathedral has fine stained glass and a crypt of its own. In the streets of the old town you will find half-timbered houses, a clock tower with an astronomical dial and plenty of small squares where cafés set out their tables. Auxerre also has a solid football tradition, thanks to AJ Auxerre and the long reign of its coach Guy Roux, which still comes up in local conversation.

For lunch, Auxerre is a good place to try classic Burgundian cooking: eggs poached in red wine sauce, known as oeufs en meurette, cheesy gougères, jambon persillé and, of course, wine. The vineyards of Chablis lie only about twenty kilometres to the east, and many restaurants serve the crisp local whites. If you are riding on, you will want to go easy, but a glass with lunch is part of the culture.

The riding around Auxerre is varied and rewarding. To the east, the roads into Chablis country climb over limestone hills striped with vines, with long views and gentle curves. To the south, the Yonne valley and the Canal du Nivernais offer pleasant riverside roads, and further on the hills of the Morvan begin, with forests and more challenging bends. Auxerre has everything you might need in terms of fuel and services. Spring and autumn are especially lovely here, with mild temperatures and the vineyards changing colour, while summer can be hot but is softened by the river.
t.la clayette@46.3,4.3:
