La Clayette is a small town in the Brionnais, the hilly southern corner of Burgundy, and its centrepiece is a castle reflected in a lake. The château, with its towers and turrets, rises straight out of the water, and on a still morning the reflection is almost perfect. It is privately owned, so you can admire it from the lakeside but not usually from the inside.

This is cattle country. The Charolais breed, the big, cream-white beef cattle you see in fields all over the world, originated in this area, and the meadows around La Clayette are full of them, grazing between hedgerows and old oaks. On market days, the farmers come to town, and the bars fill with talk of animals and prices. The local restaurants serve Charolais beef in all its forms, and if you are a meat eater, it is worth trying.

The Brionnais is also known for its Romanesque churches, small, beautiful buildings in golden stone scattered through the villages, with carved portals and tympana. Anzy-le-Duc and Semur-en-Brionnais are among the most famous, both a short ride away. To the east, the Montagne de Dun, a hill with a ruined chapel at the top, offers wide views over the countryside.

The roads around La Clayette are a joy for riders who like gentle, winding routes through rolling countryside. They are quiet, mostly well surfaced, and they meander through hills, woods and pastures, with constant changes of direction and gradient. You will meet tractors and cattle trucks, and occasionally cows on the road, so ride with care. La Clayette is a small town, so for a full range of services, you might need to head to Paray-le-Monial, about twenty-three kilometres away, famous for its Romanesque basilica. Spring and early summer, with the hedges in flower and the meadows green, are lovely.
t.la machine@46.9,3.5:
The name sounds like a joke, but it is a piece of industrial history. La Machine, in the Nièvre in central France, grew up around a coal mine, and it takes its name from the machine, a steam-driven pump installed in the eighteenth century to drain the mine shafts, which was such a novelty that it gave the place its identity. Mining continued here for centuries, and the last pit closed in the 1970s. Today, the Musée de la Mine, built around the old headframe, tells the story of the miners, with a reconstructed gallery where you can see how they worked.

It is a quiet working town, not a pretty one, and it is worth knowing that it has nothing to do with the famous Col de la Machine, the vertiginous balcony road above the Combe Laval in the Vercors, far away to the south-east near Grenoble. If your ride name led you to expect cliffs and tunnels, the plateau here will be a surprise. That said, the Nivernais countryside around La Machine is pleasant enough riding: rolling hills, woods, meadows and small villages, with quiet roads.

Decize, a few kilometres south, is the more interesting town for a stop. It sits on an island in the Loire, at the junction with the Aron and the Canal du Nivernais, and its old town has the remains of a castle and a long promenade of plane trees along the river. The canal itself, built to carry timber from the Morvan to Paris, is now used by pleasure boats, and its towpaths are popular with cyclists.

La Machine has a few bars and restaurants, and Decize has more choice and fuel. The roads in the area are generally good, quiet and easy, with gentle curves and little traffic. To the east lie the forests and hills of the Morvan, with more challenging roads, and to the west the Loire valley. The Loire here is wild and unchanneled, with sandbanks and islands that change shape with the floods, and the riverside roads have a peaceful, timeless quality. Summers are warm and pleasant; winters can be damp and grey.
t.near irigny@45.7,4.8:
South of Lyon, the Rhône broadens into a powerful, heavily engineered river, lined with locks, power stations and chemical plants on the east bank. The west bank, where around Irigny, Charly and Vernaison, is softer: a strip of villages, orchards and market gardens rising gently towards the Monts du Lyonnais. Rides begin and end here for a simple reason: it sits outside the congested core of the city but within easy reach of it.

The area was once famous for its fruit, particularly cherries and peaches, and in early summer you will still see roadside stalls selling local produce. The villages have a mixture of old stone farmhouses, nineteenth-century country houses built by wealthy Lyon families, and modern suburbs. Across the river, the industrial corridor known as the Vallée de la Chimie is one of the largest concentrations of chemical industry in France, a reminder that Lyon's prosperity was built on silk, chemicals and engineering.

Lyon itself is famous for its food, and if you are finishing a ride here, it is worth heading into the city for dinner. The traditional restaurants known as bouchons serve hearty dishes like quenelles, andouillette and salade lyonnaise, washed down with Beaujolais or Côtes du Rhône. The old town, with its Renaissance houses and hidden passageways, and the hill of Fourvière, with its basilica and Roman theatres, are worth a visit too.

The Beaujolais rides head north from here, either through the city or around it, to the vineyards and hills north-west of Lyon. Getting through or around Lyon can be slow, especially at peak times, and the motorway around the city is notoriously congested, so leave early. The local roads on the west bank are pleasant, winding through villages and orchards. The surrounding towns cover fuel and shopping. Summers in the Rhône valley are hot, and the mistral wind can blow strongly down the valley, especially in winter and spring, so be prepared for gusts.
t.near chaponost@45.7,4.7:
The Romans brought water to Lyon from the Pilat massif, some eighty kilometres away, and the most impressive surviving section of their work stands at Chaponost, a few kilometres from the point. The Gier aqueduct, as it is called, crossed the valleys on arches of stone and brick, and at Chaponost a long line of them still marches across a field, some still carrying their channels. It is a remarkable sight, all the more so for being in an ordinary suburban setting, and it is easily reached by a short detour.

The point itself lies near Brindas and Messimy, on the western edge of the Lyon agglomeration, where the city meets the first hills of the Monts du Lyonnais. These hills are a patchwork of orchards, meadows, woods and small villages, with views back over the city and, on clear days, the Alps on the eastern horizon. Mont Blanc can sometimes be seen from here, a white shape floating above the haze.

The rides that finish here come back from the east, from the Bugey, the Chartreuse and the Vercors, often after a long day of mountain roads. The final stretch involves crossing or skirting Lyon, which can be slow and frustrating at rush hour, so try to time your return for the evening, after the peak. Once you are on the west side of the city, the roads become quieter and more pleasant, winding up into the hills.

The local villages have bakeries, cafés and small restaurants, and there are fuel stations and supermarkets in the larger towns nearby. For a proper dinner, Lyon is close enough to make an evening trip worthwhile. The Monts du Lyonnais themselves are worth exploring on another day, with a dense network of small roads, tight bends and gentle climbs, and very little traffic. Spring, when the fruit trees are in flower, is particularly beautiful, but autumn, with the leaves turning and the air crisp, is lovely too.
t.brignais@45.7,4.7:
In 1362, on the slopes above Brignais, a royal army sent to clear out bands of unemployed mercenaries, the Tard-Venus, who were ravaging the Lyon area during a lull in the Hundred Years' War, was soundly defeated by them. It was an embarrassing moment for the French crown, and the mercenaries went on plundering the region for some time afterwards. Today there is little trace of the battle, and Brignais is a busy town of some twelve thousand people on the south-western edge of Lyon, in the valley of the Garon.

The town has grown rapidly as a suburb, with shopping centres, business parks and housing estates, but it has kept a small old centre with a church and a few old houses. The surrounding villages, like Orliénas and Soucieu-en-Jarrest, are more rural, with orchards, meadows and views over the Lyonnais hills. In Soucieu, more arches of the Roman aqueduct that carried water to Lyon can be seen in the fields.

The Ardèche rides that start and finish here head south, down the Rhône valley, to the gorges of the Ardèche, one of the most spectacular natural sights in France. The fastest way is the A7 motorway, but it is busy and boring, so most riders prefer the roads along the west bank of the Rhône, through the vineyards of the Côte-Rôtie and Condrieu, or across the hills of the Pilat. The Pilat massif, south of Lyon, has some excellent roads, winding through forests and over passes, with views over the Rhône valley and the Alps.

Brignais has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and fast food, and it is a convenient place to stock up before a long day. Coming back in the evening, the traffic around Lyon can be heavy, so allow extra time. The weather in the Lyon area is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and the mistral can blow strongly down the Rhône valley, making the riding gusty and tiring. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons.
t.saint saens@49.7,1.3:
Saint-Saëns is a small market town in the Pays de Bray, in Upper Normandy, and the composer Camille Saint-Saëns's family name is said to have come from here, though he was born in Paris and had little to do with the place. The town sits in the valley of the Varenne, surrounded by meadows, apple orchards and forests, and it has a quiet, rural charm, with brick and timber houses and a market square.

On its doorstep lies the Forêt d'Eawy, one of the most beautiful beech forests in Normandy. Running through it is the Allée des Limousins, a perfectly straight forest road that stretches for over a dozen kilometres between towering beeches. Riding along it, with the trees arching overhead and the light filtering through the leaves, is a strangely meditative experience, especially in autumn, when the beeches turn gold and copper.

The Pays de Bray is a distinctive landscape: a long, eroded valley in the chalk, where the underlying clay is exposed, producing lush meadows ideal for dairy farming. The region is famous for its cheese, in particular Neufchâtel, a soft, bloomy-rind cheese often shaped like a heart, made around the town of Neufchâtel-en-Bray, about thirteen kilometres away. Cider and calvados are made from the local apples, and you will see orchards everywhere, often with cows grazing beneath the trees.

The roads around Saint-Saëns are quiet and pleasant, winding through valleys, forests and villages, with little traffic. They can be wet and muddy, especially in autumn and winter, and slippery under the trees. Saint-Saëns is small, so fuel and services are limited; Neufchâtel-en-Bray is the nearest larger town. The weather in Normandy is often grey and damp, with frequent showers, but when the sun comes out, the green landscape glows. Late spring, when the apple trees are in flower, is the most beautiful time to ride here.
t.pannes@48.0,2.7:
Pannes is a small town on the northern edge of Montargis, in the Gâtinais, about a hundred kilometres south of Paris, and for most riders it is simply a fuel stop on the way south to Sancerre. It lies in a flat, agricultural landscape of wheat fields, small woods and rivers, with the suburban sprawl of Montargis and Châlette-sur-Loing to the south.

Montargis itself is worth a short detour. It is sometimes called the Venice of the Gâtinais, because the Loing river and several canals run through the town, crossed by dozens of small bridges. The canals, lined with old houses and flowers, give the town a charming, peaceful atmosphere. Montargis is also famous for the praline, a sweet of caramelised almonds, said to have been invented in the seventeenth century by the cook of the Duke of Plessis-Praslin, after whom it was named. Confectioners in the town still make them, and a small bag is a good snack for the road.

The Gâtinais is a region of gentle landscapes, with rivers like the Loing and the Ouanne winding through fields and woods, and canals like the Canal de Briare, one of the oldest canals in France, built in the early seventeenth century to link the Loire and the Seine. Further south, at Briare, the canal crosses the Loire on the Pont-Canal de Briare, a long iron aqueduct finished at the end of the nineteenth century, where boats glide across above the river. It is well worth a stop on the way to Sancerre.

The roads around Pannes are flat and straight, with little to excite the rider, but they are quiet and easy, and they cover ground quickly. Watch out for speed cameras, which are common on the main roads. Pannes, Châlette-sur-Loing and Montargis between them supply fuel, groceries and lunch. The weather is typical of the centre of France: warm summers, cool winters, with frequent changes. The light over the flat fields can be beautiful, especially in the early morning and evening.
t.sancerre@47.3,2.8:
Sancerre is a hill town in the most literal sense: a cluster of stone houses wrapped around the top of a steep, isolated hill rising above the Loire, with vineyards falling away on every side. From the old Tour des Fiefs, the last remaining tower of the castle, the view stretches across the river valley to Pouilly on the other bank and far over the rolling vineyards. On a clear day, it is one of the most beautiful views in central France.

The name is known worldwide for wine. The crisp, mineral whites made from Sauvignon Blanc on the chalky and flinty soils of these slopes are among the most famous expressions of the grape, and there are also reds and rosés from Pinot Noir. The small village of Chavignol, just outside Sancerre, gives its name to the Crottin de Chavignol, a small, round goat's cheese that is the perfect match for the wine. A plate of crottin, a slice of bread and a glass of Sancerre on a terrace in the old town is a simple pleasure that is hard to beat, even if you limit yourself to a single small glass.

The town has a dramatic history. In 1573, during the Wars of Religion, the Protestant population of Sancerre was besieged by royal troops for several months, and the people were reduced to eating leather, parchment and worse before surrendering. Today, the narrow streets and squares of the old town are peaceful, full of wine shops, restaurants and cafés.

The roads around Sancerre are a joy to ride, winding through the vineyards, up and down the steep slopes, with constant views and changes of direction. They can be narrow and steep, with tight bends, and during the harvest in September, tractors and grape pickers are everywhere. Sancerre is small, so fuel options are limited; Cosne-Cours-sur-Loire, about eleven kilometres away, has more. Below the town, Saint-Satur sits on the river, with a large viaduct, now a footpath, and the Loire, wide and wild, with sandbanks and islands.
t.macon@46.3,4.8:
Mâcon sits on the west bank of the Saône, where the river runs broad and unhurried at the southern end of Burgundy. It is a busy, practical town, often overlooked by people speeding down the A6 towards the south, but it has a pleasant riverside, a long stone bridge and a relaxed southern atmosphere. The light here already feels different, warmer and softer, a hint of the Mediterranean that lies further down the Rhône.

The poet and statesman Alphonse de Lamartine was born in Mâcon in 1790, and he is the town's great figure, with a statue, a museum and streets named after him. He spent much of his life in the surrounding countryside, at the châteaux of Milly and Saint-Point, and his romantic poetry was inspired by the landscapes of the Mâconnais. Of the old cathedral of Saint-Vincent, only the twin towers and narthex remain, after it was largely destroyed during the Revolution.

The real riches of the area lie to the west. The Mâconnais hills are covered in vineyards, producing white wines from Chardonnay, including the famous Pouilly-Fuissé. Above the vineyards, the Roche de Solutré, a dramatic limestone escarpment shaped like a ship's prow, rises above the villages. At its foot, archaeologists found the remains of thousands of horses and other animals from the Palaeolithic era, giving its name to the Solutrean culture. François Mitterrand used to climb the rock every year, and the walk to the top is well worth it for the view.

The roads through the Mâconnais vineyards are a delight, winding through the hills, between the vines and the villages, with constant views of the rocks and the valley. They are narrow and twisty in places, with little traffic outside the harvest season. Mâcon has plenty of fuel, food and services, and the riverside quays are a pleasant place to take a break. Summers are warm and sunny, and the vineyards are particularly beautiful in autumn, when the leaves turn gold and red.
t.cluny@46.4,4.7:
For about two centuries, the largest church in Christendom stood in this small Burgundian town. The abbey of Cluny, founded in 910, grew into the head of a vast network of monasteries across Europe, and its third church, begun at the end of the eleventh century, was longer than any other until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt. Popes came from its ranks, kings sought its blessing. Then came the Revolution: the abbey was dissolved, sold, and used for decades as a stone quarry. What remains is a fragment, a single soaring arm of the transept with its octagonal bell tower, and the empty space around it is almost more eloquent than the building would have been.

Walk through the abbey precinct and you can feel the scale. Digital reconstructions in the visitor centre show the church as it was, and the town around it still follows the lines of the old monastery, with Romanesque houses, towers and gates scattered through the streets. The national stud farm, established by Napoleon, occupies part of the old abbey grounds, and you may see horses being exercised.

For lunch, Cluny has a good selection of cafés and restaurants around the abbey, serving Burgundian classics and Charolais beef, which comes from the pastures just to the west. A few kilometres north, the ecumenical community of Taizé attracts thousands of young pilgrims every year, a modern echo of Cluny's spiritual pull.

Getting here from Mâcon is half the fun. The road climbs over the hills of the Mâconnais, through vineyards and woods, with tight bends and fine views, before dropping into the valley of the Grosne. Another route passes near the Roche de Solutré and the vineyards of Pouilly-Fuissé. Traffic is light, the surfaces are mostly good, and the scenery changes constantly. The old railway line between Cluny and Mâcon is now a greenway for cyclists, so expect bikes at the crossings. Cluny is small, but it has the basics; for a wider choice of fuel and shops, the towns around Mâcon are the better bet.
t.pollionnay@45.8,4.7:
The road from Lyon over the Col de la Luère is a local institution. It climbs west from the suburbs into the Monts du Lyonnais, through woods and meadows, with a series of bends that every rider and cyclist in Lyon seems to know by heart, and Pollionnay, a small village at the foot of the climb, is where many of them end their rides. It has a church, a few houses on the slopes and views back over the city, and it feels much further from Lyon than it actually is.

The Monts du Lyonnais are a range of rounded hills west of Lyon, rising to around nine hundred metres, with a dense network of small roads through farmland, forests and villages. The landscape is green and gentle, with fruit orchards, dairy farms and stone farmhouses, and the roads are quiet and winding, with constant changes of gradient. The Yzeron valley, just south, has a small reservoir and pleasant roads along the river.

The rides that end here come back from the high Alps and Provence. The Alpe d'Huez, with its twenty-one numbered hairpins, each named after a winner of the Tour de France stage that finishes there, is cycling folklore, and it is a fantastic ride on a motorcycle, though often crowded with cyclists. Mont Ventoux, the Giant of Provence, rises to around 1,900 metres from the lavender fields of the Vaucluse, its bare white summit of limestone scree visible for miles, and the memorial to the British cyclist Tom Simpson, who died on its slopes in 1967, stands near the top.

After such long days, the gentle hills of the Lyonnais are a welcome sight. Pollionnay itself is small, with limited services, but the surrounding towns, like Craponne and Tassin, have fuel, shops and restaurants. The weather in the Monts du Lyonnais can be cooler and wetter than in Lyon, and the roads can be slippery in the shade under the trees.
t.near epernon on the way back@48.7,1.7:
West of Rambouillet forest the land loosens up into a patchwork of wheat, copses and small river valleys, and this stop sits in that gentle seam between the Yvelines and the Eure-et-Loir. Épernon is the nearest proper town, a few kilometres off, built where the Guesle and the Drouette meet before they wander on towards the Eure. It is quiet country, and after a day on the Seine loops it feels like the ride is exhaling.

The name may ring a bell. The dukes of Épernon took their title from this little town, the best known being Jean-Louis de Nogaret, the swaggering favourite of Henri III who outlived several kings and most of his enemies. A short hop south-west brings you to Maintenon, where the arches of Louis XIV's unfinished aqueduct still stride across the château grounds, a monument to a plan to send the Eure to the fountains of Versailles that war and money eventually killed.

As for water you can actually get into: the rivers here are narrow, shaded and better for looking at than swimming in. The realistic option is the string of étangs de Hollande inside Rambouillet forest, to the east, which has long had a summer bathing area. Check that it is open and supervised before you plan around it, because rules on these ponds change with the season and the water quality.

The riding is easy rather than dramatic. Narrow departmental roads run between fields and through villages with grey stone churches, with the occasional slow tractor and a lot of deer warning signs, which mean it around dusk. Surfaces are generally decent but patched, and gravel collects at farm entrances. Wind can push you around on the open plateau when the forest edge falls away.

Épernon has the shops, cafés and fuel you need, and Rambouillet, with its château and the royal dairy built for Marie-Antoinette, is close enough for a longer break if the day allows. Otherwise take the cool of the trees, a drink, and the slow road home.
t.near ambierle on the way back@46.1,3.9:
The Côte Roannaise is a long east-facing slope where the Monts de la Madeleine drop towards the Loire plain, and Ambierle sits high on it, with vineyards falling away below and the forested hills at its back. On a clear morning you can see across the plain to the Monts du Lyonnais and beyond. This stop is down on the edge of that slope, between Ambierle and Renaison, at the point where the vines give way to meadows and hedges.

Ambierle is worth the short climb. Its priory church, a Benedictine foundation rebuilt in late Gothic style, holds a carved and painted altarpiece from Flanders that is far finer than anyone expects to find in a village of under two thousand people. Nearby Saint-Haon-le-Châtel is a small walled village with old houses squeezed inside its ramparts.

The wine is gamay, as in Beaujolais, but grown on granite and making lighter, peppery reds under the Côte Roannaise name. Roanne, down on the plain, has an outsized reputation for food thanks to the Troisgros family, whose restaurant put the town on the gastronomic map decades ago.

For a swim, keep your expectations sensible. Above Renaison the dams of La Tache and Chartrain hold the drinking water for Roanne, so bathing there is off limits. The nearest proper option is the Loire itself, held back by the Villerest dam south of Roanne, where the lake has had organised bathing and water sports areas in summer.

The riding is lovely. The D8 runs along the hillside through the wine villages with constant views, while roads climbing into the Monts de la Madeleine twist through pine and beech towards the passes, with bumpy patches and the odd logging truck. Renaison and Riorges have fuel and shops, Roanne everything else.
t.near beaujeu on the way back@46.2,4.5:
The Haut Beaujolais is not the Beaujolais most people imagine. North-west of Beaujeu the vineyards run out and the hills rise into forest, dark Douglas fir plantations, beech woods, steep pastures with Charolais cattle grazing on them. This stop sits in that upland country between Beaujeu and Matour, where the roads loop over ridges and down into narrow valleys with small farming villages.

Beaujeu gave the whole region its name. The lords of Beaujeu controlled this country in the Middle Ages, and Anne de Beaujeu, daughter of Louis XI, effectively ruled France as regent during her brother's minority. The town is still the wine capital of the area and celebrates the release of Beaujolais nouveau every November with bonfires and plenty of wine. Higher up, Mont Saint-Rigaud is the highest point in the Rhône department, a forested summit with views over the hills towards the Saône.

For a swim the best option is a ride away. The Lac des Sapins at Cublize, south-west of here, is a large lake with a natural-filter bathing area, which makes it one of the more unusual and reliable swimming spots in the region in summer. Closer to this stop you mostly find streams and ponds, pleasant for a rest in the shade but not for diving in.

The riding is what you came for. The roads are narrow and twisty, with sudden blind corners, gravel at junctions and occasional sheep or cattle crossing between fields. Expect cool, fresh air under the firs even on hot days, and fog in the valleys on autumn mornings. Traffic is light except for timber trucks during the week.

Matour and Beaujeu have cafés, bakeries and basic shops. For fuel, plan ahead: Belleville, down on the Saône plain, is the safest bet, and smaller villages may have nothing or only an automatic pump.
t.near neuville sur saone@45.9,4.9:
Neuville-sur-Saône sits in a bend of the river just north of Lyon, and this stop is up on the plateau east of it, between Montanay and Cailloux-sur-Fontaines. The land here is open farmland and new housing, a transition zone where the city thins out and the Dombes begins. It is not the place for scenery, but it is a sensible finish: close to the motorways, with easy access back into Lyon or out towards the Ain.

The history is subtle but real. Neuville was once the capital of the Franc-Lyonnais, a small territory along the left bank of the Saône that enjoyed tax privileges under the old monarchy. The town took its present name in the seventeenth century from Camille de Neufville de Villeroy, archbishop of Lyon, who rebuilt it and left behind a large church with twin towers that still dominates the riverside.

Across the river rise the Monts d'Or, a small limestone massif with old villages, stone walls and views over Lyon. On a clear evening the hills glow in the low sun, and the Saône below is calm and wide. The quays at Neuville are a pleasant place for a slow walk after a long ride, and the bridges give you views up and down the river.

Riding into this area at the end of a day, you come off quiet roads and into the traffic of the Lyon outskirts. The D433 and D51 can be busy, especially at rush hour, and roundabouts come thick and fast. Watch for cyclists along the river and for slow traffic on the narrow roads of the villages.

Neuville has fuel, cafés, bakeries and restaurants, and the town is busy on market days. If you want to finish with a meal, the riverfront has a few places with terraces where you can watch the barges go by.
t.fresnes@48.7,2.3:
Fresnes is a working suburb on the southern edge of Paris, between Antony, Wissous and the sprawl of Rungis. It is not a place anyone visits for its scenery, but as a start and finish it does the job well. The A6 and A86 are close, the N118 heads west towards the Chevreuse valley, and the Vexin and Seine cliffs are within reach after a short motorway dash.

The name carries weight in French history. The prison of Fresnes, one of the largest in France, was used by the Gestapo during the occupation to hold members of the Resistance and Allied agents, many of whom were tortured or deported from there. The prison is still in use, and the walls remain an imposing presence on the town's edge.

Next door, Rungis houses the vast wholesale food market that replaced the old Les Halles in central Paris in 1969. It is the largest fresh-food market in the world, and the trucks moving in and out at night give you an idea of how much the city eats. If you start early, you will see the traffic around it.

Riding out from here, the first part is all about getting clear of the city. Expect heavy traffic on the A86 and N118 at peak hours, plenty of lane changes and speed cameras. Once you are past Saclay and into the Chevreuse valley, the roads open up and the countryside begins.

Fuel stations sit on every arterial road and the bakeries open early, so there is no excuse for leaving hungry or on reserve. On the way back, aim to arrive outside rush hour if you can, or plan to filter through traffic with patience.
t.near sury le comtal on the way back@45.6:
The Forez plain is one of those places you do not notice until you are in it: a wide, flat basin of the upper Loire, ringed by the Monts du Forez to the west and the Monts du Lyonnais to the east. This stop lies on its southern half, between Précieux, Sury-le-Comtal and Saint-Romain-le-Puy, in a country of fields, hedges, scattered farms and, here and there, the glint of a pond.

Those ponds are the plain's quiet signature. Hundreds of them were dug over the centuries for fish, and today they make the Forez an important stop for migrating birds, with herons, grebes and marsh harriers working the reeds. Most belong to private estates or fishing associations, so they are scenery rather than swimming water. For a real dip, look for a designated leisure lake in the area in summer, or accept that a shady bench is all this stop will give you.

What makes the view is Saint-Romain-le-Puy. A small basalt cone, the remains of an ancient volcano, rises straight out of the flat land, and on top of it sits a Romanesque priory church that has kept watch over the plain for nearly a thousand years. Sury-le-Comtal has a château with remarkable carved wooden interiors, and Montbrison, a little further north, gives its name to fourme de Montbrison, a mild blue cheese that goes well with the local reds.

The riding here is mostly about transit, with long straight roads, roundabouts and the occasional village bend. The fun begins when you head west into the Monts du Forez, where roads climb in tight loops through pine forest to high moorland. Weather can shift quickly up there, with fog and cold wind even in summer.

Sury-le-Comtal and Saint-Romain have bakeries, cafés and the basic shops, and fuel is easy to find in the larger villages. Take the basalt cone as your landmark and you will not lose yourself.
t.brignais@45.7,4.8:
Brignais is where the ride hands you back to Lyon. It sits in the valley of the Garon on the south-western edge of the city, a busy town of shops, light industry and housing estates, with the Monts du Lyonnais rising gently behind it and the Pilat a blue shadow further south. After a day on the ridges it is an unglamorous but very practical finish.

Its name lives on in the history books for a battle that went badly wrong. In 1362 a royal French army met the free companies, bands of unpaid soldiers left over from the Hundred Years' War who were pillaging the region, near Brignais. The mercenaries, who held the high ground, crushed the knights sent to stop them, and the defeat left the Lyonnais at their mercy for years. There is little to see today, but it is a reminder that this quiet suburb was once on the front line of a very different kind of war.

The countryside around is still farming land, with orchards, market gardens and small vineyards on the slopes of the Coteaux du Lyonnais. In spring the cherry trees around Vourles and Charly flower white, and in early summer the farm stalls fill with cherries and apricots.

Coming in from the Pilat, the roads change character fast. The flowing bends of the hills give way to roundabouts, traffic lights and commuter traffic. The A450 and the old national roads funnel everything towards Lyon, and the evening rush can be dense. Watch for buses, cyclists and drivers changing lanes without warning.

Brignais has every service a town of twelve thousand needs, with fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets and plenty of cafés. If you want a last beer before the city swallows you, the centre has a few terraces where you can sit, peel off your gloves and argue about the best corner of the day.
t.enghien les bains@49.0,2.3:
Enghien-les-Bains is the only town in the Paris region that feels like a spa resort, and that is exactly what it was built to be. The town grew up in the nineteenth century around sulphurous springs and a lake, and the Parisians who came to take the waters left behind villas, promenades and a casino. This finish puts you right on the lake shore, with Montmorency forest on the hills behind.

The casino is famous for a legal quirk. French law long prohibited casinos within a hundred kilometres of Paris, and Enghien was granted an exception, which made it the gambling address of the capital for generations. The thermal baths are still in use, and the lake, with its boats, fountains and lakeside paths, makes for a gentle walk after a long ride.

The forest of Montmorency, on the ridge north of the town, is a large wood of chestnut and oak, criss-crossed by roads and tracks. Jean-Jacques Rousseau lived in Montmorency for several years and wrote some of his major works there, and his house is now a museum.

The ride into Enghien from the Seine valley takes you through the northern suburbs, with plenty of traffic, roundabouts and speed bumps. The roads are generally well surfaced but busy, and the last kilometres are about patience rather than pleasure. Parking for motorcycles is usually available near the lake.

The lakeside terraces are the obvious place to end, and on a summer evening, with the water lit and the casino glowing, Enghien has a faintly Belle Époque holiday air that is odd and rather lovely so close to the périphérique. Fuel is easier in the neighbouring towns than in the centre.
t.near pont sainte maxence on the way back:
North of Senlis the Oise runs in a broad, flat-bottomed valley between two great forests, Halatte to the south and Compiègne to the north-east. This stop lies in that valley between Verberie and Pontpoint, a few kilometres upstream of Pont-Sainte-Maxence, where barges still push along the river and gravel pits have turned old meadows into chains of lakes.

The area has a deep royal past. Verberie was a residence of Merovingian and Carolingian kings, and the forests were royal hunting grounds for centuries. At Pontpoint, the ruins of the abbey of Le Moncel, founded by Philip the Fair in the early fourteenth century, stand in a park by the river, with a huge Gothic roof structure that has survived the centuries. Compiègne, with its palace and the clearing where the 1918 armistice was signed, is a short ride away.

For a swim, the Oise itself is not an option: it is a working waterway with currents and boat traffic. The flooded gravel pits along the valley are tempting on a hot day, but most are private or used for fishing, and some are dangerous because of steep, unstable banks and very cold water at depth. Only swim where bathing is clearly allowed and supervised.

The riding is pleasant rather than thrilling. The roads along the valley are flat and fast, while the forest roads through Halatte and Compiègne are straight, shaded and often lined with beech and oak. Expect deer crossings, especially at dawn and dusk, and heavy traffic on the main roads at weekends.

Fuel is no problem in Pont-Sainte-Maxence, and Verberie has the bakery-and-bar basics. Senlis, twenty minutes south, is the better dinner: a cathedral, crooked medieval lanes and more good tables than a town that size deserves.
t.near neuville sur saone@45.9,4.8:
On the west bank of the Saône, opposite Neuville, the land rises quickly from the river into the Monts d'Or. This stop sits on that slope between Chasselay and Albigny-sur-Saône, where the last suburbs of Lyon fade into orchards, stone walls and small vineyards, and the hills begin to glow golden in the evening light.

That colour is the clue to the country just north of here. The Pierres Dorées area, the southern tip of the Beaujolais, takes its name from a local limestone rich in iron oxide that turns honey-gold in the sun. Villages like Chessy, Oingt and Theizé are built entirely of it, with castles, churches and houses that look warm even on cloudy days. It is one of the most beautiful parts of the Lyon region, and it begins only a few kilometres from here.

The Monts d'Or themselves are a small but steep massif, topped by Mont Verdun, whose summit is occupied by a military air base and an old fort. Mont Thou and Mont Cindre, nearby, offer views over Lyon and the Saône valley. The slopes are covered with woods, meadows and old stone quarries, and the area is popular with walkers and cyclists.

The riding here is pleasant and varied. Small roads climb into the hills with tight bends and steep gradients, while the riverside road is flat and fast. Traffic can be heavy near Lyon, especially at rush hour, and the narrow village roads require attention.

Neuville over the bridge covers fuel and groceries. But if the light is still good, point the bike north for twenty minutes instead: a glass of Beaujolais in a square of golden stone beats any petrol-station coffee.
t.le raincy@48.9,2.5:
Le Raincy is a small, leafy town on the eastern edge of Paris, a place of large villas, quiet streets and old trees, surrounded by much busier neighbours like Bondy and Montfermeil. It was once part of a vast estate belonging to the Orléans family, and when the land was divided in the nineteenth century, it was laid out as a residential park for the well-to-do. That gives it a calm, slightly old-fashioned feel that contrasts with the motorways a few kilometres away.

The town has one building that architects travel to see. The church of Notre-Dame du Raincy, built by Auguste Perret in the early 1920s, was one of the first churches made entirely of reinforced concrete, with walls replaced by a continuous screen of coloured glass. It was revolutionary at the time and is now considered a landmark of modern architecture. If you finish early enough, it is well worth a look.

The forest of Bondy, nearby, is a remnant of a much larger forest that once stretched across this part of the Île-de-France, famous in the Middle Ages for its brigands. Today it is a pleasant area of woods and ponds, popular with walkers.

The ride into Le Raincy is all about the eastern suburbs, with busy roads, traffic lights and roundabouts. The A3 and A86 are close, and the N3 heads east towards Meaux and the Marne valley. Expect heavy traffic at rush hour and speed cameras on the main roads.

Fuel is easiest on the arterial roads of the neighbouring towns. The little centre of Le Raincy itself has a handful of terraces, and after the N3 a quiet table under plane trees feels like a reward earned.
t.verrieres le buisson@48.8,2.3:
Verrières-le-Buisson is one of the greener towns on the southern edge of Paris, a residential place wrapped around a large wood, the Bois de Verrières, that runs along a ridge above the Bièvre valley. Antony and Châtenay-Malabry are next door, but the trees give the town a feeling of space that is rare this close to the capital.

The name is linked to a famous family of plant breeders. The Vilmorins, whose seed company became one of the most important in the world, had their estate here, and their arboretum, planted over generations, still contains rare and old trees. Louise de Vilmorin, writer and socialite, was born in the family house. In Châtenay-Malabry, the Vallée-aux-Loups was the home of Chateaubriand, who planted many of the trees in the park himself.

The Bois de Verrières is a mixed forest of oak, chestnut and beech, crossed by paths and a few roads. It is a pleasant place to walk, and in autumn the colours are rich and warm. The Bièvre valley below has been heavily built over, but the river has been reopened in places, and green corridors follow its course.

Coming back from Fontainebleau, you ride through the southern suburbs, with plenty of traffic, roundabouts and speed cameras. The N118 and A86 are close, and the roads into Verrières are narrow and winding, with speed bumps and parked cars.

My advice is to stop at the edge of the wood before the final stretch home. Ten minutes under the chestnuts does more for a tired back than any coffee. Fuel sits along the main roads, and the town centre has bakeries for a last sugar fix.
t.near ingre on the way back@48.0,1.8:
North of Orléans the Beauce begins, the great wheat plain of France, flat as a table and sown to the horizon. This stop lies on its southern edge, between Ormes, Bricy and Ingré, where the plain meets the suburbs of Orléans and the military air base at Bricy, home to the French air force's transport aircraft. You may see the big grey A400Ms lumbering overhead.

Orléans is the city of Joan of Arc, who lifted the English siege in 1429, and the city still celebrates her every May with processions and festivities. The cathedral of Sainte-Croix, rebuilt in a Gothic style after the Wars of Religion, dominates the old town, and the riverside quays along the Loire are pleasant for a stroll.

The Loire itself is beautiful but dangerous. Its sandbanks shift, its currents are strong and unpredictable, and every summer people drown trying to swim in it. Do not swim in the river. The leisure base on the Île Charlemagne, at Saint-Jean-le-Blanc, has a lake with a supervised bathing area in summer, which is a much safer option.

East of Orléans, the Forêt d'Orléans is one of the largest state forests in France, a vast area of oak and pine with ponds and quiet roads, perfect for a peaceful ride. The roads in the Beauce are straight and fast, but the wind can be strong and the views monotonous.

The suburbs around Ingré solve fuel and groceries in minutes. If you eat in Orléans, look for Olivet, a soft local cow's milk cheese often rolled in ash, and remember that the city was France's vinegar capital for centuries; a few old vinegar houses still trade on the name.
t.sorbiers on the way back@45.5,4.5:
Saint-Étienne made France's guns, bicycles and ribbons, and dug its coal from under its own streets. Sorbiers lies just north-east of the city, in the Jarez valley, where the industrial past gives way to green hills and small farms. The Monts du Lyonnais rise to the north, the Pilat to the south, and the city sprawls in the valley between.

The mining heritage is everywhere. The Puits Couriot, a former coal mine in the city, is now a museum, with the headframe and the slag heaps still standing. The Manufrance company, which made guns and bicycles and sold them through a famous catalogue, was a symbol of the city for a century. And the football club, AS Saint-Étienne, plays at the Stade Geoffroy-Guichard, known as the Chaudron, the cauldron, for its passionate atmosphere.

Swimming nearby is limited. South of the city, the Furan valley holds the Gouffre d'Enfer dam, one of the first large masonry dams in France, built in the nineteenth century to supply water to the city, but swimming is not allowed. Further afield, the Loire gorges and lakes offer options, and the municipal pools are a reliable choice.

The riding around Saint-Étienne is far better than its grimy reputation suggests. The Col de la République, on the old road to Bourg-Argental, was the first mountain pass ever climbed in the Tour de France, in 1903, and it remains a fine, steady climb through pine forest. Beyond it the Pilat opens up a whole network of smaller roads, with tight bends, steep ramps and sudden views east over the Rhône valley to the Alps. North of Sorbiers, the lanes into the Monts du Lyonnais are quieter still, threading through hamlets and pasture on surfaces that range from fresh to frankly agricultural.

Sorbiers and its neighbour La Talaudière cover fuel and shopping without fuss. If you go into the city, try a plate of râpée, the local potato pancake, or a bowl of the creamy, nutty Fourme cheese from the Forez hills, and remember that people here are proud, funny and rarely impressed by anything from Lyon.
t.chasselay@45.9,4.8:
In June 1940, as the German army swept south, a unit of Senegalese tirailleurs fighting for France defended the approaches to Lyon at Chasselay. After they surrendered, many of the African soldiers were separated from their white comrades and massacred. Two years later, a cemetery was built for them in the style of a West African tata, a walled enclosure of red earth, with gates and pointed towers. It stands on the edge of the village today, one of the most moving war memorials in France.

Chasselay itself is a quiet village on the northern slopes of the Monts d'Or, with stone houses, vineyards and views over the Saône valley. The Azergues valley, to the west, leads into the Beaujolais, and the golden-stone villages begin a few kilometres north.

This finish brings you back from the Dombes, the plateau of ponds east of the Saône, where you may have seen herons, egrets and storks among the reeds. The final stretch crosses the river and climbs into the hills, with roads that are narrow and winding.

There is a bakery in the village, and Neuville, a few minutes east, takes care of fuel. Whatever the time, give the Tata ten minutes before you go home. The red walls, the rows of graves, the silence on a summer evening: it is a short stop, and it stays with you for a long time.
t.near saint yan on the way back@46.4,4.0:
White cattle, hedges and Romanesque bell towers: that is the Brionnais, the corner of southern Burgundy where the Loire bends towards Digoin. This stop lies on the plain near Saint-Yan, a village best known in France for its airfield, where the national civil aviation school trains its pilots. Small aircraft circle overhead most days, and the open grassland around the runway gives the place an unusually wide sky.

Charolais cattle are the other local celebrity. The heavy cream-coloured beasts graze in every field, and at Saint-Christophe-en-Brionnais, a short way south-east, one of the biggest live cattle markets in France still takes place every week, with farmers in blue smocks haggling in the early morning. Between the fields stand some of the most beautiful small Romanesque churches in Burgundy, at Anzy-le-Duc, Semur-en-Brionnais and Montceaux-l'Étoile, built in a golden local stone with carved portals that reward a close look.

Paray-le-Monial, a few kilometres north, has a great Romanesque basilica modelled on the lost abbey church of Cluny, and it remains a busy pilgrimage town. Digoin, a little further, has a canal aqueduct that carries boats right across the Loire, an odd sight from the riverbank.

Swimming in the Loire is a bad idea anywhere along its course: shifting sand, sudden holes and strong currents make it treacherous even when it looks lazy. Look instead for a supervised leisure lake or the municipal pools in Paray or Digoin in summer.

The riding is soft and rolling, with good surfaces, little traffic and long views over the bocage. Watch for cattle being moved between fields and for tractors with wide implements. Fuel and food are in Paray-le-Monial and Digoin; order a Charolais steak, obviously, and do not ask for it well done.
t.near saint crepin ibouvillers on the way:
The Pays de Thelle is a low chalk plateau north of the Vexin, crossed by quiet roads and patched with woods, and this stop lies in its quieter part, between Saint-Crépin-Ibouvillers, Villeneuve-les-Sablons and Lormaison. It is undramatic, gently rolling country, with big fields, farm courtyards built of flint and brick, and small churches in every village.

Méru, the nearest town of any size, has an unexpected past. For centuries its workshops made buttons, fans, dominoes and small luxury objects from mother-of-pearl, bone and ivory, supplying the fashion houses of Paris. A museum in the town tells the story of that craft, with old machines and delicate pieces that are hard to believe were made by hand.

There is no natural swimming water worth the name here. The plateau is dry chalk, and the streams are small. The honest answer is a municipal pool in Méru or Beauvais, or a longer ride to one of the lakes along the Oise.

Beauvais, to the north, is home to a cathedral with the tallest Gothic choir ever built, so ambitious that parts of it collapsed and the nave was never finished. It is an extraordinary sight, a vast, soaring fragment of a building that defeated its builders.

The riding is easy, with straight roads across the fields and gentle bends through the villages. The surfaces are generally good, but watch for mud and gravel from farm vehicles, especially in harvest season. Méru has fuel, shops and cafés, and the villages have the odd bakery that opens early and closes for a long lunch.
t.neuville sur saone@45.9,4.8:
Julius Caesar noticed the Saône. In his account of the Gallic Wars he wrote that the river flows with such incredible slowness that the eye cannot tell in which direction it is moving, and two thousand years later, standing on the quay at Neuville, you can see what he meant. The river here is wide, brown-green and almost still, and the reflections of the plane trees on the bank barely ripple.

That calm has always shaped life in the little town. The river was a highway long before the roads, and barges still pass, along with pleasure boats heading for Burgundy. On summer evenings the quays fill with walkers, anglers and families, and the restaurants on the waterfront serve friture, small fried fish from the river, a traditional dish of the Saône valley.

Neuville is a pleasant, low-key town with a market square, old houses and a big church with twin towers looking over the water. It is a place for a slow walk after a long ride, and the bridge offers views up and down the river, with the Monts d'Or rising on the opposite bank.

This finish brings you back from the Vanoise and the Jura wine country, a long day of mountains and vineyards, and the gentle Saône is a soothing end. The roads into Neuville are busy, especially at rush hour, and the bridge can be congested.

Take a table on the quay, order something cold, and watch the river refuse to hurry. Caesar, for once, was not exaggerating.
t.near saint arnoult en yvelines on the wa:
In 1951 the poet Louis Aragon and the novelist Elsa Triolet bought an old water mill on the Rémarde river near Saint-Arnoult-en-Yvelines, and turned it into their country home. They lived and wrote there for decades, and they are buried together in the garden. The Moulin de Villeneuve is now a museum, with their library, furniture and the park where they walked.

Saint-Arnoult lies on the southern edge of the forest of Rambouillet, where the woods give way to the Beauce plain. This stop is a few kilometres away, near Bullion and Sonchamp, in a landscape of forest, meadows and small valleys, with streams winding through the trees. It is a quiet, green corner of the Île-de-France, only an hour from Paris.

Dourdan, a short ride east, has a castle built by Philippe Auguste in the early thirteenth century, with towers, moats and a keep, and a pleasant old town with a covered market. The forest of Dourdan, next to it, is another large area of oak and beech.

For a swim, the forest has ponds, but most are not for bathing. The étangs de Hollande, further north in the Rambouillet forest, have a supervised area in summer. The Rémarde and its tributaries are small streams, pleasant for a rest in the shade but not for swimming.

The riding is relaxed, with narrow forest roads, gentle bends and villages with old churches. Watch for deer and wild boar at dawn and dusk, and for the packs of Parisian cyclists who own these roads on Sunday mornings. The A10 and A11 split just south at Ablis, so this is also the last calm before motorway traffic; Saint-Arnoult is the sensible place to top up the tank first.
t.saint gratien@49.0,2.3:
Princess Mathilde, niece of Napoleon, held one of the most brilliant salons of nineteenth-century France at her château in Saint-Gratien. Flaubert, the Goncourt brothers, Sainte-Beuve, Maupassant and many other writers and artists gathered there in the summers, and the conversation, it was said, was the best in France. The château still stands, though not open to the public, on the edge of the lake of Enghien.

Saint-Gratien shares that lake with its neighbour, and it is a quiet, residential town of villas, gardens and tree-lined streets. Marshal Catinat, one of Louis XIV's best generals, retired here and died in 1712, and his name is still on streets and a school.

It is a curious end to a weekend in the Morvan. Two days ago you were on empty granite roads among beech forest and lakes where nobody spoke above a murmur; now you are threading through the northern suburbs of Paris, counting traffic lights. The last stretch is slow, stop-start and full of buses, and a little patience goes further than a lot of throttle.

The reward is the lake. From the Saint-Gratien shore you look across the water to the white casino and the old spa buildings of Enghien, and in the evening, with rowing boats tied up and ducks arguing in the reeds, it has a gentle, provincial air that seems to belong to Mathilde's century rather than ours.

Practicalities are easy. The town has fuel and shops on its main roads, and the cafés of Enghien are a five-minute walk round the shore. Leave the bike, walk a loop of the lake, and let the Morvan settle into memory.
t.roche la moliere@45.4,4.3:
Coal made Roche-la-Molière. The town sits on the western edge of the Saint-Étienne basin, and for generations its hillsides were dotted with pit heads, slag heaps and miners' terraces. The mines are long closed, the spoil tips have grassed over, and today it is a quiet residential town of around ten thousand people with a château on its hill and good views back towards the city and the dark ridge of the Pilat beyond.

If you are riding out of Saint-Étienne, this is where the urban sprawl finally loosens. Head west and north and you drop towards the Loire gorges, where the river has carved a deep, wooded trench and been dammed into the long Lac de Grangent. The roads along the gorge rim are a joy: tight, cambered and lightly used outside summer weekends, with medieval ruins perched on rocky spurs above the water. The Saint-Victor-sur-Loire side is particularly good for a pause by the lake.

South-east, across the city, rises the Massif du Pilat, a granite ridge with beech and fir forests and roads that climb to more than a thousand metres, with views over the Rhône valley to the Alps on a clear day. It makes a fine contrast with the post-industrial basin you start from.

Saint-Étienne itself is an underrated place: it built arms, bicycles and ribbons, and its old Manufrance mail-order company was once known across France. The football club and its green shirts are a local religion. For practicalities, Roche-la-Molière has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and the wider Saint-Étienne area has everything a rider could need. Traffic can be heavy at rush hour, so a mid-morning departure makes the climb out of the basin far more pleasant.
t.near mitry mory@49.0,2.6:
The aircraft give it away. Mitry-Mory lies just south of Charles de Gaulle Airport, and the planes descending over the fields are a constant presence. This is the Plaine de France, a flat, open country north-east of Paris where large-scale farming mixes with logistics parks, motorways and suburban towns. It is not a place you come to for scenery, but it is a practical gateway for riders heading out of Paris towards the north or the west.

The area has a long agricultural history. Before the airport and the motorways, it was a breadbasket for the capital, with huge farms growing wheat and sugar beet. Some of these farms still exist, with fortified courtyards and big barns, a reminder of the past. The Canal de l'Ourcq, dug in the early nineteenth century to bring water to Paris, runs a little to the south, lined with trees and a towpath.

Riding here is about getting through efficiently. Roads are wide and straight, traffic is often heavy, and roundabouts multiply. Lorries heading for the logistics hubs and the airport are common. Watch for speed cameras, which are frequent in France, and for wind on the open plain. If you are heading for the Vexin, the limestone plateau west of Paris with its Seine cliffs and villages, the most efficient route goes around the capital on the Francilienne ring road.

Fuel is readily available in Mitry-Mory and around the airport, along with supermarkets and fast food. Bakeries in the old village centre offer a better coffee and croissant. Take a short break here, check the bike, and push on towards the more interesting countryside to the west, where the roads begin to curve along the river.
t.elancourt@48.8,1.9:
Élancourt is part of Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, one of the new towns built around Paris from the 1970s to absorb the capital's growth. Its landscape of housing estates, business parks and roundabouts is not the stuff of dreams, but the town has two surprises. One is France Miniature, a theme park where the country's monuments are reproduced at small scale. The other is the Colline d'Élancourt, a man-made hill built from construction spoil and landscaped into a park, offering one of the widest views in the west of the Paris region.

From the top, you can see the Eiffel Tower and La Défense on the horizon, as well as the forests and fields that surround the new town. It is a strange but rewarding spot for a photo, especially in the evening light.

For riders, Élancourt is the threshold of some lovely countryside. To the south and west lies the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse regional park, with wooded valleys, small rivers, châteaux and villages, and beyond it the forest of Rambouillet, once a royal hunting ground. The roads there are narrow and winding, with good surfaces and plenty of curves, and are popular with Parisian motorcyclists and cyclists on weekends. Further west, the route leads towards the Seine and its great loops, with chalk cliffs and the château of La Roche-Guyon.

Traffic in Élancourt can be heavy, especially at rush hour, and speed cameras are common on the main roads. The town has plenty of fuel stations, shopping centres and fast food, so it is a convenient place to fill up before heading into the countryside. Then leave the roundabouts behind and seek out the valleys.
t.boissy le cutte@48.5,2.3:
Boissy-le-Cutté is a small village in the Essonne, south of Paris, sitting on the edge of the Juine valley in the Gâtinais français regional park. It is a place of quiet streets, stone houses and fields, far from the bustle of the capital even though it lies only an hour away. The surrounding landscape is a mix of farmland, woods and river valleys, with sandstone outcrops scattered across the hills.

The Gâtinais is known for its natural beauty and its traditions. The sandy soils and woods have shaped a distinctive landscape, with heathland, rocky outcrops and clear streams. Essonne is also famous for its watercress, grown in beds fed by springs along the valleys, and you may see the green beds shimmering in the sunlight. The Juine winds through a pretty valley with mills, wash houses and old châteaux.

The roads around Boissy-le-Cutté are relaxed and pleasant to ride, winding through valleys and over gentle hills. They are generally quiet, apart from weekends, when cyclists and day-trippers come out from Paris. The surfaces are good, but watch for gravel on some minor roads and for tractors in the fields. In autumn, the woods turn gold and the light is soft and beautiful.

There are few services in Boissy-le-Cutté itself, so plan fuel and food in Étampes, the nearest larger town, or La Ferté-Alais. Étampes is worth a stop for its medieval churches and the ruined Guinette tower, the remnant of a royal castle. From here, the route heads north-west towards the great loops of the Seine, where chalk cliffs rise above the river and the roads follow the water.
t.near ambert@45.5,3.8:
Ambert has a round town hall, and it is not the strangest thing about the place. This small town in the Livradois-Forez, deep in the Massif Central, is also the home of fourme d'Ambert, one of France's oldest cheeses, a mild blue made in tall cylinders. And in a valley just outside town, the Moulin Richard de Bas still makes paper by hand, as it has done for centuries, using water power and old wooden hammers. The writer Jules Romains set his comic novel Les Copains here, and the town has a good-natured, slightly eccentric feel.

Ambert lies in the valley of the Dore, between the forested hills of the Livradois to the west and the Monts du Forez to the east. The landscape is green, with meadows, pine and fir forests and scattered farms, and in the higher areas, the Hautes Chaumes, wide open moorlands with heather and stone shelters where cattle once spent the summer.

The riding here is superb. Roads climb out of the valley in long series of curves, crossing passes like the Col des Supeyres, with views over the hills and the plain. The surfaces are generally good, traffic is light, and the scenery changes constantly. In winter, snow can cover the higher roads, and fog is common in the valleys in autumn. In summer, the hills offer a cool escape from the heat of the plains.

Ambert has fuel, a supermarket or two and places to eat, making it a good base for exploring the region. Try the fourme in a local restaurant, perhaps in a sauce or simply with bread and a glass of wine later in the day. Next, the road continues east towards the Rhône and the Alps.
t.near beaujeu@46.2,4.6:
Beaujeu gave its name to the Beaujolais. The lords of Beaujeu ruled this land of hills and vineyards in the Middle Ages, and the little town in the valley of the Ardières remained its capital until the role passed to Villefranche. Today it is a quiet place, with a Romanesque church, old houses and a hospice with a fine collection of pharmacy jars, and it takes great pride in its wine. Every November, the release of Beaujolais Nouveau is celebrated here with festivities that draw crowds.

The landscape around Beaujeu is one of the most beautiful in the Lyon region. To the east, the vineyards of the famous crus, Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent and others, cover the slopes in neat rows, with stone villages and châteaux scattered among them. To the west, the land rises to the forested hills of the Haut-Beaujolais, with pine and fir forests and the summit of Mont Saint-Rigaud, the highest point of the region.

The riding is excellent. Roads wind through the vineyards and climb into the hills over passes like the Col du Fût d'Avenas, with superb views over the Saône valley to the Alps. The surfaces are generally good, but the roads can be narrow and steep, with tight corners. Watch for tractors in the vineyards, especially during the harvest in September, and for cyclists on the climbs.

Beaujeu has fuel, a few shops, cafés and restaurants, making it a good place for a break. For a wider range of services, Belleville-en-Beaujolais lies a short ride away in the Saône valley. Try a glass of the local wine with your meal, but only once the riding is over for the day.
t.near sury le comtal@45.5,4.1:
Sury-le-Comtal sits on the flat floor of the Forez plain, the broad basin of the Loire between the Monts du Forez and the Monts du Lyonnais. It is a small town with a big secret: its château, outwardly modest, holds some of the most remarkable seventeenth-century carved wooden interiors in France, with ceilings, panels and fireplaces carved in exuberant detail. Guided visits are possible on certain days.

The Forez plain is an old lake bed, flat and fertile, dotted with ponds and farms, and crossed by the Loire. Volcanic hills rise here and there, the most striking being the basalt peak of Saint-Romain-le-Puy a short ride away, crowned by a Romanesque priory with superb views over the plain. Montbrison, the old capital of the counts of Forez, is a few kilometres north, with a fine collegiate church and the round Salle Héraldique, decorated with coats of arms.

The riding on the plain is relaxed, with straight roads and gentle bends, and it can be windy. To the west, the roads climb into the Monts du Forez, where the scenery changes rapidly to forests, meadows and high moorland, and the riding becomes much more challenging and rewarding. To the east, the Monts du Lyonnais offer rolling hills and winding roads.

Sury-le-Comtal has fuel, shops and a few restaurants. Montbrison is the place for a wider choice and for the local cheese, fourme de Montbrison, a cousin of the blue fourme d'Ambert. From the priory of Saint-Romain-le-Puy, the view over the Forez plain to the mountains is one of the best photo opportunities in the area, particularly in the evening light.
t.balbigny@45.8,4.2:
Balbigny is a small town on the Loire, at the northern end of the Forez plain, where the river leaves the open basin and enters the hills towards Roanne. It is a crossroads: the A89 and A72 motorways meet nearby, and old roads from Lyon to Clermont-Ferrand and from Saint-Étienne to Roanne pass through. For riders, it is a practical stop for fuel and food on the way across the region.

The town has a few points of interest, including an old bridge over the Loire and a church, but the main attractions lie nearby. A few kilometres south stands the Bastie d'Urfé, a Renaissance château with Italian-style gardens and a remarkable grotto decorated with shells and sand. It was the home of Honoré d'Urfé, whose long pastoral novel L'Astrée, set in the Forez, was a sensation in seventeenth-century France.

The surrounding landscape is varied. The Loire valley is broad and green, with fields and riverside woods, while to the east and west the land rises into the Monts du Lyonnais and the Monts de la Madeleine. The roads in the hills are winding and fun, with views over the river and the plain. North of Balbigny, the Loire flows into the long reservoir of Villerest, with gorges, castles and quiet roads along its banks.

Balbigny has pumps, groceries and restaurants, so it is a convenient place to stop. The motorway junctions bring traffic, but the minor roads quickly become quiet. From here, the route heads east towards the Beaujolais, through rolling hills and small villages, at its best in the soft light of early morning.
t.near mornant@45.6,4.7:
Two thousand years ago, engineers from Lugdunum ran an aqueduct through these hills to carry water from the Gier valley to the Roman city, a channel some eighty kilometres long that bridged valleys on stone arches. Around Mornant, sections of those arches still stand in the fields, weathered and patched with ivy, and stumbling upon them on a back road is one of the quiet pleasures of riding in the Monts du Lyonnais.

Mornant itself is a small market town on the eastern slopes of the hills, with a medieval core, a fortified church and a lively square. The countryside around it is a patchwork of orchards, meadows and woods, and the area is known for its cherries, sold at roadside stands in early summer. From the higher roads, the views stretch across the Rhône valley to the Pilat and, on clear days, all the way to the Alps.

The riding is the main reason to come. The roads through the Monts du Lyonnais are an endless succession of bends, climbs and descents, with small villages and changing scenery. They are close enough to Lyon to be popular on weekends, so expect other bikes, cyclists and families out for a drive. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel and for farm traffic. In autumn, the orchards turn red and gold, and the light is wonderful.

Mornant keeps riders supplied with fuel, groceries and meals, making it a convenient stop for a top-up or a meal. Bakeries offer local pastries, including the praline tart that Lyon is famous for, pink and sticky. The roads south towards Saint-Chamond and the Pilat or east to the Rhône both make good continuations, depending on how much time you have.
t.near tournan en brie@48.7,2.8:
Brie is a cheese before it is a place for most people, but the plateau east of Paris that gave the cheese its name is a real landscape: wide, flat and fertile, with huge fields of wheat and sugar beet, scattered farms with walled courtyards and patches of forest. Tournan-en-Brie is a small town on this plateau, with an old church and a railway station that links it to the capital, and it makes a practical stop on the edge of the countryside.

The plateau may look monotonous at first, but it has its own charm. The skies are huge, the light changes constantly, and the villages, with their stone churches and farmhouses, have a quiet dignity. Nearby, the château of Ferrières, built in the nineteenth century for the Rothschild family, is a spectacular piece of Second Empire architecture set in a large park, worth a detour if you have time. To the south, the forests of Armainvilliers and Crécy offer shade and quiet roads.

Roads are straight and wide, linking villages across the plateau, with occasional curves around forests and valleys. Wind can be a factor on the open fields, and tractors are common, especially at harvest time. Traffic is moderate, but the roads near Paris can be busy at rush hour.

Tournan has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés. A slice of Brie de Meaux or Brie de Melun, the two protected versions of the cheese, with a fresh baguette makes a perfect picnic. Beyond, the ride heads west towards the Eure valley, gentler and greener, with rivers, mills and châteaux.
t.near saint just en chevalet@45.9,3.9:
In the Monts de la Madeleine, the hills between the Loire and the Allier, Saint-Just-en-Chevalet sits high on a ridge, a small village of granite houses where the main road from Lyon to Clermont-Ferrand once brought a steady stream of travellers. The motorway now runs to the south, and the village has returned to a quieter life, surrounded by forests, meadows and the occasional pond.

The landscape here is remote and green, with dense forests of fir, spruce and beech, especially in the Bois Noirs, the dark woods that cover the higher ground to the west. These forests once hid uranium mines, operated in the second half of the twentieth century, now closed and slowly being reclaimed by nature. The meadows are grazed by Charolais cattle, and in summer the air smells of hay and pine.

The riding is excellent, with roads that climb and descend through the forests and over the ridges, offering views over the Loire plain to the east and the mountains of Auvergne to the west. The old national road is wide and fast, with long curves, while the minor roads are narrower and twistier, with very little traffic. Surfaces vary, and in winter, snow and ice are possible at higher elevations. Fog is common in the valleys in autumn.

Saint-Just-en-Chevalet is small, so do not count on finding everything you need. Fuel is more reliably found in Roanne to the east or Thiers to the south-west, both larger towns with full services. Thiers, perched on a steep hillside, is the cutlery capital of France and worth a stop to see its knife workshops. Next, the road crosses towards the Chartreuse, a long day away across the Rhône valley.
t.jumieges abbey@49.4,0.8:
The two white towers of Jumièges rise above the trees in a loop of the Seine, roofless, ragged and astonishing. Founded in the seventh century by Saint Philibert, the Benedictine abbey was sacked by Vikings, rebuilt by the dukes of Normandy, and consecrated in 1067 in the presence of William the Conqueror, freshly crowned king of England. After the French Revolution it was sold off and used as a stone quarry, and what remains is often called the most beautiful ruin in France. Walking through the empty nave, open to the sky, with jackdaws circling the towers, it is hard to disagree.

The abbey sits inside one of the great meanders of the lower Seine, in the regional nature park of the Boucles de la Seine Normande. The river here is wide and tidal, carrying ships to and from Rouen, and the meander loops are filled with orchards, meadows and marshes. The road along the river from Duclair to Jumièges is known as the Route des Fruits, lined with apple and cherry orchards and stalls selling cider, juice and fruit in season.

The riding is gentle and lovely, with roads following the river and climbing onto the chalk cliffs that frame the valley. Small ferries cross the Seine at several points, free of charge and a delightful way to change banks. Traffic is light, but cyclists are common, and the roads can be narrow.

Jumièges village has cafés and restaurants catering to visitors, but fuel is limited in the meander. Fill up in Duclair, on the edge of the loop, or in the Rouen suburbs. Allow at least an hour for the abbey, and try the local cider or a slice of apple tart afterwards. The light in late afternoon is especially beautiful on the white stone.
t.near saint etienne sur chalaronne@46.2,4:
The Chalaronne winds its last few kilometres towards the Saône past Saint-Étienne-sur-Chalaronne, a quiet village of brick and timber houses at the western edge of the Dombes. Here the plateau of ponds slopes down to the broad Saône valley, and the landscape becomes a mix of meadows, woods and fields, with the hills of the Beaujolais rising on the other side of the river.

The village is small and peaceful, with a church and a few farms, and it gives a good sense of rural life in the Ain. The houses in this area are often built of pisé, rammed earth, or with brick and wooden frames, a traditional style adapted to a region with little stone. The Saône floodplain nearby is a haven for birds, especially in winter and spring, when the meadows flood and attract ducks, waders and storks.

As for the riding, it is relaxed. The roads are flat or gently rolling, linking villages through fields and woods, with very little traffic. They are a pleasant way to cross from the Dombes to the Saône valley and the Beaujolais. Watch for tractors and for the occasional sharp bend at a farm corner. In the morning, mist often hangs over the river and the meadows, creating beautiful light for photographs.

Saint-Étienne-sur-Chalaronne has few services, so fuel and food are best found in Thoissey, a small town on the Saône, or Châtillon-sur-Chalaronne, a short ride east. Across the river, the vineyards of the Beaujolais are an inviting prospect, and the bridges at Thoissey or Belleville provide easy access. After this stop the ride continues east towards the Lac du Bourget and the mountains of Savoy.
t.near aveize@45.7,4.4:
High in the Monts du Lyonnais, Aveize looks out over a rolling plateau of meadows, hedgerows and small woods, where dairy farming has shaped the landscape for centuries. It is a modest village with a church and scattered farms, typical of these hills west of Lyon, where the air is fresher than in the city and the pace of life slower.

The Monts du Lyonnais are a range of low mountains, old granite worn into rounded hills, cut by deep valleys. The land is green and fertile, with fields of grass for the cows, orchards and patches of forest. Nearby Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise is famous throughout the region for its charcuterie, especially saucisson, and the local markets are a showcase of cured meats, cheeses and fruit.

The roads wind across the plateau and plunge into valleys, with constant changes of direction and gradient. They are narrow in places, with sharp bends and occasional gravel, but traffic is light, and the scenery is lovely. On clear days, the views stretch east to the Alps, with Mont Blanc sometimes visible on the horizon, and west to the Monts du Forez. In winter, snow can fall on the higher ground, and fog can fill the valleys.

Aveize has limited services, so plan fuel and food in nearby towns such as Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise or Sainte-Foy-l'Argentière. A picnic of local saucisson, cheese and bread is the perfect lunch here. From the plateau, the route heads east towards the Jura, a long ride across the Saône plain to the vineyards and waterfalls of the Jura mountains.
t.near le peage de roussillon@45.4,4.8:
In 1564, during a royal tour of France, the young king Charles IX stayed at the château of Roussillon, on the hill above what is now Le Péage-de-Roussillon, and signed an edict there that fixed the start of the year on 1 January across the kingdom. Until then, different regions began the year at Easter, Christmas or other dates. The château still stands, a Renaissance building with an elegant courtyard, overlooking the Rhône valley.

The town of Le Péage-de-Roussillon takes its name from a toll that was once collected on the road along the river. Today it is dominated by a large chemical industrial complex, one of the oldest in the Rhône valley, and its towers and pipes are a striking sight from the road. It is a working town, useful rather than pretty, with good transport links on the A7 motorway and the old N7 road.

The surrounding landscape is more appealing than the industrial zone suggests. The Rhône flows past in a wide valley, flanked by vineyards and orchards, and the hills on both sides offer winding roads and great views. To the west, across the river, rises the Pilat massif, with forests and ridges, and to the east the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné. The mistral, the strong north wind of the Rhône valley, can blow hard here, especially in winter and spring.

Le Péage-de-Roussillon has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, making it a convenient stop. For a more pleasant break, head up to the château or to the riverside. From here, the route heads north-east towards the Jura, through the Bas-Dauphiné and the Bugey, with their winding roads and changing landscapes.
t.blaincourt les precy@49.2,2.4:
The Oise valley north of Paris is a quiet, green corridor, and Blaincourt-lès-Précy is one of its villages, a cluster of houses and farms on the edge of the river plain. It is a place where the Paris region fades into the countryside of Picardy, with fields, woods and old stone villages, and it makes a peaceful stop on a ride through the valley.

The area is rich in history. The town of Précy-sur-Oise next door has a fine Gothic church, and the river was an important route for trade and travel for centuries. To the south lies the great forest of Chantilly, with its château, home of the Condé princes, whose stables are among the most magnificent in Europe and now house a museum of the horse.
