Chantilly is also the home of the famous cream and of French horse racing. To the east, Senlis, with its Gothic cathedral and Gallo-Roman walls, is one of the best-preserved medieval towns near Paris.

From the saddle it is pleasant and relaxed. Roads follow the river and wind through the forests, with gentle curves and good surfaces. The forests are cool and shady in summer, and in autumn, the colours are spectacular. Traffic can be heavy around Creil and Chantilly, especially at weekends, but the minor roads are generally quiet.

Blaincourt has few services, so fuel and supplies are best found in Précy, Creil or Chantilly. A stop in Chantilly for a coffee and a taste of the famous cream is a classic treat. Beyond, the ride heads back towards Paris through the Chevreuse valley, or west towards the Eure, depending on the day's plan.
t.near tarare@45.9,4.4:
Muslin made Tarare's fortune. From the eighteenth century onwards the town wove fine, light cotton cloth that was sold across Europe, and every few years it still celebrates the fact with the Fête des Mousselines, when the streets and façades disappear under kilometres of draped fabric in a riot of colour. Outside festival time, Tarare is a quiet valley town in the hills between the Beaujolais and the Lyonnais, with old mill buildings and a long main street.

The road that matters here is the old Route Nationale 7, the legendary Paris to the Riviera highway of French holiday memory. West of Tarare it climbs out of the valley over the Col du Pin Bouchain, a long series of curves through forest that was feared by lorry drivers and loved by everyone else. The motorway has taken the heavy traffic away, carried on tall viaducts across the valleys, and the old road has become a pleasure to ride, with well-cambered bends and fine views back over the hills.

The surrounding hills are wooded and green, with meadows and small villages, and the roads that wander north into the Beaujolais are a delight, narrow and twisting, climbing over passes and dropping into wine villages. Weather here can be cooler and wetter than in Lyon, and fog can sit on the pass in autumn.

Tarare has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, an easy and sensible stop before or after the climb. For a coffee with character, look for a café near the town hall rather than the retail zone on the edge of town. Cross the col in the morning, when the light comes through the trees, and the Loire plain opens out ahead as you descend.
t.near evreux@49.1,1.1:
Évreux is the capital of the Eure department in Normandy, a medium-sized city on the river Iton about an hour and a half west of Paris. It has had a turbulent history, sacked by Vikings, burned during the Hundred Years' War and heavily bombed in 1940 and 1944, but it has kept a fine Gothic cathedral, Notre-Dame d'Évreux, whose stained glass is among the best in Normandy. The former bishop's palace beside it now houses the city museum, with Gallo-Roman finds from the area.

The countryside around Évreux is classic Normandy: rolling farmland, hedgerows, half-timbered farmhouses and small valleys with rivers that wander towards the Seine. The Iton runs through the city, and a pleasant riverside walk follows it through the centre. To the east lies the Eure valley, and beyond it the Seine with its chalk cliffs and the gardens of Giverny.

As a start and finish, Évreux works well. The city has plenty of restaurants, cafés and bakeries, and Norman food is rich and satisfying: cream, butter, apples, cider, calvados and cheeses like Camembert, Pont-l'Évêque and Livarot. A simple lunch of a galette or a plate of local cheese and bread with a bowl of cider is a fine reward.

The riding around Évreux is gentle, with roads winding through farmland and small valleys. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main routes. Fuel is readily available in the city. From here, rides lead south towards the Loire, west into the heart of Normandy, or east along the Seine.
t.near sergines@48.4,3.3:
Sergines is a quiet village in the north of the Yonne department, on the chalk plateau between the Seine and the Yonne, roughly where Burgundy shades into Champagne. The landscape is wide and open, with huge fields of wheat, barley, sugar beet and rapeseed stretching to the horizon, broken only by clumps of trees, church spires and the occasional water tower.

This is the Sénonais, the country around Sens, and history runs deep here. Sens, about twenty kilometres south, has one of the earliest Gothic cathedrals in France, Saint-Étienne, begun in the twelfth century. Its architect, William of Sens, later rebuilt the choir of Canterbury Cathedral after a fire. The town's treasury is one of the richest in France. To the north, Bray-sur-Seine and the Bassée wetlands along the Seine offer a different landscape of river meadows and gravel pits.

The riding on the plateau is open and fast, with long straights and gentle bends, good surfaces and very little traffic. It is the kind of country where you can see weather coming from miles away, and wind can be a factor. The roads down into the river valleys offer a bit more variety, with short descents and bends.

As a sight and photo stop, Sergines offers the big skies and vast fields of northern Burgundy. In early summer, when the rapeseed is in bloom, the plateau turns brilliant yellow. Fuel and food are available in Sens and Pont-sur-Yonne. The village has a church worth a look, and the silence of the plateau is part of the appeal.
t.near mornant@45.6,4.6:
Mornant is a small town in the Monts du Lyonnais, about twenty-five kilometres south-west of Lyon. It sits on a plateau among orchards, vineyards and farmland, with views east over the Rhône valley and, on clear days, all the way to the Alps. The town has a medieval core with a fortified church and remains of its old walls.

The area has deep Roman roots. The great aqueduct of the Gier, which carried water to Roman Lugdunum, passed through this country, and impressive remains of its arches survive at Chaponost and in other places along its route. It was one of the longest aqueducts in the Roman world, and an extraordinary piece of engineering.

As a start and fuel stop, Mornant is practical. There are service stations and shops in and around town, and it is a good place to top up before heading south into the Pilat or west into the Monts du Lyonnais, where services become sparse. The roads here climb and wind through hills, orchards and woods, with frequent bends and good views.

Surfaces are generally good, though some minor roads are narrow and patched. Traffic can be busy on the main roads towards Lyon and Givors at commuting times, but the back roads are quiet. The Monts du Lyonnais are known for their fruit, especially cherries, apples and pears, and in season you will see stalls selling fresh produce along the roads.
t.near chazelles sur lyon@45.6,4.4:
For more than a century, if you bought a good felt hat in France, there was a decent chance it came from Chazelles-sur-Lyon. This hill town in the Monts du Lyonnais was the capital of French hat-making, with factories turning rabbit fur into felt and felt into fedoras, bowlers and cloches for customers across Europe and beyond. The industry faded in the twentieth century, but one of the old factories now houses the Atelier-Musée du Chapeau, where you can watch the old machines at work and see hats worn by film stars and statesmen.

The town sits high on the western edge of the Monts du Lyonnais, where the hills look out over the wide Forez plain towards the Monts du Forez beyond. It is airy, green country: pasture, hedges, small woods and scattered farms, with the land rising and falling in long swells. The light up here is clear, and the wind can be brisk.

For riders, the high ground around Chazelles is a joy. The roads climb in short, winding sections, then run along ridges with views in every direction, before dropping into small valleys. Corners come thick and fast, many of them blind, and the surfaces are a patchwork of good and tired tarmac. Traffic is light, but watch for tractors and livestock trucks. In winter, frost and fog linger.

There is fuel in Chazelles itself and in Saint-Galmier and Feurs on the plain below. Saint-Galmier, just to the south, is home to the Badoit mineral spring, and the town is a pleasant place for a coffee. From the high point, look west across the Forez plain: on a clear day, you can see the whole of the Monts du Forez spread out like a backdrop.
t.chaleins@46.0,4.8:
Chaleins is a village on the western edge of the Dombes, close to the river Saône, about thirty-five kilometres north of Lyon. It sits on the gentle slope between the plateau of the Dombes, with its countless ponds, and the broad valley of the Saône, with its meadows and poplars. Across the river, the hills of the Beaujolais rise in a green wave of vineyards.

The landscape here is soft and pastoral. Fields of maize and wheat, hedgerows, small woods and farms built of pisé, rammed earth, give the countryside a distinctive look. Many old buildings in the Dombes and the Val de Saône are made this way, with thick earthen walls on stone foundations and wide roofs to keep off the rain. The villages often have small churches and châteaux, some dating back to the Middle Ages.

The riding is easy and pleasant. The roads around Chaleins are mostly flat, with gentle curves and good surfaces, and very little traffic. Heading east, you climb onto the Dombes plateau, where the roads wind between ponds and woods. To the west, the bridges over the Saône at Montmerle and Belleville lead into the Beaujolais, where the riding becomes more varied, with steep climbs and tight bends through the vineyards.

There are no services in Chaleins itself, but fuel and food are available in Montmerle-sur-Saône and Saint-Trivier-sur-Moignans nearby. Montmerle has a pleasant riverside setting, and the views across the Saône to the Beaujolais hills are lovely, especially in the evening light.
t.near saint uze@45.2,4.9:
Saint-Uze is a small town in the northern Drôme, tucked into the valley of the Galaure a few kilometres east of the Rhône at Saint-Vallier. For two centuries it was a pottery town. The clay here was excellent, and workshops turned out stoneware and earthenware in huge quantities, from jugs and pots to tableware, giving the place a long tradition in ceramics. Look for old kilns and potters' marks around town; the craft shaped the place.

The Galaure valley is a pleasant, green corridor running east into the low hills of the Drôme des Collines, a rolling country of orchards, walnut groves and small farms. Just up the valley lies Hauterives, home to the Palais Idéal of the Facteur Cheval, the extraordinary hand-built palace of a country postman, one of the most unusual sights in France.

As a start and food stop, Saint-Uze is modest but useful. Saint-Vallier, a few minutes away on the Rhône, has more choice, with cafés, bakeries and restaurants. The food of the Drôme is honest and good: caillettes, a kind of herb and pork patty, ravioles from Romans, walnuts from Grenoble, and peaches and apricots from the Rhône valley orchards in summer.

The riding here is a mix of valley roads and hill routes. The roads along the Galaure are gentle and pleasant, while the routes climbing into the hills offer more bends and views over the Rhône valley and towards the Vercors. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main routes. Fuel is available in Saint-Vallier.
t.near lamure sur azergues@46.1,4.5:
Lamure-sur-Azergues is a small village in the upper valley of the Azergues, in the Haut-Beaujolais, the wild, wooded northern part of the Beaujolais hills. This is not the country of vineyards that most people associate with the name: up here the hills are covered with forests of Douglas fir and beech, with pastures and small farms in the clearings. The Azergues river winds through a narrow valley, and the villages are small and scattered.

The area has a long history of timber and textiles. In the nineteenth century, small workshops in the valleys wove silk and cotton for the factories of Lyon and Tarare, and some old mills survive along the rivers. Today, the economy is based on forestry, farming and tourism.

As a start and fuel stop, treat Lamure as the last easy chance: once you climb into the hills, services become scarce, and if in doubt fill up in Villefranche-sur-Saône or Tarare before heading up the valley. The roads here are superb: they climb from the valley to passes like the Col des Écharmeaux and the Col de Crie, winding through forest with endless bends, good surfaces and very little traffic. The views from the ridges stretch over the Saône valley to the Alps on clear days.

Weather can change quickly in the Haut-Beaujolais, with fog and rain common, especially in autumn and winter. In summer, the forests provide welcome shade. Food options in the upper valley are limited and hours can be short, so a bakery stop in the morning is a wise insurance policy.
t.near pelussin@45.4,4.7:
Pélussin sits on the eastern flank of the Massif du Pilat, high above the Rhône valley south of Vienne. The town is spread across a sunny slope, among orchards, vineyards and meadows, and from its terraces you look down on the river and across to the hills of the Dauphiné, with the Alps on the far horizon on clear days.

The Pilat is a regional natural park, a granite massif of forests, high pastures and scree slopes rising from the Rhône to over 1400 metres at the Crêt de la Perdrix. Its eastern slopes, around Pélussin, are warm and sheltered, with orchards of apricots and cherries and some vineyards. Higher up, the climate is harsher, with spruce and beech forests, heather moors and long winters.

For riders, the roads climbing from Pélussin into the Pilat are among the finest in the region. The road up to the Col de l'Œillon is a classic, winding through forest with hairpins and views, and it leads to the Crêt de l'Œillon, crowned by a television mast and a viewpoint with a panorama over the Rhône valley and the Alps. The roads across the plateau, towards the Croix de Chaubouret and Le Bessat, are fast and flowing. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for cyclists, who love these climbs.

Pélussin has fuel, food and basic services. For a photo, the views from the Crêt de l'Œillon are spectacular, especially in the morning or evening light. In winter, snow can close the higher roads, so check conditions.
t.near marcigny@46.3,4.0:
Marcigny is a small market town on the right bank of the Loire in southern Burgundy, in the heart of the Brionnais, a rolling country of green pastures, hedgerows and white Charolais cattle. It is also a land of Romanesque churches: within a short ride you can visit Semur-en-Brionnais, Anzy-le-Duc, Iguerande and many others, each with carved portals and capitals from the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The great abbey of Cluny lies to the east, and its influence is everywhere.

Marcigny itself was home to a famous priory for noblewomen, founded in the eleventh century by Saint Hugh of Cluny. Little remains of it, but the Tour du Moulin, a fifteenth-century fortified tower, now houses a museum with a collection of faience and local history.

The Loire here is wide and wild, with sandbanks, islands and shifting channels. People do swim in the river in summer, but it is not a safe place to swim casually: currents are strong and unpredictable, and the sandbanks can collapse. Look for designated bathing areas, or ask locally.

The riding is relaxed and scenic. Roads wind through the Brionnais hills, past farms and churches, with gentle gradients and good surfaces. Traffic is light. Fuel and food are available in Marcigny, and the local restaurants serve Charolais beef, a local speciality. As a start and finish, Marcigny offers a peaceful setting and a taste of rural Burgundy.
t.voisins le bretonneux@48.8,2.0:
Voisins-le-Bretonneux is part of Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, one of the new towns built around Paris from the 1970s onwards, and on first sight it is all office parks, roundabouts and housing estates. But it sits right on the edge of something much older and lovelier: the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse, a regional natural park of wooded valleys, streams, villages and châteaux just south of Versailles.

A few minutes away, in Magny-les-Hameaux, lie the remains of the abbey of Port-Royal des Champs, the centre of the Jansenist movement in the seventeenth century. The playwright Racine was educated here, and Pascal had close links with the community. Louis XIV, suspicious of the Jansenists, had the abbey destroyed in the early eighteenth century, but the ruins and the museum in the old buildings are atmospheric. The Vallée de Chevreuse itself, with the castle of La Madeleine above Chevreuse and the gorges of the Vaux de Cernay, is a favourite escape for Parisians.

As a start and fuel stop, Voisins is practical. There are service stations and supermarkets close by, and the roads into the Vallée de Chevreuse start almost immediately. The routes down into the valleys and up onto the plateaux are winding and pleasant, with short climbs, tight bends in the woods and some lovely stretches along the streams. Surfaces are generally good, but expect cyclists in large numbers on weekend mornings, and speed limits are strictly enforced.

Get here early on a Sunday and you will have the valley largely to yourself, with mist in the hollows and the forest smelling of damp leaves.
t.near saint arnoult en yvelines@48.5,1.9:
Saint-Arnoult-en-Yvelines lies on the southern edge of the forest of Rambouillet, one of the largest forests in the Paris region, where the woods begin to give way to the wide, open fields of the Beauce. The village has an old church, a few streets of stone houses and the gentle air of a place where Parisians come for the weekend.

Its best-known landmark is the Moulin de Villeneuve, an old mill on the Rémarde river that was the country home of the writers Louis Aragon and Elsa Triolet. They bought it after the war and lived here for many years, and they are buried together in the garden. The house is now a museum, with their furniture, books and paintings, and the garden is a peaceful place to wander.

The forest of Rambouillet surrounds the area, with oak, beech and pine woods, ponds and clearings. It was a royal hunting forest for centuries, and the château of Rambouillet, a former royal residence and later a presidential retreat, lies a short ride to the north. The forest is home to deer and wild boar, so be careful on the roads at dawn and dusk.

As a food stop, Saint-Arnoult has bakeries, cafés and restaurants, and the nearby towns offer more choice. The riding around here is relaxed, with roads winding through the forest and across the fields, good surfaces and generally light traffic. Fuel is available in the area. After a meal, the roads south into the Beauce offer wide horizons and long straights, a change from the enclosed forest roads.
t.near nandy@48.6,2.6:
Nandy is a small town on the edge of the forest of Sénart, south-east of Paris, on the high ground above the Seine between Corbeil-Essonnes and Melun. From the edge of the plateau, you can look down on the river as it winds through its wide valley, with barges moving slowly along it and the wooded slopes rising on the far side.

The forest of Sénart is one of the great green spaces of the Paris region, a large expanse of oak and hornbeam woods, ponds and open heath. It was a royal hunting forest, and Louis XV is said to have met Madame de Pompadour here, when she arranged to cross his path during a hunt. Today it is a popular place for walkers, cyclists and horse riders, and its paths and clearings are busy on weekends.

The riding here is gentle. The roads through the forest are straight or gently curving, with good surfaces, and the routes down to the Seine offer a bit more variety, with short descents and bends. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads around Melun-Sénart, a large new town, but the roads along the river and through the smaller villages are quieter.

Fuel and food are available in Nandy and the surrounding towns. As a scenic stretch, the view over the Seine valley from the plateau is the highlight, and the forest provides welcome shade on hot days. The river towns of Saint-Fargeau-Ponthierry and Seine-Port are pleasant places for a short break.
t.near montbrison@45.6,4.0:
Montbrison was for centuries the capital of the Forez, the old county that occupies the upper Loire basin west of Lyon, and the town still carries itself with a certain dignity. Its great Gothic church, the Collégiale Notre-Dame-d'Espérance, rises above the rooftops, and just beside it stands La Diana, a medieval hall whose wooden vaulted ceiling is painted with hundreds of coats of arms of the noble families of the region. Few rooms in France give you such a direct sense of medieval heraldry.

The town sits at the meeting point of two very different landscapes. To the east stretches the Forez plain, flat and dotted with ponds, the course of the young Loire marked by trees. To the west rise the Monts du Forez, a long granite ridge climbing to the Hautes Chaumes, high, open moorland grazed by cattle in summer and buried in snow in winter, with views across half of central France.

The riding is excellent. Roads climb from Montbrison into the mountains in long, winding sections through pine and beech forest, and once you reach the high moors, the views open up dramatically. The road to the Col de la Croix de l'Homme Mort and the routes across the Hautes Chaumes towards Pierre-sur-Haute are among the best in the Massif Central. Surfaces vary, and winter closes the highest roads.

Montbrison is also the home of the fourme de Montbrison, a mild, creamy blue cheese with an orange rind, made in the surrounding mountains. Pick up a piece in town for a picnic with a view. Fuel, food and coffee are plentiful. For a photo, the climb into the mountains above the town gives a fine view over the Forez plain.
t.near le peage de roussillon@45.3,4.8:
The Rhône corridor south of Vienne is one of the busiest transport arteries in Europe, with the river, the A7 motorway, the railway and the N7 all squeezed into the valley, and Le Péage-de-Roussillon sits right in the middle of it. The town grew up as a toll station on the old road, hence the name, and in the twentieth century it became home to a large chemical platform whose chimneys and pipework still dominate the riverbank.

Neighbouring Roussillon has a more elegant claim to fame. In 1564, during a royal tour of France, the young King Charles IX stayed at the Renaissance château here and issued the Edict of Roussillon, which fixed the first of January as the start of the year throughout the kingdom. Before that, different regions began the year on different dates, often at Easter. The château, a fine Italianate building, still stands.

For riders, the valley floor is about getting through rather than enjoying, and the N7, the old road to the south made famous by summer holidays of the 1950s and 60s, can be slow. But the hills on either side are another matter. To the west, across the Rhône, the roads climb steeply into the Ardèche and the Pilat, with tight bends and spectacular views over the valley. To the east, the Drôme des Collines offers quieter, rolling roads through orchards and woods.

Fuel and food are plentiful in the valley. As a scenic stretch, it is the views from the hills above, looking down on the great river and its traffic, that make the biggest impression.
t.near sarras@45.2,4.7:
Sarras lies on the Ardèche bank of the Rhône, opposite Saint-Vallier, where the valley narrows between steep granite slopes. Behind the village, the river Ay comes tumbling out of the Ardèche hills through a deep, wooded gorge, and that gorge is the reason to be here.

The road up the valley of the Ay towards Satillieu and Lalouvesc is one of the finest in the northern Ardèche. It climbs steadily through the gorge, with the river rushing below, then emerges onto the high plateau, where the views open up over a sea of wooded hills. Above the river, perched on a rocky spur near Saint-Romain-d'Ay, stands the sanctuary of Notre-Dame d'Ay, a place of pilgrimage since the Middle Ages, with a chapel and a castle ruin overlooking the gorge.

This is the Ardèche Verte, the green northern part of the department, very different from the limestone gorges of the south. The rock here is granite, the forests are of chestnut, pine and beech, and the villages are built of dark stone. Lalouvesc, at the top of the climb, is a pilgrimage town dedicated to Saint John Francis Regis, with a large basilica.

The roads are winding and often narrow, with plenty of bends, steep gradients in places and surfaces that range from good to rough. Traffic is light. Fuel and food are available in Sarras and Saint-Vallier, and in Satillieu and Lalouvesc higher up. As a high point, the plateau above the gorge offers views across the Rhône valley to the Alps on clear days.
t.near noiretable@45.8,3.9:
Noirétable is a small town in the Monts du Forez, close to the border between the Loire and Puy-de-Dôme departments, on the old route between Lyon and Clermont-Ferrand. Its name comes from the dark forests of the Bois Noirs that cover the surrounding hills, and the town has the feel of a mountain market town, with granite houses, a church and a cool, fresh climate even in summer.

Above the town, on the slopes of the mountains, stands the chapel of Notre-Dame de l'Hermitage, a pilgrimage site with a sweeping view over the Forez plain and the surrounding hills. Pilgrims have climbed here for centuries, and the site is still visited, especially in summer.

The A89 motorway now passes nearby, linking Lyon and Clermont-Ferrand, but the old roads are far more interesting. They wind through the forests and over the hills, with plenty of bends, climbs and descents, and generally light traffic. To the south, the roads lead into the heart of the Monts du Forez and up to the high moors of the Hautes Chaumes. To the north, the Bois Noirs and the Monts de la Madeleine offer more forest riding.

Noirétable has fuel, food and basic services. As a start and finish, it is a good base for exploring the mountains of the Forez and the Livradois. The weather can be changeable, with fog and rain common, and winters are snowy, so check conditions before setting out.
t.septeuil@48.9,1.7:
Septeuil is a small village in the Yvelines, west of Paris, tucked into the valley of the Vaucouleurs, a small river that runs north towards the Seine at Mantes. The village has an old church, a few shops and cafés, and a pleasant rural atmosphere, surrounded by fields, woods and gentle hills.

The area is part of the Mantois, a region of farmland and small villages between the Seine and the forests of the south. To the south lies Houdan, an old market town with a massive twelfth-century keep and a famous breed of chicken. To the north, the Seine valley and the cliffs of the Vexin offer dramatic scenery. The villages around Septeuil are quiet and unspoilt, with old farms, churches and manor houses.

As a food stop, Septeuil has a bakery and a few places to eat, and nearby towns like Houdan and Mantes-la-Jolie offer more choice. As a start and finish, it is a convenient base for rides into the Vexin and along the Seine. The roads around the village are winding and pleasant, with short climbs, bends and views over the fields.

Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main roads. Fuel is available in the larger towns nearby. The valley of the Vaucouleurs is a pleasant ride, following the river through meadows and woods, and the plateaux above offer wide views over the countryside.
t.near pacy sur eure@49.0,1.4:
Pacy-sur-Eure sits on the river Eure in Normandy, about an hour west of Paris, in a valley of meadows, poplars and chalk hillsides. The town is a modest market centre with a Gothic church, a riverside setting and good access to the A13 motorway. It is also the starting point of a heritage railway, the Chemin de fer de la vallée de l'Eure, which runs along the valley on summer weekends.

The Eure valley is lovely riding country. The road along the river winds through villages, past watermills and manor houses, with the chalk slopes rising on either side. A short ride north lies Vernon on the Seine, with the Château de Bizy, and across the river, the village of Giverny, where Claude Monet lived and painted his water lilies. His house and gardens are among the most visited sights in Normandy, and in spring and summer they are spectacular, though very crowded.

The riding is gentle and pleasant, with roads following the valleys and climbing onto the plateaux, where the fields stretch to the horizon. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main routes. The Seine valley offers more dramatic scenery, with chalk cliffs and the ruins of Château Gaillard at Les Andelys, built by Richard the Lionheart.

Pacy-sur-Eure has fuel, food and basic services. As a photo stop, the river and the valley offer lovely views, especially in the morning light, when mist rises from the water.
t.near lagny sur marne@48.9,2.8:
Lagny-sur-Marne sits on the river Marne about thirty kilometres east of Paris, a busy town with an old centre, a riverside quay and a large, unfinished Gothic church, Notre-Dame-des-Ardents, all that was completed of an ambitious abbey church begun in the thirteenth century. The town was an important market in the Middle Ages, part of the network of Champagne fairs, and Joan of Arc fought near here in 1430, shortly before her capture at Compiègne.

Today, Lagny is part of the Marne-la-Vallée area, and Disneyland Paris lies just to the south. The Marne itself is a lovely river, with wooded banks, islands and locks, and the riverside paths are popular with walkers and cyclists. The towns along the river have a gentle, old-fashioned charm.

As a start and fuel stop, Lagny is convenient. There are service stations and supermarkets nearby, and the A4 motorway provides quick access to Paris and the east. The roads north towards the Multien and the forests of Chantilly and Ermenonville are pleasant, with gentle curves through farmland and woods.

Traffic can be heavy around Lagny and Marne-la-Vallée, especially at commuting times and on weekends near Disneyland. Once you are out in the countryside, the roads become quieter. Surfaces are generally good. The Marne valley upstream, towards Meaux and Château-Thierry, offers a scenic route through vineyards and villages.
t.near creil@49.3,2.5:
Creil is an industrial town on the Oise, about fifty kilometres north of Paris, and it would be easy to pass it by. Yet within a few kilometres lie some of the finest forests and châteaux in northern France, and the high ground around the town gives you a good sense of how the river has carved its way through the chalk and limestone plateaux of the Île-de-France.

Creil has its own heritage, too. In the nineteenth century it was famous for its faience, fine earthenware decorated with printed designs, and examples can be seen in the local museum. The town grew with the railway and with industry, and it still has a working, unpretentious feel.

Just to the south-west lies Chantilly, with its château, its great stables and its famous racecourse. The Musée Condé in the château holds one of the finest collections of old master paintings in France, and the Grandes Écuries, built for the Prince de Condé's horses, are almost as grand as the château itself. The forests of Chantilly and Halatte surround the area, with oak and beech woods, ponds and long, straight rides cut for hunting.

The riding around Creil is pleasant once you escape the town. Roads climb from the river onto the plateaux, then run through the forests in long, straight lines or gentle curves. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light on the forest roads, though busy around the towns. As a high point, the edge of the plateau above the Oise offers wide views over the valley.
t.near meulan en yvelines@49.0,1.9:
Meulan-en-Yvelines sits on a bend of the Seine, about forty kilometres north-west of Paris, where the river divides around an island. The old town climbs steeply up the hillside from the water, and from the top you get a fine view over the river, the bridges and the valley. Across the water, Les Mureaux has a long aerospace history, and parts of the Ariane rockets are made there.

The Seine here is a working river, with barges carrying sand, gravel and grain, but it is also lovely, with wooded islands, chalk cliffs and riverside villages. To the north rises the Vexin français, a regional natural park of rolling farmland, wooded valleys and stone villages, which feels a world away from the suburbs of Paris.

The riding here is a mix of river roads and plateau routes. The roads along the Seine are scenic, with views over the water and the islands, but they can be busy. The routes north into the Vexin climb onto the plateau, where the roads run through fields and woods with long, gentle curves. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is lighter in the Vexin.

Meulan has fuel, food and basic services. As a scenic stretch, the views over the Seine are the highlight, especially from the high ground above the town. The Vexin villages, with their old churches and farms, make pleasant stops along the way.
t.saint martin en haut@45.7,4.5:
Saint-Martin-en-Haut lives up to its name: it sits high in the Monts du Lyonnais, on a plateau around seven hundred metres up, about thirty kilometres west of Lyon. On a clear day, the views from the village stretch east over the Rhône valley to the Alps, with Mont Blanc visible on the horizon, and west over the rolling hills to the Monts du Forez.

The Monts du Lyonnais are a land of small farms, pastures, orchards and woods, with villages scattered along the ridges. The climate is cooler and wetter than in Lyon, and the landscape is greener. Dairy farming is important, and local cheeses and charcuterie are excellent. The area is also known for its fruit, especially apples, pears and cherries.

As a start and fuel stop, Saint-Martin-en-Haut has the basics, including a service station, shops and cafés. From here, the roads lead in every direction through the hills, with endless bends, climbs and descents, and wide views from the ridges. The routes towards Yzeron, Duerne and Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise are particularly fine.

Surfaces are generally good, though some minor roads are narrow and patched. Traffic is light, but watch for tractors, cyclists and livestock. In winter, the plateau can be snowy and icy, and fog is common in autumn. The cool air and green landscape make this a refreshing escape from the heat of Lyon in summer.
t.near la ricamarie@45.4,4.4:
La Ricamarie is a former mining town on the south-western edge of Saint-Étienne, where the coal basin meets the first slopes of the Pilat. For more than a century, the pits here produced the coal that fed the factories of the Stéphanois region, and the town still carries the marks of that history: workers' houses, old slag heaps grown over with trees, and a strong sense of community.

In June 1869, during a miners' strike, troops opened fire on a crowd at a place called Le Brûlé, killing more than a dozen people, including women and a child. The massacre shocked France and became a symbol of the struggles of the working class. Émile Zola drew on events like this when he wrote Germinal. A memorial in the town recalls the victims.

Behind La Ricamarie, the land climbs quickly into the Pilat regional natural park, a granite massif of forests, pastures and moors rising to over 1400 metres. The road over the Col de la République, south-east of Saint-Étienne, is part of cycling history: it was the first mountain pass ever climbed in the Tour de France, in 1903. The roads through the Pilat are winding and scenic, with views over the Saint-Étienne basin and the Rhône valley.

As a photo stop and finish, La Ricamarie offers a striking contrast between the industrial past and the green hills beyond. Fuel and food are available in the town and in Saint-Étienne. The light in the evening, falling across the old mining landscape, can be surprisingly beautiful.
Saint-Didier-sur-Chalaronne sits just above the Saône, where the little Chalaronne river ends its slow journey across the Dombes and slips into the bigger river near Thoissey. From the edge of the village the land drops to the Val de Saône, a broad floodplain of meadows and poplar rows, and across the water the slopes of the Beaujolais rise in neat green ranks of vines.

This is a good place for a long lunch. The Saône valley has a tradition of riverside cooking, and friture, small fried fish from the river eaten with your fingers and a glass of white wine, is a classic summer dish here, alongside the frogs' legs and poultry of the Dombes and the Bresse. Thoissey, a few minutes away, is a small, old town with a few places to eat, and the Beaujolais wine villages across the river are full of cellars where you can taste, though the rider will want to keep that to a sip.

The river is the dominant presence. It floods regularly in winter and spring, spreading across the meadows and turning the valley into a shallow lake, and the villages are built on higher ground for that reason. In summer, the riverbanks are green and shady, and the old towpaths are good for a walk after lunch.

The riding is easy. Flat roads follow the valley, with good surfaces and little traffic, and the bridges at Thoissey, Montmerle and Belleville lead across into the Beaujolais, where the roads climb sharply into the vineyards and the fun begins. Fuel is available in the nearby towns. Start here with a full stomach and the hills of the Beaujolais in view.
t.near belleville@46.1,4.8:
Belleville-en-Beaujolais lies on the Saône at the foot of the Beaujolais hills, and it has one treasure that surprises most visitors: an eighteenth-century Hôtel-Dieu, a charitable hospital with great wards lined with curtained beds, a chapel and an apothecary with its original jars. It served the sick for more than two centuries and is now a museum, one of the best-preserved hospitals of its kind in France.

Behind the town, the hills rise steeply, and the slopes are covered with vineyards. This is the heart of the Beaujolais crus, the ten villages whose wines carry their own names: Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Régnié, Morgon, Fleurie and the rest. The highest point nearby is Mont Brouilly, a volcanic hill crowned by a small chapel, Notre-Dame-aux-Raisins, built in the nineteenth century by winegrowers to protect their vines from disease. The view from the top over the vineyards, the Saône valley and, on clear days, the Alps, is superb.

The roads up Mont Brouilly and through the vineyards are narrow, steep and twisting, with hairpins and blind corners, and they are a joy on a motorcycle, if you take them gently. Surfaces vary, and in harvest season, in September, tractors and grape pickers are everywhere. The routes through the cru villages, from Brouilly to Fleurie and Juliénas, are a classic tour.

Belleville has fuel, food and basic services. For a high point, the summit of Mont Brouilly is unbeatable, and the wine villages offer plenty of places to stop for a coffee, a meal or a tasting for a passenger.
t.near chandon@46.1,4.3:
Chandon is a small village in the far north of the Loire department, close to the borders of Burgundy and the Rhône, in a landscape of green pastures, hedges and gentle hills. The white Charolais cattle grazing in the fields tell you that you are on the edge of the Brionnais, and the farms, churches and villages are built of warm, honey-coloured stone.

The nearest town of any size is Charlieu, a few kilometres to the north-east, and it is well worth a visit. Its Benedictine abbey, founded in the ninth century, has a magnificent Romanesque portal, among the finest in Burgundy, and the town was once a centre of silk weaving, with a museum dedicated to the craft. The old streets, with half-timbered houses and Gothic façades, are lovely.

As a food stop, Charlieu is the best choice nearby, with restaurants and cafés serving the hearty food of the region: Charolais beef, local cheeses and charcuterie. Roanne, about twenty kilometres to the south-west, is a larger town with a long gastronomic reputation and plenty of choice.

The riding around Chandon is relaxed and scenic. Roads wind through the hills, past farms and villages, with gentle bends and good surfaces. Traffic is light. The Loire valley to the west and the hills of the Beaujolais to the east offer more varied riding. Fuel is available in Charlieu and Roanne.
t.near mouy@49.3,2.4:
Mouy is a small town in the valley of the Thérain, in the Oise department, about sixty kilometres north of Paris, halfway between Creil and Beauvais. The valley is green and pleasant, with water meadows, poplars and old mills along the river, and the town has a modest centre with a church and a market square.

The Thérain valley was once an industrial corridor, with textile mills and workshops powered by the river, and some old factory buildings survive. Today, the area is mostly rural, with farms on the plateaux above the valley and villages scattered along the river.

Beauvais, about twenty-five kilometres to the north-west, is home to the Cathedral of Saint-Pierre, which has the tallest Gothic choir in the world, an astonishing feat of medieval engineering that partially collapsed in 1284 and was never completed. Its astronomical clock is also remarkable. To the south, Chantilly and its forests offer more sights.

As a food stop and start, Mouy has bakeries, cafés and a few restaurants, and the larger towns nearby offer more choice. The riding around Mouy is pleasant, with roads following the valley and climbing onto the plateaux, where the fields stretch to the horizon. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main roads. Fuel is available in town. Coming out of the valley in the early morning, with mist lifting off the water meadows and the smell of wet grass and woodsmoke in the air, it is easy to forget that the Paris ring road is barely an hour behind you.
t.near persan@49.2,2.3:
Persan sits on the river Oise, about thirty-five kilometres north of Paris, facing Beaumont-sur-Oise across the water. The two towns have grown together along the river, and the old part of Beaumont, with its church and remains of a castle, stands on a hill above the valley.

Just south lies the forest of Carnelle, a large expanse of oak and beech woods covering a hill above the Oise. In the forest stands the Pierre Turquaise, a remarkable Neolithic covered alley grave, one of the best-preserved megalithic monuments in the Paris region. A little to the north-east, at Asnières-sur-Oise, the Abbey of Royaumont was founded in the thirteenth century by Saint Louis. Its cloister, refectory and gardens are beautiful, and the abbey is now a cultural centre with concerts in summer.

As a high point, the forest of Carnelle and the plateaux above the Oise offer views over the valley. The roads through the forest are winding and shady, and the routes across the plateaux are open and fast. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light away from the main roads.

Persan has fuel, food and basic services. The Oise valley is a pleasant ride, with riverside villages, old churches and views over the water. To the north, the forests of Chantilly and Ermenonville offer more riding through the woods.
t.near ablis@48.5,1.8:
Ablis lies right where the forest of Rambouillet gives way to the Beauce, and the change is almost theatrical. Ride south out of the trees and the land flattens into an immense, open plain of wheat, barley and rapeseed that runs to the horizon in every direction, the granary of France. On a clear day you can sometimes make out the spires of Chartres Cathedral far to the south-west, rising out of the fields like a ship on the sea, the way pilgrims saw them for centuries.

The village itself is small and practical, close to the junction of the A10 and A11 motorways. There is a church, a few shops and services, and a sense of being on the edge of two very different landscapes. The writer Charles Péguy made the pilgrimage from Paris to Chartres across the Beauce in the early twentieth century, and his poems about the walk across the endless plain are still read by the many pilgrims who follow the route today.

The riding here is about wide horizons. South of Ablis, the roads run straight across the plain, with gentle curves and long sightlines. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light on the minor roads. Wind can be a factor on the open plain. To the north, the roads through the forest of Rambouillet are shady and winding, with oak and beech woods and the chance of meeting deer.

As a photo stop, the view across the Beauce is the highlight, especially in early summer, when the fields are green or golden. Fuel and food are available in Ablis and nearby towns.
t.near vaux le penil@48.5,2.7:
Vaux-le-Pénil sits on the high ground above the Seine, just east of Melun, in the Seine-et-Marne department. From the edge of the plateau, you can look down on the river as it winds through its valley, with Melun on its island and the forest of Fontainebleau stretching away to the south.

The town has a château, rebuilt in the eighteenth century, and a few old streets, but it is mostly residential, part of the Melun urban area. The plateau around it is part of the Brie, the flat, fertile region east of Paris famous for its cheese. Brie de Melun, stronger and saltier than its better-known cousin, Brie de Meaux, is made in the area.

As a high point, the edge of the plateau above the Seine offers views over the valley and the forest. The roads down to the river are short and winding, and the routes across the plateau are open and fast. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic can be heavy around Melun, but quieter on the minor roads.

The forest of Fontainebleau, just to the south, is one of the most beautiful forests in France, with oak, beech and pine woods, sandstone boulders and gorges. Its roads are long and straight or gently curving, and they are a pleasure to ride, though weekend traffic and speed limits require care. Fuel and food are available in Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun.
t.near melun@48.6,2.7:
On the night of 17 August 1661, Nicolas Fouquet, the superintendent of finances, threw a party at his new château of Vaux-le-Vicomte, a few kilometres north-east of Melun, for the young Louis XIV. There were fireworks, a new comedy by Molière, music by Lully and a banquet served on gold plate. Three weeks later, Fouquet was arrested by d'Artagnan of the musketeers, and he spent the rest of his life in prison. Louis took his architect, painter and garden designer, Le Vau, Le Brun and Le Nôtre, and set them to work on Versailles.

Vaux-le-Vicomte still stands, one of the most perfect châteaux in France, with formal gardens that stretch far into the distance. It is an essential stop if you have the time, and the candlelit evenings in summer are magical.

Melun itself is an old town on the Seine, with its historic heart on an island in the river, a Romanesque church and a pleasant riverside. It is the capital of the Seine-et-Marne department and a busy place, with plenty of services.

The riding around Melun is varied. The roads along the Seine are scenic, the routes across the Brie plateau are open and fast, and the forest of Fontainebleau, just to the south, offers long, shady roads through the woods. Traffic can be heavy around Melun, especially at commuting times. As a finish, Melun offers fuel, food and a chance to reflect on a day in the forests and valleys south of Paris.
t.near vaux le penil@48.6,2.7:
Vaux-le-Pénil sits on the high ground above the Seine, just east of Melun, in the Seine-et-Marne department. From the edge of the plateau, you can look down on the river as it winds through its valley, with Melun on its island and the forest of Fontainebleau stretching away to the south.

The town has a château, rebuilt in the eighteenth century, and a few old streets, but it is mostly residential, part of the Melun urban area. The plateau around it is part of the Brie, the flat, fertile region east of Paris famous for its cheese. Brie de Melun, stronger and saltier than its better-known cousin, Brie de Meaux, is made in the area.

As a high point, the edge of the plateau above the Seine offers views over the valley and the forest. The roads down to the river are short and winding, and the routes across the plateau are open and fast. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic can be heavy around Melun, but quieter on the minor roads.

The forest of Fontainebleau, just to the south, is one of the most beautiful forests in France, with oak, beech and pine woods, sandstone boulders and gorges. Its roads are long and straight or gently curving, and they are a pleasure to ride, though weekend traffic and speed limits require care. Fuel and food are available in Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun.
t.near irigny@45.6,4.8:
South of Lyon, the Rhône broadens into a powerful, heavily engineered river, lined with locks, power stations and chemical plants on the east bank. The west bank, where around Irigny, Charly and Vernaison, is softer: a strip of villages, orchards and market gardens rising gently towards the Monts du Lyonnais. Rides begin and end here for a simple reason: it sits outside the congested core of the city but within easy reach of it.

The area was once famous for its fruit, particularly cherries and peaches, and in early summer you will still see roadside stalls selling local produce. The villages have a mixture of old stone farmhouses, nineteenth-century country houses built by wealthy Lyon families, and modern suburbs. Across the river, the industrial corridor known as the Vallée de la Chimie is one of the largest concentrations of chemical industry in France, a reminder that Lyon's prosperity was built on silk, chemicals and engineering.

Lyon itself is famous for its food, and if you are finishing a ride here, it is worth heading into the city for dinner. The traditional restaurants known as bouchons serve hearty dishes like quenelles, andouillette and salade lyonnaise, washed down with Beaujolais or Côtes du Rhône. The old town, with its Renaissance houses and hidden passageways, and the hill of Fourvière, with its basilica and Roman theatres, are worth a visit too.

The Beaujolais rides head north from here, either through the city or around it, to the vineyards and hills north-west of Lyon. Getting through or around Lyon can be slow, especially at peak times, and the motorway around the city is notoriously congested, so leave early. The local roads on the west bank are pleasant, winding through villages and orchards. The surrounding towns cover fuel and shopping. Summers in the Rhône valley are hot, and the mistral wind can blow strongly down the valley, especially in winter and spring, so be prepared for gusts.
t.near miribel@45.9,4.9:
East of Lyon, the Rhône splits into channels and lakes on its way into the city, and the vast Grand Parc de Miribel-Jonage has been made out of that watery landscape. This finish lies just above it, on the edge of the Côtière, the steep slope that separates the river plain from the Dombes plateau, between Thil, Beynost and Saint-Maurice-de-Beynost.

The park is the main reason to linger. It covers more than two thousand hectares of lakes, woods and meadows, with a large lake, the Lac des Eaux Bleues, that has supervised bathing beaches in summer. On hot weekends it is packed with Lyonnais, but on a weekday evening it can be surprisingly calm. It also plays a serious role as a flood plain and drinking water reserve for the city.

Above Miribel, on the Côtière, stands a tall statue of the Virgin on a tower, the Madone du Mas Rillier, built in the mid-twentieth century and visible from miles around. The view from up there takes in the Rhône plain, Lyon, and on clear days the Alps and Mont Blanc.

The riding is a mix of busy and quiet. The A42 and the old national road run along the bottom of the slope, with plenty of traffic, while small roads climb the Côtière in tight bends to the plateau. Up top, the Dombes roads are straight and quiet, with ponds and farms on either side.

On a warm evening the order of events writes itself: a swim in the Eaux Bleues, a slow climb up the Côtière to the Madone as the plain turns orange, then dinner in Miribel, where fuel and supermarkets are also close at hand.
t.near wolowaru@-8.7,121.8:
Wolowaru is a market town in the mountains of central Flores, strung out along the Trans-Flores Highway east of Kelimutu, and on market day the road through it fills with trucks, bemos and people in hand-woven sarongs carrying sacks of rice, coffee and vegetables. It is not a place most travellers stop for long, but it is a good one to pause in: a slice of ordinary life on an island where tourism has only touched a few spots.

The villages around Wolowaru are known for ikat weaving, among the finest on Flores. The Lio people, who live in this part of the island, weave cloth with intricate patterns, dyed with natural colours from roots, bark and leaves, and the designs carry meanings tied to clan, status and ceremony. In villages such as Jopu and Nggela, women sit at backstrap looms on the verandas of their houses, and visitors can watch them work and buy cloth directly. Traditional Lio houses, with steep thatched roofs and carved posts, survive in some villages, along with stone megaliths used in ancestral rituals.

The landscape here is steep and volcanic, with deep valleys, forested ridges and terraces of rice and vegetables carved into the slopes. Kelimutu, the volcano with three coloured crater lakes, lies just to the west, and its slopes rise above the town. The soil is fertile, and coffee, cloves, cacao and candlenut grow in the gardens around the villages. The Flores landscape is dramatic everywhere, but in the centre of the island it is at its most rugged.

The Trans-Flores Highway through Wolowaru is the island's main road, running from Labuan Bajo in the west to Larantuka in the east, and it is a rider's road in the truest sense: endless curves, steep climbs and descents, and constantly changing views. The surface varies, from good asphalt to potholes and landslide damage, and the road is narrow, with trucks and buses taking up most of it. Ende, about twenty-three kilometres away on the south coast, is the nearest large town with full services. Wolowaru has small shops and fuel sold from bottles at roadside stalls, but it is best to fill up properly when you can. The rainy season, from November to March, brings landslides and road closures, so the dry season is better.
t.nuits saint georges@47.1,4.9:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the working capital of the Côte de Nuits, a town of about five thousand people that has made its living from wine for centuries, and it feels less like a museum than the pretty villages around it. Behind the main street, the old streets are full of cellars, wine merchants and négociants, the firms that buy grapes and ferment, blend and bottle them. The wines are mostly red, made from Pinot Noir, and are known for being structured, earthy and long-lived, with a firm backbone that rewards patience. There are no grands crus in the appellation, but there are many outstanding premiers crus, such as Les Saint-Georges, regarded by many as the equal of a grand cru.

The town also holds a charity auction of its wines every spring, the Hospices de Nuits sale, a smaller sibling of the famous Hospices de Beaune event in November. The proceeds fund the care of the sick, as they have since the eighteenth century. In a more modern turn, Nuits is also the centre of the Burgundy blackcurrant trade, and a visitor centre called the Cassissium explains how the fruit is turned into crème de cassis, the liqueur that, mixed with white wine, gives the drink called kir.

The Route des Grands Crus runs through the town on the D974, and on a bike it is a calm, scenic ride rather than a technical one. The road follows the slope of the Côte, with vineyards rising to the west and the plain of the Saône to the east, and the traffic in summer can be heavy and slow. Early mornings in May, June, September and October are the best times, with soft light and cool air. In the harvest, from September, tractors and trailers fill the lanes, and the smell of fermenting must hangs in the air.

Vineyard tracks lead up into the combes, the little valleys that cut into the limestone escarpment, where oak and box woods give way to scrub and rocky outcrops. Above the vines, the plateau is mostly forest and farmland, and the hills are riddled with caves.

As a proper town, Nuits-Saint-Georges has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, bakeries, and a good range of restaurants and cafés. It is also a convenient overnight stop, with a selection of small hotels and guesthouses. Try local specialities such as jambon persillé, ham in parsley jelly, and a glass of Aligoté or a local Crémant de Bourgogne.
t.ezy sur eure on the way back@48.9,1.4:
Ézy-sur-Eure is a modest town of three thousand on the river Eure in Normandy, close to the border of the Eure and Eure-et-Loir, and its neighbour, Saussay, is a hamlet. The place is a few kilometres from Anet, a small town with one of the most celebrated châteaux of the French Renaissance, built in the 1540s by the architect Philibert de l'Orme for Diane de Poitiers, the favourite of King Henri II. The château, with its elegant courtyard and its famous carved entrance gate, is open to the public, and the story of Diane, who was about twenty years older than the king and ruled his heart for decades, is told in the rooms.

The Eure is a calm, clear river that runs among meadows and poplars, past mills and washhouses, and in summer people swim in the shallows and picnic on the banks, so the point is tagged for swimming. The water is generally cool and the current gentle, but check for signs, since not all stretches are supervised. The Chantilly and Ermenonville, named in the ride, lie well to the north-east, in the Oise, so this valley is a quiet western detour.

For a rider the Eure valley is a gentle place. The road follows the river with long, easy curves, passing small villages with stone houses and church towers, and now and then climbs onto the plateau for a view over the wheat fields. The surface is mostly good, and traffic is light on weekdays, with more cyclists and walkers on weekends. Because the lanes are narrow and the hedges high, watch for blind corners and farm vehicles. Fuel is available in Anet and Pacy-sur-Eure, and bakeries and cafés in the villages offer simple meals.

The region is famous for its cereals, and the plateau is covered with a patchwork of golden wheat in July. Evening is a lovely time, when the sun slants through the poplars and the river is still. In autumn the mist sits in the valley, and in winter fog and frost are common, so allow extra time. A visit to the château in the morning, before the crowds arrive, is worth the detour if you have an hour to spare.
The Lignon du Forez comes out of the Monts du Forez with a cold, clean hurry, and by the time it reaches the plain around Boën it has cut itself a shallow gorge through old volcanic rock. This is the country west of Lyon and north of Saint-Étienne that most people cross on the autoroute without noticing, and that is exactly why it is pleasant. The Forez plain is a wide, flat bowl of pasture and orchards, and the mountains stand along its western edge like a wall with the road folded into the foot of it.

Sail is the one to remember: above the village a ruined medieval castle, Couzan, perches on a rock spur, and you can see it from the road long before you reach it. Boën is the practical neighbour, a small town with shops, a bakery or two and the usual fuel station, and it sits in the middle of the little Côtes du Forez wine area, a thin-skinned red country built on gamay. Saint-Germain-Laval, a bit further north, is a pleasant old market town. For anything larger, Montbrison is about twenty kilometres away and has everything.

The riding here is gentle rather than dramatic. Departmental roads run along the river and up into the hills with tight little bends, short climbs and a lot of blind crests where the hedges close in, so keep the speed honest. Surfaces are generally decent but patched, and farm traffic is the real hazard: tractors, loose gravel at field entrances, and mud after rain in the lower lanes. The best hours are early, when the mist lies on the plain and the hills above are already clear, and late in the day, when the light goes yellow on the stone farms.

The river is why this stop is marked for swimming. In summer the Lignon has pools below the bridges where locals wade in, but the water is mountain water, so it is bracing even in August, and levels change quickly after storms upstream. Pick a spot with a gravel bank, leave the leathers in the shade and give yourself time to warm up afterwards.

This is a fine place to start or end a day if you are heading for the Vanoise or the Jura, because you are on the quiet side of Lyon and the roads east are an easy morning's transfer away. Bring cash for the smaller villages, where the one bar may not take cards.
t.near hurigny on the way back@46.4,4.8:
You are in the Mâconnais, the southern end of Burgundy, where chardonnay vines cover the limestone hills and the villages are built of honey-coloured stone. Hurigny, La Roche-Vineuse and Sancé are small places within a few kilometres of each other, each with a church and a bakery, and Charnay-lès-Mâcon, with about seven thousand people, offers fuel and a supermarket. Mâcon itself lies a short way to the east on the Saône. The label calls this a swim stop, which is optimistic, but the countryside is lovely for a quiet pause.

The great landmark of the district is the Rock of Solutré, a limestone crag topping out at nearly five hundred metres above sea level that rises abruptly from the vineyards a few kilometres to the south-west, with its neighbour the Rock of Vergisson. At Solutré, archaeologists found a huge prehistoric site where hunters, tens of thousands of years ago, are thought to have driven wild horses over the cliff, and the bones of thousands of animals have been found at the base. The rock gives its name to a whole prehistoric culture, the Solutrean, and is among the best known sites of the Stone Age in Europe. A walk to the top takes about half an hour and offers a vast view.

North-west of here, about twenty-five kilometres off, lies Cluny, where in the Middle Ages the greatest monastery in Christendom stood. Its abbey was the head of a network of over a thousand monasteries across Europe, and its church was the largest in the world until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt. Only fragments remain, but they are impressive. The wines of the Mâconnais, especially Pouilly-Fuissé and Saint-Véran, are the white wines that pair so well with the local goat's cheeses, which come in small cylinders and are sold in every market.

The roads here are made for gentle touring, with rolling hills, vineyard lanes and farm tracks, and the surface is generally good. In September and October the harvest brings tractors and lorries, but also a lovely atmosphere. Spring and autumn are best.
Blérancourt is a village of about twelve hundred in the Aisne, in the green country between Soissons and Noyon, and it houses an unexpected museum: the Musée national de la Coopération franco-américaine, in the remains of a seventeenth-century château. It was founded by Anne Morgan, the daughter of the American banker J. P. Morgan, who came here after the First World War to help the villagers rebuild, and the museum tells the story of the friendship between France and the United States, from the American Revolution to the world wars. A fine garden and a pair of pavilions survive from the old château.

Folembray, a village of about fifteen hundred, lies on the edge of the forest of Saint-Gobain, a large area of oak and beech woodland, and not far from the medieval castle of Coucy, which once had the largest keep in Europe, a cylindrical tower fifty-five metres tall, before the retreating German army blew it up in 1917. The ruins of the walls and towers still make a dramatic sight above the village of Coucy-le-Château. The country is a mix of woodland, farmland and small valleys, in the shadow of the First World War, with cemeteries and memorials scattered across it.

The point is part of a ride that centres on Paris and the Île-de-France, and it is tagged for swimming, with lakes and ponds scattered around the forest, though you should look for signed and supervised places. Laon, the hilltop cathedral city, is about thirty kilometres to the east, and Soissons and Compiègne are within easy reach. For fuel and food, Chauny, Noyon and Soissons are the nearest places of any size, and the villages may have only a bakery.

Roads through the Saint-Gobain forest are among the best in the region for a quiet ride, with long, gentle curves under tall trees and little traffic. The surface is mostly good, although forestry vehicles can leave mud, and deer cross the road without warning, especially at dusk. In autumn the colours are rich, with the smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke, and in spring the woods ring with birdsong. Fog is common in winter, and the shaded roads can be icy. Please treat the memorials and cemeteries with respect.
t.near cluny@46.4,4.7:
For about two centuries, the largest church in Christendom stood in this small Burgundian town. The abbey of Cluny, founded in 910, grew into the head of a vast network of monasteries across Europe, and its third church, begun at the end of the eleventh century, was longer than any other until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt. Popes came from its ranks, kings sought its blessing. Then came the Revolution: the abbey was dissolved, sold, and used for decades as a stone quarry. What remains is a fragment, a single soaring arm of the transept with its octagonal bell tower, and the empty space around it is almost more eloquent than the building would have been.

Walk through the abbey precinct and you can feel the scale. Digital reconstructions in the visitor centre show the church as it was, and the town around it still follows the lines of the old monastery, with Romanesque houses, towers and gates scattered through the streets. The national stud farm, established by Napoleon, occupies part of the old abbey grounds, and you may see horses being exercised.

For lunch, Cluny has a good selection of cafés and restaurants around the abbey, serving Burgundian classics and Charolais beef, which comes from the pastures just to the west. A few kilometres north, the ecumenical community of Taizé attracts thousands of young pilgrims every year, a modern echo of Cluny's spiritual pull.

Getting here from Mâcon is half the fun. The road climbs over the hills of the Mâconnais, through vineyards and woods, with tight bends and fine views, before dropping into the valley of the Grosne. Another route passes near the Roche de Solutré and the vineyards of Pouilly-Fuissé. Traffic is light, the surfaces are mostly good, and the scenery changes constantly. The old railway line between Cluny and Mâcon is now a greenway for cyclists, so expect bikes at the crossings. Cluny is small, but it has the basics; for a wider choice of fuel and shops, the towns around Mâcon are the better bet.
t.near crepy en valois@49.3,2.9:
Crépy-en-Valois was once the capital of the Valois, the old county whose name passed to a whole dynasty of French kings. Today it is a busy market town of some fifteen thousand people on the plateau north-east of Paris, a natural place to refuel before heading on to Laon and the Aisne valley.

The remains of the old castle house a museum of archery and the Valois, a reminder that archery companies were once important social institutions in this part of France, and some still exist. The old town has narrow streets, a few half-timbered and stone houses and the ruined church of Saint-Thomas, its unfinished façade standing on its own like a stage set. It is not a place that demands a long stop, but it rewards a short walk.

The countryside around Crépy is good riding country if you know where to look. To the north lies the Forest of Compiègne, to the east the Forest of Retz around Villers-Cotterêts, and between them a gently rolling landscape of wheat and beet fields, small valleys and villages built of pale stone. Villers-Cotterêts is where Alexandre Dumas was born, and it is also where King Francis I signed the ordinance of 1539 that made French, rather than Latin, the language of official documents. Morienval, a few kilometres from Crépy, has an abbey church with some of the earliest Gothic rib vaults in France, tucked away in a quiet village.

Roads here are generally quiet D-roads, smooth and well signed, with long, open straights across the plateau and more interesting stretches where they drop into valleys and wind through woods. Wind can be a factor on the exposed parts, and the long straights invite speed, but speed cameras are common in this part of France. Crépy has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries in good supply, so fill up, grab something to eat and enjoy the run north towards the Aisne.
t.near gisors@49.2,1.7:
Gisors is a Norman town that stands guard on the border with the Île-de-France. It lies on the Epte, the old border river, and its great castle, a motte-and-bailey fortress with a tall octagonal keep, was built by the Normans in the late eleventh century and strengthened by the kings of England, before it fell to the French king Philip Augustus in the twelfth. It was one of the key strongholds on the frontier, and the walls and keep still dominate the town. A local legend says that the Knights Templar hid treasure in the castle, and it has kept treasure hunters busy for generations, though nothing has been found.

The church of Saint-Gervais-et-Saint-Protais, a large, richly decorated building that mixes Gothic and Renaissance styles, stands in the centre, and its richly carved facade is among the finest in the region. The town has about twelve thousand people, a market, a handful of restaurants and a pleasant, slightly sleepy feel. In the nearby village of Neaufles-Saint-Martin, the ruin of a huge round tower stands on a mound above the houses.

As a return gate, Gisors is practical: it has fuel, supermarkets and a railway station, and the road to Paris is clear. The route home follows the valley of the Epte and the plateau of the Vexin, a quiet, open landscape with a good surface and light traffic. The air smells of hay and warm stone in summer, and woodsmoke in autumn.

The riding in this region is relaxed and unhurried, with long views and not much to disturb you. The Lyons Forest, to the north, is among the finest beech forests in France, and the cliffs of the Seine, to the south, are a dramatic sight, which makes this a good place to turn for home with a sense of a day well spent.

A word of caution: fuel stations in the smaller villages can be few, so take advantage of Gisors before heading south. The temperature here can be several degrees colder than Paris in winter, and fog is common in the valleys.
t.near vienne@45.5,4.9:
Vienne has been a city for two thousand years and it still shows it. On the east bank of the Rhône, about thirty kilometres south of Lyon, the Romans built a prosperous colony here, and the temple of Augustus and Livia still stands in the centre, as complete as when it was built, with its Corinthian columns facing a small square of cafés. Nearby a Roman theatre climbs the hillside, and every July it fills with music for a jazz festival that has become one of the best known in Europe.

For a rider, Vienne is a very practical stop. With over 32,000 people, it has fuel stations on the approaches and a good range of cafés and shops, and it is on the main route between Lyon and the south, so it is a natural place to refill and eat. Be aware that the one-way system in the centre is confusing, and that traffic backs up on the bridges across the Rhône. Park near the river and walk in.

Across the water, on the right bank, the steep terraces of Côte-Rôtie climb from the village of Ampuis, and the wines made from Syrah on those slopes are among the most celebrated in France. A little further south, Condrieu produces its fragrant white Viognier. Behind them, the Pilat massif rises in a long wooded ridge, which is one of the better riding areas in the region, with roads that twist up through chestnut woods to open crests. Vienne is the gateway.

There is a modest Roman pyramid standing alone in a field near the old circus, a curious monument whose purpose is still debated, and the cathedral of Saint-Maurice, a long Gothic building at the foot of the hill, is worth a look if you have the time. Evenings are lively in the centre, with restaurants serving Lyon-style food, and the Rhône at dusk is a pleasant place to unwind.
t.near epernay@49.1,3.9:
Épernay is the sort of town that makes a bubble feel like an institution. It sits on the Marne river, in the heart of Champagne, and its main street, the Avenue de Champagne, is lined with the grand houses of famous producers: Moët and Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger, Mercier and others, in mansions of stone, brick and wrought iron, set behind gardens and gates. The avenue is sometimes called the most expensive street in the world, a joke based on the value of the bottles stored beneath it.

That is the real secret of Épernay: the cellars. Under the town, chalk galleries stretch for tens of kilometres, cool and damp, where millions of bottles lie on their sides, slowly developing the fine bubbles that give the wine its character. Several houses offer tours, which include a descent into the dark, a lecture on the méthode champenoise and, naturally, a glass at the end. It is best to book ahead in summer, and remember that tasting and riding do not mix.

The hills around, planted with chardonnay and pinot noir and pinot meunier, form the landscape that was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015 for its vineyards, houses and cellars. A few kilometres to the north, in the village of Hautvillers, the monk Dom Pérignon is traditionally credited with refining the techniques of champagne production in the late seventeenth century, though the myth that he invented the wine is just that. His grave lies in the abbey church.

The riding here is a pleasure. The scenic route through the vineyards winds along the slopes of the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Blancs, with good roads, gentle gradients, and long views over rows of vines. The best time is autumn, when the harvest is under way and the vineyards turn red and gold, but spring, with its fresh green growth, is just as good. During the harvest, expect tractors and workers on the roads.

Épernay is a town of twenty-seven thousand, with fuel stations, restaurants and parking, and the centre is compact enough to explore on foot. The suburb of Magenta is named after the battle of 1859, a small piece of Franco-Italian history in a very French town.
t.near cambremer@49.2,0.1:
Cambremer is where apple country begins to show its hand. The village lies in the Pays d'Auge, in the Calvados department of Normandy, a green, rolling land of orchards, hedgerows, half-timbered farmhouses and fat dairy cows, and the roads that wind between them are lined with apple trees. There are only about a thousand people, so it is a small place, with a church, a few shops and the sense of being in no hurry. The surrounding farms are the true attraction, because this is the heart of the Route du Cidre, a signposted trail past dozens of producers who sell cider, pommeau, perry and calvados directly from the farm.

The cider is not the sweet fizzy drink of the English pub. It is a dry, complex, slightly cloudy drink, made from a blend of bitter, sweet and acid apples, often with a gentle sparkle, and the best bottles come from small producers with old orchards. Calvados is the apple brandy distilled from it and aged in oak, and in the Pays d'Auge the spirit is double-distilled, giving it depth. Pommeau, a blend of apple juice and young calvados, is sweet and rich. Of course, a rider should taste with discipline, spit or sip, and buy a bottle to take home.

The region is also famous for cheese, with Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque all made within a short distance, and a lunch of cheese, bread, butter and cider is the correct thing here. The half-timbered buildings, called colombages, have walls of oak beams and white or ochre plaster, and many of them are centuries old. In late April and early May, the orchards bloom in white and pink, and in autumn the fruit is picked and the air smells of fermentation.

The riding is about leisure. The lanes are narrow and winding, with high hedges, farm gates and tractors, and it is easy to find yourself on a tiny road with grass down the middle. Take it slowly, because there are cows crossing and mud on the corners after rain. Fuel is not in the village, so top up in Lisieux, thirteen kilometres away, or Dozulé, and expect shops to close at lunch. The weather is mild and often damp, and a waterproof jacket is wise even in summer.
